rd-school-c9-english-a.ch2-sound-of-musi.title: The Sound of Music — Evelyn Glennie & Bismillah Khan
rd-school-c9-english-a.ch2-sound-of-musi.subtitle: A deaf girl who hears with her whole body, and a boy whose shehnai woke a free nation

sections.md:
Put your palm flat on a table while someone taps the other end. You *feel* the tap before you think about it. Now imagine building an entire world-class career on that feeling.

This chapter has two parts, two musicians, two continents:

- **Part I — "Evelyn Glennie Listens to Sound without Hearing It"** (by Deborah Cowley): a Scottish girl who lost most of her hearing by age eleven and became one of the world's greatest solo **percussionists**.
- **Part II — "The Shehnai of Bismillah Khan"**: the story of how a humble instrument rose to the concert stage, and of **Ustad Bismillah Khan**, whose shehnai greeted India's independence from the Red Fort.

What links them? **Devotion, practice, and refusing to accept limits** — whether the limit is deafness or the belief that an instrument is 'too ordinary' for classical music.

> This read covers both parts in full order: background, scene-by-scene retellings, key facts, themes, a science link, a comparison, the chapter's language work, speaking and writing tasks, and model answers.

Both texts are modern, copyrighted prose. Read the originals in *Beehive* (free on ncert.nic.in); this companion explains them in its own words.

sections.md:
**Opening scene.** The text opens with Evelyn, now a celebrated musician, arriving for a lesson or performance — an ordinary-looking young woman. You would not guess that she is profoundly deaf; she has learned to lip-read and speaks fluently.

**Childhood.** Evelyn Glennie grew up on a farm in **Aberdeenshire, Scotland**. When she was about **eight**, her mother noticed something wrong when Evelyn was waiting to play the piano: she didn't respond when her name was called. Her hearing was deteriorating, slowly and steadily — and she hid it well; teachers thought she was just being inattentive.

**Diagnosis.** By **eleven**, her marks had dropped. Her headmistress urged her parents to take her to a specialist. The diagnosis: she was **profoundly deaf** as the result of gradual nerve damage. She was advised to wear hearing aids and be sent to a school for the deaf. 'Suddenly everything looked black,' is the feeling the text conveys.

**Refusal to give up.** Evelyn was determined to lead a normal life and pursue her interest in music. At school she noticed a girl playing a xylophone and decided she wanted to play too. Most teachers discouraged her — but percussionist **Ron Forbes** spotted her potential. He began by tuning two large drums to different notes. 'Don't listen through your ears,' was his advice in effect; 'try to sense it some other way.' Evelyn suddenly realised she could feel the higher drum from the waist up and the lower one from the waist down. She learned to open her mind and body to sounds and vibrations.

**Rise.** She never looked back. She toured the United Kingdom with a youth orchestra and, at **sixteen**, decided to make music her life. She auditioned for the **Royal Academy of Music** in London and scored one of the highest marks in the academy's history. She moved gradually from orchestral work to **solo performance**, and by the end of her three-year course she had captured most of the top awards.

**How she does it.** She plays **barefoot** on stage, feeling the vibrations through the floor. She senses sound through her skin, hair and cheekbones — the text says she can feel the different parts of her body responding. When she plays the xylophone, she can sense the sound passing up the stick into her fingertips. Leaning against a piano, she feels its sound; she has described her body as a kind of resonating chamber.

**Hard work and giving.** Evelyn works tirelessly. Besides regular concerts she gives **free concerts in prisons and hospitals**, and she gives high priority to classes for young musicians. The text says that she is a shining inspiration for deaf children; as a teacher of the deaf is quoted as saying in effect, she shows them that there is nothing they cannot do. She has packed more into her life than most people do in a lifetime.

sections.h: Part I: what the story teaches
sections.md:
**Determination over disability.** Evelyn was advised to go to a school for the deaf; she chose an ordinary school and a music career. The chapter frames deafness not as a full stop but as a challenge she redefined.

**A new way of 'listening'.** Sound is vibration — physics agrees. A drumhead vibrates, pushes air and also the floor. Our ears detect air vibrations; our skin and bones can detect strong, low vibrations too. Evelyn trained herself to read these signals with remarkable precision.

**Hard work.** Her success came from practice, not miracles — the text stresses how much she works and travels.

**Giving back.** Free concerts in hospitals and prisons; mentoring young musicians.

**Science link (Class 9 Science, 'Sound'):** Sound is a mechanical wave that needs a medium; it travels faster in solids than in air (roughly 343 m/s in air at 20 °C, but several thousand m/s in many solids). That is one reason the floor carries rhythm so clearly to Evelyn's bare feet. Low-pitched sounds (low frequency) are felt more easily in the body — which is why she felt the lower drum lower down.

**Did you know?** Evelyn Glennie was later made a Dame (DBE) in the UK for services to music, and has commissioned many new percussion concertos — percussion as a *solo* instrument was rare before her. She plays well over a thousand instruments from around the world, including Indian ones.

sections.h: Part II: from pungi to shehnai
sections.md:
Part II opens with a legend. The Mughal emperor **Aurangzeb** banned the playing of the **pungi** in the royal residence because its sound was shrill and unpleasant. The pungi became a generic name for reeded noisemakers.

A **barber** from a family of professional musicians, who had access to the royal palace, decided to improve it. He chose a pipe with a **natural hollow stem**, longer and broader than the pungi, and made **seven holes** on its body. When he played it, closing and opening some holes, a soft, melodious sound came out. He played before royalty and everyone was impressed.

The new instrument was named **shehnai**. The chapter explains the name traditionally: it was played in the **Shah's** chambers and was invented by a **nai** (barber) — 'shah' + 'nai'.

For centuries, the shehnai was part of the **naubat** (traditional ensemble of nine instruments) found at royal courts, and it became associated with **temples and weddings** — the sound of auspicious beginnings. Until recently it was used only on such occasions, not on the classical concert stage.

One man changed that: **Ustad Bismillah Khan**, who brought the shehnai onto the classical stage.

**A note on the legend:** The 'shah + nai' origin is a popular story told in the chapter; music historians trace reed instruments of this family across Persia and India over a long period. Treat the legend as tradition, not proven history.

check.why: The chapter says Aurangzeb banned the pungi in the royal residence because it had a shrill, unpleasant sound.

sections.h: Part II: Bismillah Khan's life, retold
sections.md:
**Birth and family.** Bismillah Khan was born on **21 March 1916** in **Dumraon, Bihar**, into a well-known family of musicians. His grandfather Rasool Bux Khan was a shehnai player for the king of Bhojpur, and his father, Paigambar Bux, and other paternal ancestors were also great shehnai players.

**The laddu.** As a small child he went to the nearby **Bihariji temple** to sing the Bhojpuri *chaita*, and at the end of it he would receive a big **laddu** weighing about 1.25 kg — a prize given by the local Maharaja. The young boy sang for the sweet as much as for the song.

**Benaras and the Ganga.** At the age of **five** or six, he moved to **Benaras (Varanasi)** to live with his maternal uncle **Ali Bux**, who played the shehnai at the **Vishnu temple** (often called the Balaji temple). Young Bismillah practised for hours on the banks of the **Ganga**, in the temples of Balaji and Mangala Maiya. The flowing waters of the river inspired him to improvise and invent ragas that were earlier considered beyond the range of the shehnai.

**Breakthrough moments:**
- At **14**, he accompanied his uncle to the **Allahabad Music Conference**, and his performance was widely admired. At the end of his recital, the great singer Ustad Faiyaz Khan patted him on the back and encouraged him to keep working hard.
- With the opening of **All India Radio, Lucknow**, in **1938**, his big break came; he soon became an often-heard shehnai player on radio.
- On **15 August 1947**, as India became free, he became the first Indian to greet the nation with his shehnai, playing **Raag Kafi** from the **Red Fort** to an audience that included **Mahatma Gandhi** and **Jawaharlal Nehru**, who would later give his famous 'Tryst with Destiny' speech.

**International fame:** He was the first Indian to be invited to perform at the prestigious **Lincoln Center Hall** in the USA. He also took part in the **World Exposition in Montreal**, the **Cannes Art Festival** and the **Osaka Trade Fair**. An auditorium in **Tehran** was named after him — *Tahar Mosiquee Ustad Bismillah Khan*.

**Films:** He played for Vijay Bhatt's Hindi film **'Gunj Uthi Shehnai'** (1959), whose song 'Dil ka khilona hai toot gaya…' became a nationwide hit. He also played for the Kannada film **'Sanadi Appanna'**, directed by Vikram Srinivas. But he disliked the artificiality and glamour of the film world and didn't continue.

**Love for Benaras:** One of his students wished him to head a shehnai school in the USA and promised to recreate the atmosphere of Benaras by building replicas of its temples. Bismillah Khan asked, in effect, whether they could also transport the river Ganga. Whenever he was abroad, he said, he longed to see Hindustan; when in Mumbai he thought only of Benaras and the holy Ganga, and in Benaras he missed Dumraon.

**Honours:** Padma Shri, Padma Bhushan, Padma Vibhushan, and in **2001** the **Bharat Ratna**, India's highest civilian award. With the award, he urged young people to teach their children music, which he saw as India's richest tradition. He died on **21 August 2006**.

sections.h: The shehnai: how it makes music
sections.md:
The shehnai is a **double-reed** wind instrument. Air blown between two thin reeds makes them vibrate rapidly; the vibrations set the air column inside the wooden tube vibrating. Opening and closing the finger holes changes the **effective length** of the air column — a shorter column vibrates faster, giving a **higher pitch**. The flared metal bell at the end helps project the sound.

That is exactly what the barber in the legend did: a longer, broader tube than the pungi and seven holes to control pitch, producing a softer, richer tone.

**Indian instrument families (a quick map):**
| Family | How sound is made | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Sushira (wind) | vibrating air column | shehnai, bansuri, nadaswaram |
| Tata (string) | vibrating string | sitar, veena, sarod |
| Avanaddha (membrane) | stretched skin struck | tabla, mridangam, dholak |
| Ghana (solid) | solid body struck | ghatam, manjira, jaltarang |

Evelyn's percussion belongs to the last two families; Bismillah Khan's shehnai to the first.

sections.md:
Both parts are biographical sketches, but they show success from different starting points. Evelyn had to overcome a **personal physical challenge**; Bismillah Khan had to raise the **status of an instrument** and stay true to his roots while the world called.

**Common values:** relentless practice (Evelyn's long hours; Bismillah's riverside riyaz), love of music above fame, generosity to others (free concerts; urging parents to teach children music), humility.

**A thought:** Evelyn changed how the world thinks about *who* can be a musician; Bismillah Khan changed how India thinks about *which instruments* belong on the classical stage.

**Bismillah Khan and harmony.** A devout Muslim, he played every morning at Hindu temples in Benaras and saw music as a bridge between communities. The chapter presents him as a symbol of India's composite culture.

**1. Nouns from adjectives and verbs (suffixes).** The chapter is full of abstract nouns. Notice how suffixes build them:

| Base word | Noun | Suffix |
|---|---|---|
| determine | determination | -ation |
| perform | performance | -ance |
| deaf | deafness | -ness |
| achieve | achievement | -ment |
| able | ability | -ity |
| inspire | inspiration | -ation |
| impair | impairment | -ment |

Practice: form nouns from *improve, popular, hard, judge, serious*.

**2. Words with more than one meaning.** Use a dictionary to see how context decides meaning:
- *Hard* — 'hard work' (difficult) vs 'hard wood' (firm).
- *Note* — a musical note vs a written note.
- *Break* — his 'big break' (opportunity) vs to break a cup.
- *Stage* — a platform for performers vs a phase ('at this stage').

**3. Phrasal verbs.** The text uses everyday verb + particle combinations: *look back* (Evelyn never looked back = never regretted, kept progressing), *pack in* (packed more into her life), *give up*, *take part in*, *turn down*. Try sentences with each.

**4. Tenses in biography.** Biographies move between the **simple past** for events ('He played at the Red Fort') and the **present perfect** for achievements that continue to matter ('She has become a legend'). Notice also the **past perfect** for earlier events ('By eleven her hearing had deteriorated').

**5. Vocabulary**

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| deteriorating | getting worse |
| profoundly | deeply, extremely |
| impaired | damaged, weakened |
| resonant / resonate | vibrating with sound |
| ensemble | group of musicians |
| auspicious | lucky, favourable |
| maestro | a great master of music |
| improvise | create on the spot |
| riyaz | disciplined musical practice |
| replica | an exact copy |

check.why: 'Never looked back' is an idiom meaning she kept succeeding and moving forward.

sections.md:
**Speaking — 'A musician I admire'.** Speak for one minute about any musician — a classical maestro, a film singer, a folk artist from your state, or someone in your family who sings at festivals. Cover: who, what instrument or style, one story from their life, and why you admire them.

**Group discussion.** *Should children learn music in school as a compulsory subject?* Use evidence from the chapter: Bismillah Khan's appeal to teach children music; Evelyn's free classes.

**Writing — a paragraph on overcoming difficulty.** Write 100–120 words about a person (famous or from your life) who overcame a difficulty, like Evelyn. Plan: difficulty → turning point → effort → achievement → lesson.

**Writing — newspaper report.** Imagine you are a reporter at the Red Fort on 15 August 1947. Write a 120-word report on the shehnai performance. Include a headline, date-line ('New Delhi, 15 August'), who, what, where and the mood of the crowd.

**Project.** Make a poster of the four Indian instrument families with one picture and one famous player for each.

**Q1. How was Evelyn's deafness discovered?** *(30–40 words)*
**Model:** When Evelyn was about eight, her mother noticed she did not respond when called while waiting to play the piano. Her hearing worsened; at eleven a specialist found she was profoundly deaf due to nerve damage.

**Q2. How does Evelyn hear music?** *(40 words)*
**Model:** Evelyn feels music as vibrations through different parts of her body — her skin, hair and cheekbones. She plays barefoot to sense vibrations through the floor, and can feel higher notes in her upper body and lower notes below the waist.

**Q3. Why was the shehnai traditionally played at temples and weddings?** *(30 words)*
**Model:** Its sound was considered auspicious, so it was part of the naubat at royal courts and was played at temples and weddings to mark sacred, joyful beginnings.

**Q4. How did Bismillah Khan's love for Benaras show?** *(40 words)*
**Model:** He spent his childhood practising by the Ganga and playing at the Vishnu/Balaji temple. Even after world fame, he refused to settle abroad, saying in effect he could not live without the Ganga and Benaras, which inspired his music.

**Q5. Evelyn's achievements.** Admission to the Royal Academy of Music with very high marks; top awards there; career as a leading solo percussionist; extensive touring; free concerts in prisons and hospitals; inspiration to deaf children.

**Q6. 'Both Evelyn and Bismillah Khan reached the top through devotion.' Discuss.** *(120 words)* — Introduction; Evelyn: deafness, Ron Forbes, practice, Royal Academy; Bismillah: riyaz by the Ganga, AIR, Red Fort, refusal to leave Benaras; common qualities; conclusion.

**Tip:** For 'character sketch' questions, give 3–4 traits each backed by one event from the text.

rd-school-c9-english-a.ch3-little-girl.title: The Little Girl — Katherine Mansfield
rd-school-c9-english-a.ch3-little-girl.subtitle: A frightened child, a stern father, and one stormy night that changes everything

sections.md:
Have you ever heard a parent's footsteps on the stairs and felt your stomach tighten? For **Kezia**, the small girl in this story, that sound means her father is home — and that the house must fall silent.

**"The Little Girl"** is a short story by **Katherine Mansfield**, first published in 1912. It traces how a child's **fear** of her father slowly turns into **understanding** and **love**. Nothing dramatic happens — no adventure, no villain — and yet by the end, a whole relationship has shifted.

Mansfield's genius is in **small moments**: the way a girl stutters when nervous, the way a pin-cushion becomes a disaster, the way a nightmare opens a door between two people.

> In this read: the author, a scene-by-scene retelling with the meaning of every part, characters, the turning point, themes, style notes, the chapter's language work, speaking and writing tasks, and exam answers.

Mansfield died in 1923, so the story is in the public domain — but this companion does not reproduce it, because exact wording matters and your *Beehive* textbook (free on ncert.nic.in) has the authorised version. Read it alongside this guide.

check.q: What is Kezia's main feeling towards her father at the beginning?
check.why: At the start Kezia is afraid of her father — his loud voice, stern looks and rules make her nervous.

sections.md:
**Katherine Mansfield (1888–1923)** was born in **Wellington, New Zealand**, and moved to London as a young woman. She is one of the great masters of the **modern short story**. Her stories focus on inner feelings, small domestic moments and the hidden tensions of family life.

She often wrote about childhood in New Zealand, and a girl named Kezia appears in several of her stories (*Prelude*, *At the Bay*), loosely modelled on Mansfield's own childhood. Her father, Harold Beauchamp, was a successful businessman — perhaps one source for the busy, authoritative father in this story.

She died young, of tuberculosis, at just **34**. Famous collections include *In a German Pension* (1911), *Bliss* (1920) and *The Garden Party* (1922).

**Did you know?** Mansfield was admired (and a little envied) by Virginia Woolf, who wrote that Mansfield's was the only writing she had ever been jealous of.

check.q: Katherine Mansfield was born in —
check.why: Mansfield was born in Wellington, New Zealand, and many of her stories draw on her childhood there.

sections.md:
**Scene 1 — Mornings.** To Kezia, her **father** is a person to be feared and avoided. Every morning before he leaves for work, he comes into her room and gives her a casual kiss, and she answers 'Goodbye, Father'. When she hears the noise of his carriage going away down the road, she feels a wave of relief.
*Meaning:* the kiss is a ritual without warmth. Kezia's relief tells us the house is more relaxed without him.

**Scene 2 — Evenings.** In the evening, when he returns, the whole household changes. Standing near the staircase, Kezia hears his loud voice in the hall. He wants his tea brought to the drawing-room, his slippers, his newspaper. Her **mother**, delicate and often resting, calls Kezia to come and take off his boots. To Kezia he seems like a **giant**: big hands, big neck, and especially a big mouth when he yawns. Thinking about him is like thinking about a giant.
*Meaning:* through a child's eyes, ordinary size becomes monstrous. Mansfield shows fear exaggerating things.

**Scene 3 — The stutter and Sunday afternoons.** When her father looks at her over his newspaper and asks her a question, she cannot answer properly. When nervous, **Kezia stutters**. Her father is annoyed: if she can't say what she means, he tells her in effect, she shouldn't speak at all. His impatience makes the stutter worse. On Sunday afternoons Grandmother sends her down to the drawing-room to have a 'nice talk' with her parents — but she usually finds Mother reading and Father stretched out asleep on the sofa, a handkerchief over his face, his feet on one of the best cushions, snoring. Kezia sits on a stool and watches him gravely until he wakes, and the 'talk' never really happens.
*Meaning:* a cycle — his impatience → her nervousness → more stuttering → more impatience. Even the time set aside for closeness ends in distance.

**Grandmother.** Kezia's **grandmother**, who lives with them, is kind and gentle — the one adult Kezia can run to. She tries to ease the relationship.

check.q: Why did Kezia stutter in front of her father?
options: She was nervous and afraid of him
She was trying to be funny
check.why: Fear made her nervous, and her father's impatience made the stutter worse.

sections.md:
One day Grandmother suggests that Kezia make a **pin-cushion** as a present for Father's birthday, from a piece of beautiful **yellow silk**. Kezia sews three sides carefully. But what should she fill it with? Grandmother is out in the garden. Kezia wanders into her parents' bedroom to look for scraps, and on the bed-table she finds a great many sheets of fine paper. She gathers them up, tears them into tiny pieces and stuffs her cushion, then sews up the fourth side.

Those papers were Father's **'great speech'** for the Port Authority. That night the house is searched for it. When Father learns what happened, he is furious. He calls Kezia to his room. Terrified, she explains — stammering — that she wanted to make him a present. He decides she must be taught a lesson: he **beats her hands with a ruler**. Kezia does not understand why she is being punished for making a gift. She cries and runs to Grandmother, who holds her.

Through her sobs Kezia asks a question that shows her confusion about the world: *What did Jesus make fathers for?* (This is the one short line we quote; it is funny and heartbreaking at once.)

*Meaning:* the pin-cushion is a symbol of **miscommunication**. Kezia acts out of love; Father sees only destruction. Neither understands the other's intention. Kezia's innocent question shows how a child tries to fit harshness into her picture of a good world.

sections.md:
Kezia often watches the **Macdonalds**, the family next door, who have **five children**. Through the hedge she sees Mr Macdonald playing with them in the garden in the evening — running about and playing tag with them, the children shrieking with laughter, the little ones climbing on him and pulling at his beard, and the father laughing as loudly as they do.

Kezia is astonished. She concludes that there must be **different kinds of fathers** in the world.

*Meaning:* the Macdonalds give Kezia — and us — a measure. Her own father is not 'what fathers are'; he is one kind of father. This sows a seed: if fathers can be different, perhaps hers could be different too. It also sharpens her sense of loss.

options: He was very strict and too busy and tired to play
check.why: Kezia's father worked very hard and was strict, so he never played with her as Mr Macdonald played with his children.

sections.h: Scenes 6–7: the stormy night and the turning point
sections.md:
**The night alone.** One day Kezia's **mother falls ill** and has to go to hospital, and **Grandmother goes with her**. Kezia is left at home with **Alice**, the cook. When Alice puts her to bed, Kezia is afraid of the dark.

She has a recurring **nightmare**: a **butcher** with a knife and a rope coming closer and closer to her, smiling a dreadful smile, while she cannot move. Usually when she has this dream, Grandmother comes to comfort her. That night the nightmare comes again. She wakes screaming.

**The turning point.** It is not Grandmother who comes — it is **Father**. He picks her up, holds her and asks what the matter is. Seeing how frightened she is, he carries her to his own bed and lies down beside her. He covers her up and, half-asleep himself, holds her close. Kezia lies with her head against his chest, feeling the warmth of his body and hearing his **heart beat**. He tells her to rub her feet against his legs to warm them. Exhausted, he soon falls asleep.

**The realisation.** Kezia, wide awake, notices how tired he is, how hard he works — so tired that he cannot play like Mr Macdonald. She remembers, with regret, that she tore up his beautiful speech. And she feels that her father has a **big heart**. Her thought ends with the famous phrase *'not so big, after all'*.

*Meaning:* the ending is beautifully double. 'Not so big' means he is **not as frightening** as he seemed — the 'giant' of Scene 2 has shrunk to human size. It also means he is **human**: tired, overworked, even a little vulnerable, with nobody to look after *him*. The heartbeat is the key image: she literally hears the human inside the giant.

check.q: Who comforted Kezia after her nightmare?
check.why: With Mother and Grandmother at the hospital, it was her father who came, took her to his bed and comforted her.

sections.md:
**Kezia** — a sensitive, imaginative, timid child. Her fear makes her **stutter** in front of her father. She is honest (she admits the pin-cushion), curious about other families, and capable of deep feeling. Her growth is the story's arc: from fear → confusion → envy of the Macdonalds → understanding → affection.

**Father** — strict, busy, impatient, used to being obeyed. He punishes Kezia harshly for the speech. But he is not cruel at heart: he works very hard for the family, and when it matters, he gently comforts her. His sternness hides tiredness and love.

**Mother** — delicate and often unwell; she sends Kezia to take off Father's boots. She is somewhat distant in the story.

**Grandmother** — warm, loving, Kezia's refuge. She suggests the pin-cushion and comforts Kezia afterwards.

**Mr Macdonald** — the playful father next door, a contrast showing Kezia that fathers can be different.

**Alice** — the cook, who looks after Kezia when the others are away; practical, but she cannot replace Grandmother's comfort.

sections.md:
**1. Parent–child relationships and communication.** Kezia and her father do not know how to reach each other. His strictness makes her stutter; her silence makes him impatient. One night of closeness does what years of formal greetings could not.

**2. Fear vs. understanding.** Fear grows in distance. When Kezia lies close enough to hear his heartbeat, she sees the real man. The story suggests we often fear what we do not understand.

**3. Appearances can mislead.** Father *seems* hard; really he is tired and quietly caring. The Macdonalds *seem* perfect; we don't know their struggles.

**4. The burden of adult work.** Kezia's realisation that he works hard is a moment of childhood growing up — seeing an adult's world from the inside.

**5. Discipline and its limits.** The ruler punishment is harsh. Today we would say a calm talk works better than hitting; the story was written in 1912, when such punishment was common. It is worth discussing how families and schools now prefer kinder discipline.

**Did you know?** Child-rights law in India today, including the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act (2009), prohibits physical punishment and mental harassment in schools.

check.q: What does the line 'not so big, after all' finally suggest?
options: Father is human and not as frightening as he seemed
check.why: Kezia now sees her father as a tired, caring human being rather than a frightening giant.

sections.md:
- **Point of view:** third person, but we stay close to **Kezia's thoughts**. We see Father as she sees him — a 'giant' with huge hands — so our picture changes when hers does.
- **Small concrete details:** the yellow silk, the ruler, the slippers, the stutter. Mansfield makes small objects carry big feelings.
- **Contrast:** two fathers (hers vs Macdonald); two nights (the beating vs the comfort).
- **Childlike questions:** *What did Jesus make fathers for?* — humorous and sad at once.
- **Symbol:** the heartbeat stands for the hidden tenderness in Father; the pin-cushion for love misunderstood.
- **Quiet climax:** the turning point is not loud; it is a child listening to a heartbeat.
- **Circular structure:** we begin with fear of the father's arrival and end in his arms.

**Writing exercise:** Describe someone you were once afraid of (a teacher, a coach, a relative) from a *child's* point of view, then show one moment that changed your view.

check.q: Through whose eyes do we mostly see the events?
check.why: The narration stays close to Kezia's thoughts, so we see her father as she sees him.

sections.md:
**1. Words for feelings.** Mansfield never says 'Kezia was traumatised'; she shows it. Build a feelings word-bank from the story: *afraid, relieved, nervous, timid, frightened, puzzled, sorrowful, comforted, tender*. Arrange them from most negative to most positive and use five in sentences about Kezia.

**2. 'Too … to' and 'so … that'.** The key realisation can be put in two structures:
- Father was **too tired to** play with her.
- Father was **so tired that** he could not play with her.
Practice: rewrite 'Kezia was very frightened; she could not speak' both ways.

**3. Reported questions.** Turn direct questions into reported speech:
- Direct: Father asked, "What have you been doing today?"
- Reported: Father asked Kezia what she had been doing that day.
- Direct: Kezia asked, "Why did Father punish me?"
- Reported: Kezia asked why Father had punished her.
Note: no question mark, no 'do/did', statement word order, tense moves back.

**4. Phrasal verbs from the story.** *take off* (his boots), *tear up* (the papers), *look after* (the house), *put to bed*, *fall asleep*, *calm down*. Make a sentence with each.

**5. Vocabulary**
| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| stutter / stammer | speak with pauses and repetitions |
| timid | shy and easily frightened |
| relief | release from worry |
| delicate | weak in health |
| grave(ly) | serious(ly) |
| hedge | row of bushes forming a fence |
| nightmare | a frightening dream |
| tremble | shake with fear |

check.q: Which is the correct reported form of: Father asked, "What have you been doing today?"
options: Father asked what had she been doing that day?
Father asked Kezia what she had been doing that day.
Father asked what you have been doing today.
Father asked did she do anything today.
check.why: Reported questions use statement word order, no question mark, a back-shifted tense and changed time words.

sections.md:
**Speaking — pair role-play.** One student is Kezia, the other is her father, the morning after the nightmare. Kezia tries to apologise for the speech without stuttering; Father tries to explain why he was angry and why he works so hard. Aim for a calm, kind conversation — the talk they never had in the story.

**Group discussion.** *Parents today are friendlier than parents of the past.* Use examples from the story and from your own experience; respect every speaker's family.

**Writing — a letter.** You are Kezia, now grown up. Write a letter to your father on his birthday remembering the pin-cushion and the stormy night, and telling him what you understand now. (120 words)

**Writing — paragraph.** 'Love is sometimes hidden behind strictness.' Write 100–120 words with one example from the story and one from your life or observation.

**Writing — a different ending.** Imagine Grandmother had not gone to hospital that night. How might Kezia's relationship with her father have developed? (100 words)

**Q1. Why was Kezia afraid of her father?** *(40 words)* Her father was strict and impatient. He scolded her for stuttering, demanded quiet when he came home, and looked at her sternly over his newspaper. He seemed huge to her, and his punishment over the pin-cushion made her even more frightened.

**Q2. Who was Kezia's comforter? Why?** *(30 words)* Her grandmother. She was gentle and loving, suggested the pin-cushion, held Kezia after the punishment and usually came when Kezia had nightmares.

**Q3. What lesson did Kezia's father want to teach her? Was he fair?** *(40 words)* He wanted to teach her not to touch things that weren't hers. It was unfair, because Kezia's intention was loving and she did not know the papers mattered; a calm explanation would have taught better than a ruler.

**Q4. How did Kezia's attitude towards her father change?** *(120 words)*
Plan: (1) Early fear — morning kiss, evening rituals, stutter. (2) Pin-cushion incident and punishment; her bitter question to Grandmother. (3) The Macdonalds show her another kind of father. (4) The night of the nightmare — Father comforts her, she hears his heartbeat. (5) Realisation — he works hard, is tired, has a big heart. Conclude: fear gives way to sympathy and love.

**Q5. Was Kezia's father a bad father?** — A balanced answer: he was strict and harsh, which hurt her; but he worked hard for the family and showed real tenderness when she needed him. Teachers reward answers that weigh both sides.

**Q6. Explain the title.** The title stresses Kezia's smallness and vulnerability; the whole story is seen from the height of a little girl, which is why her father looks like a giant until, at the end, he becomes 'not so big'.

summary: 'The Little Girl' is a 1912 short story by Katherine Mansfield (1888–1923), New Zealand-born.
Kezia fears her strict, busy father; his morning kiss and evening demands (tea, slippers, newspaper, boots) feel cold.
She stutters when he speaks to her; his impatience makes it worse; Sunday 'nice talks' end with him asleep.

Mr Macdonald next door plays joyfully with his five children; Kezia sees fathers can differ.
When Mother falls ill, Grandmother goes with her to hospital; Kezia is left with Alice the cook.
Kezia's nightmare of a butcher with a knife and rope returns; Father comforts her and takes her to his bed.
She hears his heartbeat, sees how tired he is and realises he has a big heart.
'Not so big, after all' — fear turns into understanding and love.

rd-school-c9-english-a.ch4-truly-beautif.title: A Truly Beautiful Mind — Albert Einstein
rd-school-c9-english-a.ch4-truly-beautif.subtitle: The 'boring' boy who hated rote learning and rewrote our idea of space and time

sections.md:
A baby is born in Germany with a head so large and angular that his mother is alarmed and thinks him deformed. By the age of two and a half he still hasn't spoken a word. When he finally talks, he repeats sentences slowly under his breath before saying them aloud. His playmates call him **'Brother Boring'**.

That boy became **Albert Einstein** — perhaps the most famous scientist of the 20th century, whose name is now a word for 'genius'.

**"A Truly Beautiful Mind"** is a short biographical chapter in *Beehive*. It traces his journey: a late-talking child, a rebellious student, a patent clerk who changed physics in his spare time, a Nobel laureate, a refugee, and finally a **peace activist** troubled by the bomb his ideas helped make possible.

The title points to two kinds of beauty: the beauty of his **scientific imagination**, and the beauty of his **conscience**.

> In this read: a retelling of the whole chapter in sequence, the science made simple with worked numbers, his letter to Roosevelt, character and themes, the chapter's language work, speaking and writing tasks, and exam answers.

The chapter is modern copyrighted prose; read it in *Beehive* (free on ncert.nic.in). This companion explains it in its own words.

check.q: What nickname did Einstein's playmates give him?
check.why: Because he was slow to speak and didn't join their games, his playmates called him 'Brother Boring'.

sections.md:
Albert Einstein was born on **14 March 1879** in **Ulm**, Germany. His family soon moved to **Munich**. His late talking worried his parents. He preferred to play by himself and was not keen on games with other children. At around **six**, his mother arranged for him to learn the **violin** — and music became a lifelong companion. He became a good violinist and continued playing all his life.

At school he was not the dull boy of legend; he did well, especially in **mathematics**. But he **hated the regimentation** of the Munich gymnasium (high school): drill-like teaching, rote memorisation, teachers who behaved like drill sergeants. He clashed with teachers because he liked to think for himself.

When his family moved to **Milan, Italy**, for business, fifteen-year-old Albert was left behind in Munich to finish school. Unhappy and lonely, he soon **left the gymnasium** without a diploma and joined his family. (The chapter notes that he left partly because of the school's atmosphere; one account also says a teacher felt his presence undermined respect in class.)

He then went to **Switzerland**, finished secondary school in **Aarau**, where the teaching was more liberal, and entered the university in **Zurich** — the Swiss Federal Polytechnic (today ETH Zurich).

**Lesson for us:** Einstein shows that disliking rote learning doesn't mean disliking learning. He was a ferocious learner — just not of the copy-and-repeat kind.

check.q: Why did Einstein dislike his school in Munich?
options: It was too far from home
He hated its rigid, regimented, rote-learning style
He had no friends at all
check.why: He disliked the school's strict regimentation and rote methods, which crushed creative and independent thinking.

sections.h: University, Mileva and the patent office (1896–1905)
sections.md:
In Zurich, Einstein studied physics and mathematics — though he often skipped lectures and studied on his own from books. Among his classmates was **Mileva Marić**, a Serbian student, one of very few women studying physics then. They shared a love of science and became close; he admired her as a clever fellow thinker.

After graduating in **1900**, Einstein could not get a university post. For a while he worked as a tutor and substitute teacher. In **1902** he joined the **patent office in Bern** as a technical expert, examining other people's inventions. His family opposed his relationship with Mileva, but they married in **1903**; they had two sons.

The patent office job turned out to be a gift: it was steady, it left him time to think, and assessing inventions sharpened his ability to see the essence of an idea. In his spare time — and sometimes secretly at his desk — he worked on physics.

**1905 — the 'miracle year'.** Einstein published several groundbreaking papers, including one on what became known as the **Special Theory of Relativity**. In it, time and space are not absolute; they depend on the observer's motion. From it followed the most famous equation in the world: **E = mc²**. He also earned his doctorate in 1905.

sections.md:
You don't need to master relativity for this chapter, but understanding the basics makes Einstein's story richer.

**Special Relativity (1905):**
- The **speed of light** in vacuum is the same for every observer — about **3 × 10⁸ m/s** (300,000 km per second).
- As a result, **time runs slower** for something moving very fast relative to you, and lengths contract along the direction of motion. These effects are tiny at everyday speeds, huge near light speed.
- **E = mc²** — mass and energy are interchangeable; a small mass is equivalent to an enormous energy (see the worked examples below). That is why nuclear reactions release so much energy from so little mass.

**General Relativity (1915):** Einstein extended his ideas to **gravity**: massive objects **curve space-time**, and that curvature tells objects how to move. One prediction: light bends around the Sun. In **1919**, British astronomers measured starlight bending during a solar eclipse — the result matched Einstein's prediction, and he became a world celebrity overnight. Newspapers announced a revolution in science.

**Photoelectric effect (1905):** light falling on a metal can knock out electrons, but only if each 'packet' of light (photon) has enough energy. This showed light behaves like particles too, and helped found quantum physics — it is what won him the Nobel Prize.

**Everyday link:** GPS satellites must correct for relativity — their clocks tick at a slightly different rate from ours — or your phone's map would drift by kilometres within a day. Solar panels and automatic doors with light sensors rely on the photoelectric effect.

sections.h: Fame, the Nobel Prize and exile (1905–1933)
sections.md:
After 1905, recognition came step by step. Einstein got university posts — Zurich, Prague, and then **Berlin** (1914), one of the great scientific centres of Europe, where he was elected to the Prussian Academy of Sciences.

His marriage to Mileva broke down; they **divorced in 1919**, and the same year he married his cousin **Elsa**.

In **1915** he published the **General Theory of Relativity**. After the 1919 eclipse confirmation, newspapers worldwide hailed him; he was suddenly the most famous scientist alive, mobbed by crowds wherever he lectured.

In **1921** he was awarded the **Nobel Prize in Physics** (presented in 1922) — notably not for relativity, but **for his explanation of the photoelectric effect**.

**1933 — exile.** When **Adolf Hitler** came to power, Einstein, who was **Jewish** and a well-known critic of the Nazis, was visiting the USA. He did not return to Germany. He settled in **Princeton, USA**, at the Institute for Advanced Study, and in 1940 became an American citizen.

Throughout these years he was also a public figure, speaking for democracy and against nationalism and militarism. He supported the League of Nations and pacifist causes after the horrors of the First World War.

check.q: Einstein's Nobel Prize was awarded for —
check.why: The 1921 Nobel Prize was given for his explanation of the photoelectric effect, not for relativity.

sections.h: The letter, the bomb, and a conscience (1939–1955)
sections.md:
In **1939**, physicists learned that uranium atoms could be split (**nuclear fission**), releasing vast energy. Some feared Nazi Germany might build a bomb. Einstein, persuaded by fellow physicists (notably Leó Szilárd), signed a **letter to U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt** warning of this possibility and urging the U.S. to start its own research.

This contributed to the U.S. effort that became the **Manhattan Project**. Einstein himself did **not** work on building the bomb.

In **August 1945**, atomic bombs were dropped on **Hiroshima** and **Nagasaki** in Japan, killing huge numbers of people. Einstein was deeply shaken by the destruction. He spent his remaining years campaigning for **peace**, **nuclear disarmament**, and a **world government** to prevent war. The chapter mentions that he wrote an open letter to the **United Nations** proposing a world government. He was even offered the presidency of Israel in 1952, which he declined.

He died on **18 April 1955** in Princeton, aged 76. His brain was preserved by a pathologist for study — a sign of how people saw him as the very model of genius.

**The 'truly beautiful mind':** not only because he understood the universe, but because he cared about **what humans did with that understanding**. He was a rebel against authority, but a gentle one; a man who saw science as a way of wonder, not of power.

**Character traits with evidence:**

| Trait | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Independent thinker | Rejected rote learning; studied on his own at university |
| Persistent | Worked on physics while employed as a clerk |
| Creative | Imagined riding beside a light beam; new ideas of time and space |
| Musical / sensitive | Lifelong violinist |
| Principled | Left Nazi Germany; spoke against war and nationalism |
| Conscientious | Campaigned for peace after Hiroshima |
| Modest | Lived simply; declined the presidency of Israel |

**Themes:**
1. **Education should nurture curiosity**, not just obedience.
2. **Late bloomers** — slow starters can achieve greatly.
3. **Science and responsibility** — knowledge can heal or destroy; scientists (and citizens) must think about consequences.
4. **Peace over power.**

**Indian connection:** Einstein met **Rabindranath Tagore** in Berlin in 1930 and their conversations were published. He admired **Mahatma Gandhi**, writing in 1944 that future generations would scarcely believe that such a man had walked the earth. And Indian physicist **Satyendra Nath Bose** sent Einstein a paper in 1924; Einstein translated it and extended it, giving us 'Bose–Einstein statistics' — which is why particles called **bosons** are named after Bose.

check.q: Particles called 'bosons' are named after which Indian scientist who worked with Einstein?
check.why: Satyendra Nath Bose's work with Einstein led to Bose–Einstein statistics, and particles obeying them are called bosons.

sections.md:
**1. Words describing people.** Biographies describe character with adjectives. From the chapter and this guide: *backward, boring, rebellious, brilliant, independent, gentle, principled*. Notice how the same person can be called 'Brother Boring' and 'genius' — the description depends on who is speaking and when.

**2. Suffixes for people (-ist, -er, -or, -ian).**
| Base | Person |
|---|---|
| science | scientist |
| physics | physicist |
| peace / pacifism | pacifist |
| violin | violinist |
| invent | inventor |
| music | musician |
| teach | teacher |
Practice: form the 'person' word for *art, mathematics, chemistry, politics, research*.

**3. Noun phrases.** A biography packs facts into phrases: *a technical expert at the patent office*, *the most famous scientist of the century*, *a letter to the American President*. Expand these into sentences, or compress sentences into such phrases.

**4. Reported speech in biography.** The chapter reports what people said rather than quoting much directly.
- Direct: His teacher said, "Your presence spoils the respect of the class."
- Reported: His teacher said that his presence spoiled the respect of the class.
Remember: change pronouns, shift tense back, remove quotation marks.

**5. Linking events in time.** Useful connectors: *soon after, by the age of, at the age of, in the same year, later, eventually, by then, from then on*. Rewrite Einstein's timeline as a paragraph using at least five of these.

**6. Vocabulary**
| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| regimentation | strict organisation and control |
| rote learning | memorising by repetition without understanding |
| genius | exceptional intellectual or creative power |
| patent | legal right to an invention |
| relativity | theory that space and time depend on the observer's motion |
| pacifist | person opposed to war |
| disarmament | reducing or giving up weapons |
| deformed | abnormally shaped |

check.q: Which word means 'a person who is opposed to war'?
check.why: A pacifist opposes war and violence, as Einstein did in his later years.

sections.md:
**Speaking — 'A scientist I admire'.** Speak for one minute about any scientist — Einstein, C. V. Raman, Kalpana Chawla, A. P. J. Abdul Kalam, Janaki Ammal, Marie Curie. Cover their early life, main discovery, a challenge they faced, and one quality you want to learn from them.

**Debate.** *'Scientists should be held responsible for how their discoveries are used.'* Use the 1939 letter and Einstein's later peace campaign as evidence.

**Writing — biographical sketch.** Write a 150-word biography of someone in your family or neighbourhood, using the chapter as a model: birth and early life → school → turning point → achievements → what makes them special. Use time connectors.

**Writing — letter.** Imagine you are Einstein in 1946. Write a short letter to a young student explaining why you now campaign for peace. (120 words, in your own words.)

**Writing — newspaper report.** 'Starlight bends! Einstein's theory proved' — write a 100-word report as if it were November 1919, including what was measured and why it matters.

**Q1. Why did Einstein's mother worry about him as a baby?** *(30 words)* His head was unusually large and angular, and he did not speak until he was about two and a half. Even then, he repeated sentences softly before speaking, so his parents feared he was backward.

**Q2. Why did Einstein leave school in Munich?** *(40 words)* He disliked the school's strict regimentation and rote learning, and clashed with teachers. When his family moved to Milan, he was left alone, became unhappy and left without completing school, later finishing in Aarau, Switzerland.

**Q3. How did the patent office help Einstein?** *(40 words)* The job gave him a steady income and plenty of time to think. Examining inventions trained him to find the core of an idea, and he worked on physics in spare moments — leading to his famous papers of 1905.

**Q4. 'Einstein was not only a great scientist but also a great human being.' Justify.** *(120 words)* Plan: scientific achievements (1905 papers, E = mc², general relativity, Nobel 1921) → moral stance (left Nazi Germany, spoke against militarism) → 1939 letter and later dismay after Hiroshima → peace activism and call for world government → conclusion on 'beautiful mind'.

**Q5. Why is the chapter titled 'A Truly Beautiful Mind'?** *(40 words)* The title praises both the brilliance of Einstein's scientific imagination and the goodness of his conscience. He revealed the beauty of the universe's laws and also worked for peace, so his mind was beautiful in thought and in values.

**Did you know?** *Time* magazine named Einstein its **'Person of the Century'** in 1999.

rd-school-c9-english-a.ch5-snake-and-mir.title: The Snake and the Mirror — Vaikom Muhammad Basheer
rd-school-c9-english-a.ch5-snake-and-mir.subtitle: A vain young doctor, a hot Kerala night, and a snake that liked mirrors

sections.md:
Picture a tiny rented room, a hot, sticky night in Kerala, a single kerosene lamp. A young doctor is admiring himself in a mirror, smiling at his own face and planning a glamorous future. Then — a soft *thud* behind him. Something has fallen from the rafters. It is not a rat.

**"The Snake and the Mirror"** is one of the funniest pieces in *Beehive*. It was written in **Malayalam** by the beloved storyteller **Vaikom Muhammad Basheer** and translated into English by **V. Abdulla**. Told in the first person, a homeopath narrates the night a snake coiled around his arm — and how the encounter scared the vanity right out of him.

It is a story to enjoy for its **humour**, especially **self-mocking humour**, and to think about for its message: **pride and vanity look very silly when you face death**.

> In this read: the author and his world, the setting, a full scene-by-scene retelling with the meaning of each part, the humour explained, character, themes, the chapter's language work, speaking and writing tasks, and model answers.

Basheer died in 1994, so the story and its translation are under copyright. Read it in *Beehive* (free on ncert.nic.in); this companion retells and explains it in its own words.

check.q: The story was originally written in which language?
check.why: Vaikom Muhammad Basheer wrote in Malayalam; the story was translated into English by V. Abdulla.

sections.md:
**Vaikom Muhammad Basheer (1908–1994)** was born in **Thalayolaparambu, near Vaikom**, in present-day Kerala. As a young man he left home to join the **freedom struggle**, was jailed for his participation, and later spent years wandering India and beyond, doing odd jobs — cook, hotel worker, palmist's assistant, even living among wandering ascetics. Those travels filled him with characters and stories.

He wrote in simple, everyday Malayalam — a revolution at the time, when literary writing was often heavy and formal. He is affectionately known as the **'Beypore Sultan'** (after Beypore, near Kozhikode, where he lived in later life).

**Famous works:** *Balyakalasakhi* (Childhood Friend), *Pathummayude Aadu* (Pathumma's Goat), *Ntuppuppakkoranendarnnu* (Me Grandad 'ad an Elephant!), *Mathilukal* (Walls), *Premalekhanam* (Love Letter).

He received the **Padma Shri** in **1982**.

**Did you know?** *Mathilukal* (Walls), based on his prison days, was made into an award-winning film by Adoor Gopalakrishnan in 1990.

**About translation.** A translator must carry not only words but jokes, rhythm and culture into another language. Humour is the hardest thing to translate — so when you laugh at this story in English, credit V. Abdulla too.

check.q: Basheer is affectionately called —
check.why: He is fondly known as the 'Beypore Sultan', after Beypore near Kozhikode where he lived.

sections.h: The setting: one room, one lamp, many rats
sections.md:
Basheer sets the whole adventure in a single small rented room, and every detail of it matters:

- **An unpainted ceiling** — really no ceiling at all: you can see the wooden **rafters** and the tiled roof. Rats run about up there. (This explains how the snake could drop down.)
- **No electricity** — a **kerosene lamp** gives a small circle of light; the rest of the room is shadowy.
- **Few belongings** — a box of books, a table, a chair, a bed, a few clothes and some medicines. The doctor's practice is tiny and his income small.
- **A hot, humid night** in Kerala — the window is open; the air is heavy.

**Why this setting works:** it is ordinary and a little shabby, which makes the doctor's grand daydreams funnier; and the dim light and open rafters make the snake's sudden arrival believable and frightening.

**Homeopathy note.** Homeopathy is a system of medicine that came to India in the 19th century and is widely used. In the story, the joke is that the narrator's little box of homeopathic medicines would be of no use against a snakebite.

check.q: Why could the snake drop into the room so easily?
options: The room had no proper ceiling, only open rafters
There was a hole in the floor
It came in a box of books
check.why: The 'unpainted ceiling' meant open rafters under the roof, where rats — and snakes — could move about and fall down.

sections.h: The story, retold — Part 1: a vain young doctor
sections.md:
**The frame.** The story begins with the homeopath being asked by listeners whether he has ever had an encounter with a snake. He says he has — and tells this tale. So the whole story is a yarn shared among friends.

**Coming home.** That night he returns from the hospital at about **eight o'clock**, after dinner at a hotel. It is hot. He opens the window, lights the lamp and settles at his table.

**The mirror.** He has a fine **mirror**, and he is very pleased with himself. He looks at his face in it and admires himself — he thinks he is rather handsome. He's careful about appearance: he shaves regularly and keeps a thin, fashionable **moustache** (he mentions a film star's moustache — the joke being that his own looks are ordinary).

**The big decisions.** As he gazes at himself, he makes two important decisions:
1. He will **shave every day** and grow a thin moustache, and always look smart and stylish.
2. He will **get married** — to a **woman doctor with plenty of money** and a good practice. She should be a little fat — so that, he jokes, if he makes a silly mistake and she runs after him, he will be able to escape!

*Meaning:* Basheer paints a young man who is poor but proud, ambitious in a comic, practical way. Even his idea of marriage is about money and convenience. The mirror is the symbol of his vanity.

He is imagining all this, smiling at himself, when he hears a **dull thud** behind him…

check.q: What kind of woman did the doctor plan to marry?
options: A woman doctor with plenty of money and a good practice
check.why: He daydreamed of marrying a well-off woman doctor with a busy practice, preferably a little fat so he could outrun her.

sections.md:
**The snake.** He turns slightly. A **snake** has fallen from the rafters onto the back of his chair. In a moment, it slides over his shoulder and **coils around his left arm, above the elbow**. Its hood is spread, its head just a few inches from his face.

**Fear.** He is paralysed with fear — he sits as still as a stone statue. He doesn't dare move or shout. His breath almost stops. He knows one bite could be the end, and there's no antidote in his little box of homeopathic medicines (a delicious self-joke).

**Prayer.** His mind races. He tries to pray — and here Basheer adds a lovely comic touch: the terrified narrator finds even his thoughts of God coming out in a jumble. He thinks of God in his own way and quietly wishes he were not in such a fix. His grand plans of a minute ago suddenly seem very small.

**Numbness.** The snake's grip on his arm tightens; his arm begins to feel numb, as if it no longer belonged to him. Its head is close; time seems to stop.

**The turn.** Then — something remarkable. The snake **turns its head and looks into the mirror**. It sees its own reflection. The narrator wonders, comically, whether the snake is admiring its own beauty — perhaps it too is thinking of shaving or finding a rich partner! The snake slowly unwinds from his arm and moves onto the table, towards the mirror, gazing at itself.

**Escape.** This is his chance. Silently, carefully, he rises from the chair, slips out of the room, and **runs**.

*Meaning:* in the face of death, vanity drops away; what remains is a frightened human being. The snake now plays the role the man played a moment ago — admiring itself in the mirror. Basheer turns the mirror on human pride.

sections.h: The story, retold — Part 3: the morning after
sections.md:
He runs out of the house into the night and goes to a friend's place, where he spends the night.

The next morning he returns with friends to look for the snake. They search the room — but the snake has gone. The ending has a final comic twist that the original story tells best (read it in your textbook!), and it once again punctures the narrator's dignity.

The narrator closes by laughing at himself — the grand plans of the previous evening now seem ridiculous. Whether he really gave them all up is left playfully open; Basheer's narrator is too honest to pretend he became a saint overnight.

**Why the frame matters:** The story is told to an audience, like a yarn shared among friends. This conversational frame makes the humour warmer — we feel we are sitting with him as he tells it, and we know he survived, so we can laugh at his fear without worrying.

sections.md:
Basheer's humour is **gentle, self-deprecating and situational**. Look at the techniques:

**1. Self-mockery.** The narrator laughs at his own poverty (a box of books, a table, a chair), his vanity (comparing his moustache to a film star's), his unromantic marriage plans (a 'fat' rich wife he can outrun).

**2. Bathos** — sudden drop from grand to trivial. Facing death, his prayers come out muddled; the snake, meanwhile, admires itself in the mirror like a vain young man!

**3. Comic exaggeration.** He sits like a stone statue; his arm feels like it isn't his; his heart pounds.

**4. Irony.** The mirror that fed his vanity is the very thing that saves him — by feeding the *snake's* vanity.

**5. Understatement and timing.** He tells the scariest moment calmly, letting the absurdity speak.

**6. Parallelism.** Man admires himself in the mirror → snake admires itself in the mirror. Basheer holds up a mirror to human pride.

**7. Direct address.** The narrator speaks to his listeners, inviting them to laugh with him.

check.q: Which is an example of irony in the story?
options: The mirror that fed his vanity saves his life by distracting the snake
check.why: It is ironic that the mirror, a symbol of his vanity, distracts the snake and lets him escape.

sections.md:
**The homeopath — character sketch:**
- **Vain** — admires himself, plans to look smart.
- **Poor but ambitious** — modest practice, but dreams of a rich marriage.
- **Imaginative** — builds a whole future in a minute.
- **Honest and humorous** — tells the story against himself.
- **Human** — terrified, prays, shaken out of his illusions.
- **Quick-witted when it matters** — seizes the one moment to escape silently.

**Themes:**
1. **Vanity and its folly.** Pride evaporates in the face of real danger.
2. **Fear and survival.** The mind races, priorities shift instantly.
3. **Humour as wisdom.** Laughing at oneself is a sign of maturity.
4. **The ordinary life.** Basheer celebrates the small rented room and the struggling young professional.

**Nature note (safety!):** India has many snakes; only a few are dangerously venomous (the 'big four': Indian cobra, common krait, Russell's viper, saw-scaled viper). The narrator's stillness was actually wise — sudden movement can provoke a bite. In real life: stay still, move slowly away, never try to handle a snake, and go to a hospital immediately for any bite (anti-venom is given there). Snakes are also important to farmers because they eat rats.
keyTerms: homeopath — practitioner of homeopathy
vanity — excessive pride in one's appearance
self-deprecating — making fun of oneself
bathos — comic fall from serious to trivial

check.q: Why did the narrator not shout or move when the snake coiled around his arm?
options: He was frozen with fear and knew movement might provoke a bite
check.why: He sat motionless out of fear, and sensibly so, since sudden movement could have provoked the snake to strike.

sections.md:
**1. Past continuous for background, simple past for events.** Stories set the scene with the past continuous and drop the action in with the simple past:
- *I **was looking** into the mirror* (background) *when I **heard** a thud* (event).
- *The rats **were running** about on the rafters when the snake **fell**.*
Practice: join with *when* — 'He was smiling at himself. The snake dropped onto the chair.'

**2. Active and passive voice.**
- Active: *The snake coiled round his arm.*
- Passive: *His arm was coiled round by the snake.* (clumsy — which is why active is better here!)
- Active: *A thief may have stolen his things.* → Passive: *His things may have been stolen.*
Use the passive when the doer is unknown or unimportant.

**3. Sound words (onomatopoeia).** *thud, hiss, rustle, squeak* (rats), *thump* (heart). Write three sentences about a scary night using sound words.

**4. Words for fear, from mild to extreme.** uneasy → nervous → frightened → terrified → petrified. Place the narrator's feelings on this scale at each stage of the story.

**5. Idioms and phrases.** *frozen with fear*, *a narrow escape*, *in a fix*, *to hold one's breath*, *to take to one's heels* (run away). Use each in a sentence.

**6. Vocabulary**
| Word / phrase | Meaning |
|---|---|
| rafters | sloping beams supporting a roof |
| unpainted ceiling | bare roof without boards |
| coil | wind into rings |
| petrified | so frightened one can't move |
| a stone image | a statue (frozen still) |
| strenuously | with great effort |
| demise | death |
| vain | too proud of one's looks |

check.q: Choose the sentence that correctly uses the past continuous and simple past.
options: I looked into the mirror when I was hearing a thud.
I was looking into the mirror when I heard a thud.
I am looking into the mirror when I heard a thud.
I had look into the mirror when I hear a thud.
check.why: The ongoing background action uses the past continuous ('was looking'); the sudden event uses the simple past ('heard').

sections.md:
**Speaking — tell a 'narrow escape' story.** In groups, each student tells a true or imagined narrow escape (a stray dog, a near-miss on a bicycle, a wasp in the classroom) in two minutes. Use the frame technique: 'Have I ever told you about the time…?' Try to make your listeners laugh at *you*, as Basheer does.

**Pair work — interview.** One student is a newspaper reporter, the other the homeopath, the morning after. Ask: What happened? What were you thinking? What will you do differently now?

**Writing — the snake's point of view.** Rewrite the climax from the snake's point of view in 100–120 words: the fall, the warm arm, the strange shining surface, the handsome creature in it.

**Writing — a notice.** Write a short notice for your housing society or school on 'What to do if you see a snake' (50 words, with a heading, date and issuing authority).

**Writing — diary.** Write the homeopath's diary entry for that night (100 words), ending with whether he still plans to marry a rich doctor.

**Q1. Describe the narrator's room.** *(40 words)* It was a small rented room with an unpainted ceiling — only rafters, where rats ran about. There was no electricity, just a kerosene lamp. He owned only a box of books, a table, a chair, a bed and some medicines.

**Q2. What were the two 'important decisions' the doctor made while looking in the mirror?** *(40 words)* He decided to shave daily and grow a thin, stylish moustache to look smart; and he decided to marry a well-off woman doctor with a good practice, preferably a little fat so he could escape if she chased him.

**Q3. How did the narrator feel when the snake coiled around his arm?** *(40 words)* He was terrified and frozen like a statue, scarcely breathing. He knew one bite meant death and that his medicines were useless. He tried to pray, his arm went numb, and his proud plans suddenly seemed meaningless.

**Q4. How did the mirror save the narrator?** *(30 words)* The snake turned its head, saw its reflection in the mirror and moved towards it, unwinding from his arm. This gave the narrator the chance to slip out silently.

**Q5. How does the story show that pride is foolish?** *(120 words)* Plan: describe his vanity → the snake's sudden arrival and his helpless fear → his prayers and abandoned plans → the parallel of the snake admiring itself → conclusion: in the face of death, appearance and wealth mean nothing; humility and humour remain.

**Q6. Give two examples of humour and explain them.** — (a) The plan to marry a fat woman doctor so he can outrun her: absurdly practical, mocking his own vanity. (b) The snake admiring itself in the mirror: it mirrors the narrator's vanity, turning the danger into comedy.

check.q: 'Petrified' most nearly means —
check.why: Petrified means so frightened that one cannot move, exactly how the doctor felt with the snake on his arm.

summary: Written in Malayalam by Vaikom Muhammad Basheer (1908–1994), translated by V. Abdulla.
Basheer, the 'Beypore Sultan', was a freedom fighter and wrote in simple, everyday Malayalam; Padma Shri 1982.
The story is framed as a homeopath telling listeners about his encounter with a snake.
His small rented room has open rafters with rats, no electricity, a kerosene lamp and few belongings.
Admiring himself in a mirror, he decides to shave daily, keep a stylish moustache and marry a rich, slightly fat woman doctor.
A snake falls from the rafters and coils around his left arm above the elbow.
He sits frozen like a statue, tries to pray, and his arm goes numb.
The snake turns to look at its own reflection in the mirror and moves away.
He escapes quietly and spends the night at a friend's house.
Next morning, with friends, he finds the snake gone — with a final comic twist.
Humour: self-mockery, irony, bathos, exaggeration, parallelism, conversational frame.
Themes: vanity, fear, humility, laughing at oneself.
Language focus: past continuous vs simple past, active/passive voice, sound words, fear vocabulary, idioms.

glossary.d: one who practises homeopathy, a system of medicine
roof beams
excessive pride in looks or achievements
outcome opposite to what is expected
rendered from one language into another
a story told within a scene of someone telling it

practice: Describe the narrator's room and what it tells us about his life.
What did the narrator do when he heard the 'thud'?
Describe the narrator's feelings when the snake coiled around his arm.
What 'two decisions' did he make before the snake appeared?
How did the mirror save the narrator's life?
Give two examples of humour in the story and explain why they are funny.
Write a character sketch of the homeopath.
Join using 'when' with the past continuous: He was combing his hair. The snake fell.
What lesson about vanity does the story teach? (100 words)
Rewrite the climax of the story from the snake's point of view (100–120 words).
Why is it important to stay calm and still near a snake? What should one do after a snakebite?

rd-school-c9-english-b.beehive-poetry.title: Beehive Poetry — All Eight Poems Explained
rd-school-c9-english-b.beehive-poetry.subtitle: From Frost's two roads to Wordsworth's slumber: meaning, devices and exam answers

sections.h: How to read a poem (in five questions)
sections.md:
Poems pack big feelings into few words. For every poem in *Beehive*, ask:

1. **Who is speaking, and to whom?** (the *speaker* or *poet-persona*)
2. **What is the situation?** (a walk in a wood, a storm, a tree being cut)
3. **What is the central idea / theme?**
4. **What tools does the poet use?** — imagery, metaphor, simile, personification, alliteration, repetition, rhyme scheme.
5. **How does it make me feel, and why?**

**Quick device guide:**

| Device | What it is | Example (our own) |
|---|---|---|
| Simile | comparison with *like/as* | The clouds rolled like elephants. |
| Metaphor | direct comparison | Exams are a mountain. |
| Personification | human qualities to non-human | The wind whispered. |
| Alliteration | repeated initial consonant | silver sand slipped |
| Anaphora/Repetition | repeated words at line starts | Remember… Remember… |
| Enjambment | sentence runs over the line-end | — |
| Imagery | appeals to senses | the smell of wet earth |

This read covers all **eight poems** in the current *Beehive*: The Road Not Taken · Wind · Rain on the Roof · The Lake Isle of Innisfree · A Legend of the Northland · No Men Are Foreign · On Killing a Tree · A Slumber Did My Spirit Seal. We **explain** the poems; read the full texts in your textbook.

check.q: 'The wind whispered secrets' uses which device?
check.why: Whispering secrets is a human action given to the wind, which is personification.

sections.h: 1. The Road Not Taken — Robert Frost
sections.md:
**Poet:** Robert Frost (1874–1963), American, four-time Pulitzer winner, poet of New England's woods and farms. Published 1916.

**Situation:** A traveller stands where a road in a **yellow (autumn) wood** splits in two. He can take only one. He looks down the first as far as he can, then takes the other — which seemed **grassier and less worn**, though, honestly, both were worn about the same, and both lay covered in fresh leaves that morning.

He tells himself he'll keep the first for another day — yet knows that one way leads on to another and he will probably **never come back**. He imagines that, years later, he'll say **with a sigh** that he took the one less travelled by, and that **made all the difference**.

**Theme:** **choices** in life and their **irreversibility**; how we later tell stories about our choices.

**Subtlety:** Frost shows the roads were actually *about the same*. The 'difference' may be a story the speaker tells himself. The **sigh** can be read as regret or as satisfaction — the poem leaves it open.

**Form:** 4 stanzas of 5 lines; rhyme scheme **ABAAB**; mostly iambic tetrameter.

**Devices:** **Metaphor** — the roads = life choices; **imagery** — yellow wood, undergrowth; **repetition** — 'two roads diverged'.

check.q: What is the rhyme scheme of each stanza of 'The Road Not Taken'?
check.why: Each five-line stanza rhymes ABAAB, which gives the poem its musical, reflective flow.

sections.md:
**Poet:** Subramania Bharati (1882–1921), the great Tamil poet and freedom fighter ('Mahakavi Bharati'). Translated from Tamil by A. K. Ramanujan.

**What happens:** The speaker addresses the wind directly. He asks it to **come softly**, not to break shutters, scatter papers or throw books down from the shelf. He scolds it for tearing pages and bringing down rain. Then he notes the wind's destructive power: it breaks crumbling houses, rotting rafters, weak bodies and **hearts**.

**The turn:** The **wind god winnows** — like separating grain from chaff, it crushes only the weak. So the lesson: **make strong homes, firm bodies, steady hearts**. Then the wind becomes our **friend** — it can't put out strong fires; it makes them roar and flourish. **We praise it every day.**

**Theme:** **Strength and resilience**. The wind = **hardships of life**. Weak people are broken by difficulties; strong ones grow stronger.

**Devices:** **Personification/Apostrophe** — wind addressed as a person/god; **metaphor** — 'winnowing' (from farming), 'fire' = inner strength; **imagery** — broken shutters, scattered papers; **free verse** (no regular rhyme).

**Did you know?** Bharati, persecuted by the British for his patriotic writing, lived in the French colony of Pondicherry for years. His songs are still sung across Tamil Nadu.

check.q: In 'Wind', what does the wind symbolise?
check.why: The wind represents adversity — it breaks the weak but strengthens those who are firm.

sections.h: 3. Rain on the Roof — Coates Kinney
sections.md:
**Poet:** Coates Kinney (1826–1904), American poet, lawyer and journalist. The poem was very popular in 19th-century America.

**Situation:** On a night when **humid shadows hover** over the starry sky and **melancholy darkness** weeps, the speaker lies in bed in his cottage, listening to the **patter of soft rain** on the shingled roof.

**Memory flows:** Every tinkle on the roof echoes in his heart; a thousand **dreamy fancies** weave themselves into a busy pattern. **Recollections** of the past come back.

**His mother:** Above all, he remembers his **mother**, who used to look at him lovingly as he fell asleep — 'fondly' tending her dreamers. Her loving face returns to him with the sound of the rain.

**Theme:** **Nature triggers memory**; the warmth of **childhood and a mother's love**; nostalgia.

**Devices:**
- **Personification** — darkness 'weeps'; shadows 'hover'.
- **Alliteration** — *patter … pillow*, *dreamy … darkness*.
- **Onomatopoeia** — *patter*, *tinkle*.
- **Imagery** — auditory (rain sounds), visual (starry spheres), tactile (pressing the pillow).
- **Rhyme** — regular, musical (abab-style).

**Indian link:** Who hasn't lain awake during the monsoon, listening to rain on a tin roof or tiled ceiling, half-dreaming of grandparents or childhood? This poem captures that universal feeling.

check.q: What memory does the rain bring back most strongly to the speaker?
check.why: The rain's patter makes him remember his mother lovingly watching over him as he fell asleep.

sections.h: 4. The Lake Isle of Innisfree — W. B. Yeats
sections.md:
**Poet:** William Butler Yeats (1865–1939), Irish poet, Nobel Prize in Literature 1923. Written c. 1888–90 while he lived in London.

**Situation:** Standing on the **grey pavements** of a city, the speaker longs to go to **Innisfree**, a small island in **Lough Gill** in Ireland, which he loved as a child.

**His dream there:**
- Build a small **cabin of clay and wattles** (woven sticks).
- Grow **nine bean-rows**, keep a **hive for honey-bees**.
- Live alone in the **bee-loud glade**.
- Find **peace**, which comes **dropping slow** like dew from the morning's veils to where the cricket sings.
- **Midnight's glimmer**, noon's **purple glow** (heather), evening full of **linnets' wings**.
- Hear **lake water lapping** with low sounds by the shore — which he hears 'in the deep heart's core' even in the city.

**Theme:** **Longing for nature and simplicity**; escape from urban stress; inner peace.

**Devices:** **Imagery** (sound: bee-loud, cricket, lapping water; sight: purple glow); **alliteration** — *lake water lapping with low sounds*; **metaphor** — peace 'dropping slow'; **repetition** — 'I will arise and go now'; rhyme scheme **ABAB**.

**Did you know?** Yeats said the poem was inspired when he heard a little tinkle of water from a fountain in a London shop window, which reminded him of lake water.
