options: On the grey pavements of a city
check.why: He stands on the roadway or grey pavements of a city, yet hears the lake water in his heart.

sections.h: 5. A Legend of the Northland — Phoebe Cary
sections.md:
**Poet:** Phoebe Cary (1824–1871), American poet. A **ballad** — a story-poem with regular rhyme, often of folk origin.

**Setting:** The far **Northland** (Lapland/Scandinavia), where nights are long and children wear furs. A legend told there.

**The story:** Once, **Saint Peter** — travelling the earth when the Lord was 'down on earth' preaching — came, hungry and faint, to a cottage. A little woman was **baking cakes**. He asked her for just **one cake**.

She made a very small cake — but it seemed too large to give away. She made a smaller one; that too seemed too big. She made the smallest — still too much. Finally, she put them all on the shelf and gave him **nothing**, saying her cakes seemed too large to give away, even the smallest.

Saint Peter was angry. He said she was too **selfish** to dwell in human form and have both food and shelter and fire to keep her warm. So he cursed her: she would build as **birds do**, and get her scanty food by **boring and boring** all day in hard, dry wood.

She went **up through the chimney** as a bird — a **woodpecker**. Her little cap of **scarlet red** stayed on her head; the rest of her was **burned black as coal** by the chimney's soot. And every schoolboy in the land can see her still, **boring** in the trees.

**Theme/moral:** **Greed and selfishness are punished**; **generosity** and kindness to the needy are virtues.

**Form:** 16 quatrains; rhyme scheme **ABCB**; simple, narrative ballad style. Devices: **simile** — 'black as coal'; **repetition** — 'boring and boring'; legend/myth explaining a natural fact (why the woodpecker looks as it does).

check.q: What did the woman become as punishment?
check.why: Saint Peter turned her into a woodpecker, with a red cap and sooty black body, forced to bore into wood for food.

sections.h: 6. No Men Are Foreign — James Kirkup
sections.md:
**Poet:** James Kirkup (1918–2009), British poet who lived in Japan and elsewhere; a pacifist. Poem written in the shadow of world wars.

**Message:** The speaker urges us to **remember** that no men are strange and no countries foreign. Beneath all uniforms, every body breathes as ours does. We walk on the **same earth**, in which we'll all lie. They too know sun, air and water; are fed by **peaceful harvests**, starved by **war's long winter**. Their hands are like ours; their eyes **wake and sleep**; their **strength can be won by love**.

So, **remember**: when we're told to **hate our brothers**, it is ourselves we betray, dispossess and condemn. When we take up arms against each other, we **defile the earth**; hells of fire and dust outrage the innocence of air.

**Theme:** **Universal brotherhood**, **anti-war**, common humanity.

**Devices:**
- **Repetition/Anaphora** — 'Remember'.
- **Metaphor** — 'war's long winter' (hardship), 'uniforms' (outer differences).
- **Imagery** — sun, air, water, harvest.
- **Free verse**, two stanzas, no regular rhyme.
- **Synecdoche** — 'hands', 'eyes' stand for whole people.

**Link to India:** The ideal of **'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam'** — *the world is one family* — from the Maha Upanishad, expresses the same idea; it was the theme of India's G20 presidency in 2023.

check.q: What does 'war's long winter' suggest?
options: The long suffering and hardship caused by war
check.why: The metaphor compares war to a harsh, long winter that starves and freezes people's lives.

sections.h: 7. On Killing a Tree — Gieve Patel
sections.md:
**Poet:** Gieve Patel (1940–2023), Mumbai-based poet, playwright, painter and doctor.

**Irony from the start:** The poem is written like **instructions** for killing a tree — and its very coldness shocks us into seeing the tree's **resilience** and our **cruelty**.

**The argument:**
1. A simple **jab of the knife won't do it**. The tree has grown slowly, consuming the earth, rising out of its crust, absorbing **years of sunlight, air, water**, and from its **leprous hide** sprouting leaves.
2. Even if you **hack and chop**, the bleeding bark will heal; from close to the ground will rise **curled green twigs** that grow back to former size.
3. **No** — the **root** must be pulled out of the earth, out of the 'anchoring' cave it lived in. It must be **exposed** — the strength of the tree revealed, the **white and wet** source, the most sensitive, hidden part.
4. Then the **scorching and choking** in sun and air, browning, hardening, twisting, withering — and **it is done**.

**Theme:** Trees are **living, resilient beings**; destroying them needs deliberate brutality. The poem is an **ecological** protest against **deforestation**.

**Devices:** **Irony** (instructional tone); **personification** — the tree 'bleeds', has a 'hide', 'anchoring earth'; **imagery** — tactile and visual; **free verse**; **alliteration** — *scorching and choking*.

**Science link:** Many trees regrow from stumps ('coppicing'); the root system and its stored food make that possible — which is exactly the poem's point.

sections.h: 8. A Slumber Did My Spirit Seal — William Wordsworth
sections.md:
**Poet:** William Wordsworth (1770–1850), English Romantic poet; one of the 'Lucy poems' (c. 1798–99). Who 'Lucy' was is unknown — critics disagree whether she was real.

**Stanza 1:** The speaker says a **slumber** sealed his spirit — he was lulled into a sense of security. He had **no human fears**; she seemed a thing that could **not feel the touch of earthly years** — as though she could never age or die.

**Stanza 2:** Now she has **no motion, no force**; she neither hears nor sees. She is **rolled round in earth's diurnal course** (daily rotation) **with rocks, and stones, and trees**. She has died and become part of nature.

**Theme:** **Death and loss**; the shock of realising mortality; also a consoling sense of **union with nature**.

**Devices:**
- **Contrast** between stanzas — then (alive, seemingly timeless) and now (dead, motionless).
- **Metaphor** — 'slumber' (unawareness/complacency); 'seal' (closed).
- **Alliteration** — *slumber … spirit seal*; *rocks … rolled round*.
- **Imagery** — earth's diurnal course.
- Rhyme scheme **ABAB**; two quatrains.

**Diurnal:** daily. The earth turns once a day; Lucy, buried, turns with it.

check.q: 'Rolled round in earth's diurnal course' means she —
options: Has died and moves with the earth's daily rotation
check.why: Buried in the ground, she moves only as part of the earth's daily rotation, along with rocks, stones and trees.

rd-school-c9-english-b.ch6-my-childhood.title: My Childhood — A. P. J. Abdul Kalam
rd-school-c9-english-b.ch6-my-childhood.subtitle: A boy from Rameswaram, three friends of three faiths, and lessons that built a President

sections.h: Tamarind seeds and a newspaper bundle
sections.md:
It is 1939. In a small island town at India's southern tip, an eight-year-old boy scours the streets for **tamarind seeds** — suddenly in demand — and sells them to a shop for one *anna* a day. A little later he catches bundles of newspapers thrown from a moving train and helps distribute them. These are his **first earnings**, and he will remember the pride of them for the rest of his life.

That boy was **Avul Pakir Jainulabdeen Abdul Kalam** — the 'Missile Man of India' and the **11th President of India**.

**"My Childhood"** is an extract from his autobiography **Wings of Fire** (1999, written with Arun Tiwari). In a few pages, Kalam paints his home, his parents, his friends, his teachers — and quietly makes a powerful case for **religious harmony** and **standing up against prejudice**.

**Before you read (the textbook's warm-up idea):** think of the people who shaped you — a parent, a friend, a teacher. Which single incident do you remember most clearly? Autobiography works exactly like that: a grown man looks back and picks the moments that made him.

> In this read: Kalam's life, an original retelling of the whole chapter in order, the people who shaped him, character sketches, themes, the language exercises (vocabulary, passive voice, phrasal verbs), writing tasks and model answers. The chapter is copyrighted, so this read retells it in our own words — open the free official PDF from the link at the end to read Kalam's own sentences.

sections.md:
**A. P. J. Abdul Kalam (15 October 1931 – 27 July 2015)** was born in **Rameswaram**, then in the Madras Presidency, now in Tamil Nadu. He studied physics at St Joseph's College, Tiruchirappalli, and aerospace engineering at the Madras Institute of Technology.

**Career highlights:**
- Worked at **DRDO** and then **ISRO**, where he was project director of **SLV-III**, India's first indigenous satellite launch vehicle, which put the **Rohini** satellite into orbit in **1980**.
- Led the **Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme** (Agni, Prithvi) — hence 'Missile Man'.
- Played a key role in the **Pokhran-II** nuclear tests (1998).
- **President of India, 2002–2007** — known as the 'People's President', especially loved by students.
- **Bharat Ratna, 1997.**

He died while delivering a lecture to students at IIM Shillong — doing what he loved most: teaching young people to dream.

**Did you know?** Kalam's birthday, 15 October, is celebrated in many places as a day for students and reading.

sections.md:
Kalam was born into a **middle-class Tamil Muslim family** in Rameswaram. The family lived in their **ancestral house** on **Mosque Street**, built in the middle of the 19th century — a large, solid house of limestone and brick.

**His father, Jainulabdeen**, had neither much formal education nor wealth. But he possessed great **innate wisdom** and a **generosity of spirit**. He lived an austere life: he avoided all inessential comforts and luxuries, yet made sure the family had food, medicine and clothes.

**His mother, Ashiamma**, was his father's ideal partner. Kalam recalls that she fed far more outsiders every day than family members — a picture of generous hospitality.

Kalam describes himself as one of **many children**, a **short boy with rather undistinguished looks**, born to tall and handsome parents. He says he had a very secure childhood, both materially and emotionally.

He says he inherited **honesty and self-discipline** from his father, and **faith in goodness and deep kindness** from his mother — as did his three brothers and sister.

**Reading between the lines:** notice that Kalam never complains about money. 'Secure' for him means love, food and values — not luxury. That is the first quiet lesson of the chapter: a rich childhood is not the same as a wealthy one.

check.q: What qualities did Kalam inherit from his father?
check.why: Kalam writes that he inherited honesty and self-discipline from his father, and faith in goodness and kindness from his mother.

sections.h: Part 2 retold: war, tamarind seeds and first wages
sections.md:
When the **Second World War broke out in 1939**, Kalam was eight. For reasons he didn't fully understand, there was suddenly a **demand for tamarind seeds** in the market. He collected them and sold them to a provision shop on Mosque Street — earning **one anna** a day. (An anna was 1/16 of a rupee.)

**His brother-in-law, Jallaluddin**, told him stories about the war; Kalam would later try to trace them in the headlines of *Dinamani*, a Tamil newspaper. Rameswaram was an isolated island, so the war felt far away — yet it reached even this quiet town.

Because of the war, the train **stopped halting at Rameswaram station**. Newspapers now had to be **bundled and thrown out from the moving train** on the Rameswaram–Dhanushkodi road. Kalam's cousin **Samsuddin**, who distributed newspapers in Rameswaram, needed a helping hand to catch the bundles — and Kalam filled the slot. So he earned his **first wages**.

Half a century later, he says, he could still feel the surge of pride in earning his own money for the first time.

**Why it matters:** Even as a child, Kalam saw work as dignity. Small jobs taught responsibility and self-reliance. A future scientist first learnt to be curious by trying to match his brother-in-law's war stories with newspaper headlines.

sections.h: Part 3 retold: three friends, three traditions
sections.md:
As a child, Kalam had **three close friends**:

- **Ramanadha Sastry** — son of **Pakshi Lakshmana Sastry**, the high priest of the **Rameswaram temple**.
- **Aravindan** — who later went into the business of arranging transport for visiting pilgrims.
- **Sivaprakasan** — who became a catering contractor for the Southern Railways.

All three were from **orthodox Hindu Brahmin families**. Kalam writes that as children, none of them **ever felt any difference** among themselves because of their religious differences and upbringing.

**A festival of togetherness:** Kalam's family arranged boats with a special platform for carrying the idols of the Lord during the annual **Shri Sita Rama Kalyanam** ceremony, from the temple to the marriage site, situated in the middle of a pond called **Rama Tirtha**, near the house.

His mother and grandmother told the children bedtime stories from the **Ramayana** and from the life of the **Prophet**.

**Kalam's father and Lakshmana Sastry** were close friends, often discussing spiritual matters together — Kalam remembers the two in their traditional attire, a picture of friendship across faiths.

**Notice the pattern:** harmony here is not a slogan — it is daily life: a Muslim family serving a Hindu festival, a Muslim grandmother telling Ramayana stories, a Muslim father and a Hindu priest as best friends.

sections.h: Part 4 retold: the new teacher — prejudice confronted
sections.md:
When Kalam was in the **fifth standard** at the **Rameswaram Elementary School**, a **new teacher** came to the class. Kalam wore a **cap** that marked him as a Muslim, and he always sat in the **front row next to Ramanadha Sastry**, who wore the **sacred thread**.

The new teacher could not stomach a Hindu priest's son sitting with a Muslim boy. In accordance with his idea of social ranking, he asked Kalam to **go and sit on the back bench**. Kalam felt very sad, and so did Ramanadha, who looked utterly downcast as Kalam shifted. The image of his friend weeping stayed with Kalam forever.

After school, the boys went home and told their parents. **Lakshmana Sastry summoned the teacher** and, in their presence, told him he should not spread the poison of **social inequality and communal intolerance** in the minds of innocent children. He asked the teacher to either **apologise or quit the school and the island**.

The teacher not only regretted his behaviour, but the strong sense of conviction Lakshmana Sastry conveyed ultimately **reformed** him.

**The lesson:** Prejudice must be confronted — calmly, firmly, and by people with moral authority. Here, the challenge came not from Kalam's own family but from a **Hindu priest** defending a Muslim child. That is the heart of the chapter.

check.q: What did Lakshmana Sastry ask the new teacher to do?
options: Leave Kalam alone and teach maths
Either apologise or quit the school and the island
check.why: He told the teacher to apologise or leave the school and the island, refusing to let him spread communal intolerance.

sections.h: Part 5 retold: Sivasubramania Iyer breaks barriers
sections.md:
Kalam's **science teacher, Sivasubramania Iyer**, though an orthodox Brahmin with a very conservative wife, was something of a **rebel**. He did his best to break social barriers so that people from varying backgrounds could mingle easily.

He used to spend hours with Kalam and would say he wanted Kalam to develop so that he would be on par with the highly educated people of the big cities.

One day he **invited Kalam home for a meal**. His **wife was horrified** at the idea of a Muslim boy being invited to dine in her ritually pure kitchen. She **refused to serve him**.

Sivasubramania Iyer was **not perturbed**, nor did he get angry with his wife. Instead, he **served Kalam with his own hands** and sat down beside him to eat his meal. His wife watched from behind the kitchen door. Kalam wondered whether she noticed any difference in the way he ate rice, drank water or cleaned the floor after the meal.

When Kalam was leaving, Iyer **invited him again for dinner the next weekend**. Seeing Kalam hesitate, he told him not to get upset: once you decide to change the system, such problems have to be confronted.

The next week, when Kalam went, **Iyer's wife took him inside her kitchen and served him food with her own hands**. Change had come — gently, patiently, through example.

check.why: Without anger, he served Kalam with his own hands and sat with him, quietly showing that the barrier was wrong.

sections.h: Part 6 retold: leaving home — 'you have to go away to grow'
sections.md:
The Second World War ended (1945), and India's freedom was imminent. Kalam asked his father's permission to **leave Rameswaram** and study at the district headquarters in **Ramanathapuram**.

His father, like a friend thinking aloud, told him: *"Abdul! I know you have to go away to grow. Does the seagull not fly across the sun, alone and without a nest?"* (This is the one short line we quote; it captures the spirit.)

When Kalam's mother hesitated, his father quoted **Khalil Gibran** — the Lebanese-American poet — on how children come *through* parents but are not their possessions; parents may give them love, but not their thoughts, for children have their own.

**Kalam's take-away:** Love includes letting go. His parents, despite limited means and deep attachment, encouraged him to pursue education far from home.

**The seagull image explained:** a seagull leaves the shore and flies alone over the sea towards the sun. Growing up, too, means leaving the safe nest. The father turns a sad moment into a brave one.

check.q: Which poet did Kalam's father quote when Kalam's mother hesitated?
check.why: His father quoted Khalil Gibran's idea that children have their own lives and thoughts, to reassure Kalam's mother.

sections.h: The people who shaped him — character sketches
sections.md:
**Jainulabdeen (father):** simple, wise, generous, spiritual; a friend of the temple's high priest; brave enough to let his son leave. *Key word: wisdom.*

**Ashiamma (mother):** kind and hospitable, fed outsiders daily, emotional about her son leaving. *Key word: kindness.*

**Pakshi Lakshmana Sastry:** high priest of the Rameswaram temple; firm and fearless in defending a Muslim child; reformed the prejudiced teacher. *Key word: conviction.*

**The new teacher:** narrow-minded at first, but able to change — a reminder that people are not fixed as villains. *Key word: reform.*

**Sivasubramania Iyer:** a 'rebel' Brahmin teacher who believed in Kalam, acted calmly, and changed his wife by example. *Key word: patience.*

**Iyer's wife:** conservative but open to change; her second-week welcome is one of the most hopeful moments in the chapter. *Key word: change.*

**Ramanadha Sastry:** Kalam's bench-mate whose tears show that prejudice hurts everyone, not only its target.

**Young Kalam:** hard-working, curious, sensitive, observant — he notices small things (the weeping friend, the wife behind the door) and remembers them all his life.

sections.md:
1. **Religious harmony** — friends and families across faiths share festivals, stories and friendship.
2. **Courage against prejudice** — Lakshmana Sastry confronts openly; Iyer confronts quietly. Both work.
3. **Values from parents** — honesty, discipline, kindness.
4. **Dignity of labour** — first wages, earned with pride.
5. **Education and growth** — teachers who believe in you; parents who let you go.
6. **Children are naturally free of prejudice** — the boys 'never felt any difference'; adults bring the barriers.

**Craft:** the chapter is a **first-person autobiographical memoir**. Kalam's tone is **gentle, grateful and non-bitter**: even the prejudiced teacher is not condemned forever. He uses **concrete details** (limestone house, tamarind seeds, Rama Tirtha pond) to make a small town come alive, and **contrast** (new teacher vs Iyer) to make his point without preaching.

**Did you know?** Rameswaram's Ramanathaswamy temple and Kalam's house on Mosque Street are a short walk apart; Kalam's home is now a museum visited by thousands of students.

check.q: What is the tone of Kalam's narration?
check.why: Kalam looks back with gratitude and calm reflection, even when describing prejudice.

sections.h: Thinking about language: words, passive voice, phrasal verbs
sections.md:
**Vocabulary from the chapter**

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| austere | simple, without comforts |
| innate | inborn |
| inessential | not necessary |
| orthodox | following traditional religious beliefs strictly |
| segregation | separation of groups |
| conviction | firm belief |
| perturbed | worried, disturbed |
| imminent | about to happen |
| erupt | break out suddenly |
| surge | a sudden strong rush (of feeling) |
| undistinguished | ordinary, not special |
| downcast | sad, low in spirits |

**Passive voice practice.** In memoirs, the doer is often obvious or unimportant, so the passive is common.
- Active: *The war stopped the train at Rameswaram.* → Passive: *The train's halt at Rameswaram was stopped.*
- Active: *Someone threw the bundles out of the train.* → Passive: *The bundles were thrown out of the train.*
- Active: *Iyer's wife served him food.* → Passive: *He was served food by Iyer's wife.*
Rule: object becomes subject + **be** (in the right tense) + **past participle** (+ by agent, if needed).

**Phrasal verbs** (verb + particle with a new meaning):
- *break out* — begin suddenly (war broke out)
- *fill the slot / fill in* — take a vacant place
- *look down on* — treat as inferior
- *take over* — assume responsibility (Ramanadha took over the priesthood)
- *come up* — arise, appear

**Adverbs of manner from the story's feel:** quietly, firmly, patiently, proudly. Try writing one sentence about each character using one.

check.q: Change to passive: 'Lakshmana Sastry reformed the teacher.'
options: The teacher was reformed by Lakshmana Sastry.
The teacher is reforming by Lakshmana Sastry.
check.why: Object 'the teacher' becomes subject, followed by 'was' + past participle 'reformed' + by-agent.

sections.md:
**Q1. Where was Kalam's house? (short)** On Mosque Street in Rameswaram, in Tamil Nadu — an ancestral house of limestone and brick built in the mid-19th century.

**Q2. What do you think Dinamani is?** A Tamil newspaper; Kalam traced Jallaluddin's war stories in its headlines.

**Q3. How did Kalam earn his first wages? (40 words)** When the war stopped the train halting at Rameswaram, newspaper bundles were thrown from the moving train. Kalam helped his cousin Samsuddin catch and distribute them, earning his first wages, which made him proud.

**Q4. Had Kalam's friends been aware of differences between them? Why does he say they did not feel any?** As children they were aware of their different traditions — the cap and the sacred thread — but it never mattered to them. Their families respected each other, so the boys grew up seeing friendship, not religion.

**Q5. Why did Lakshmana Sastry's reaction matter?** He was the high priest; his moral authority showed the teacher that prejudice had no religious support. A Hindu priest defending a Muslim child made the lesson unforgettable.

**Q6. 'Kalam's childhood shows that India's strength is its harmony.' Discuss. (120 words)** Plan: friends from Brahmin families → shared festivals (Sita Rama Kalyanam) and stories (Ramayana, Prophet) → fathers' friendship → teacher's prejudice opposed by a Hindu priest → Iyer's patient example → conclusion: harmony is built by individuals who refuse prejudice.

**Writing task idea (from the exercises):** Write a paragraph on whether discrimination based on religion, caste or gender still exists today and how young people can resist it. Use one real example from school life, one reason, and one action you can take.

check.q: Which newspaper did Kalam use to trace war stories?
check.why: Kalam tried to trace Jallaluddin's war stories in the headlines of the Tamil paper Dinamani.

summary: Extract from Wings of Fire by A. P. J. Abdul Kalam (1931–2015), 11th President of India.
Born in Rameswaram into a middle-class Tamil Muslim family; ancestral house on Mosque Street.
Father Jainulabdeen: austere, wise, generous; mother Ashiamma: kind, fed many outsiders.
He inherited honesty and self-discipline from his father, kindness and faith from his mother.

Themes: religious harmony, opposing prejudice, family values, dignity of labour, education.
Language: passive voice and phrasal verbs (break out, take over, look down on).

rd-school-c9-english-b.ch7-reach-for-the.title: Reach for the Top — Santosh Yadav & Maria Sharapova
rd-school-c9-english-b.ch7-reach-for-the.subtitle: A Haryana girl who climbed Everest twice, and a Siberian girl who won Wimbledon at seventeen

sections.md:
One summit is 8,849 metres high, frozen and swept by wind. The other is a grass court in London, ringed by thousands of spectators. Two girls — from very different worlds — climbed them both.

**"Reach for the Top"** is a chapter in two parts:

- **Part I — Santosh Yadav**: from a village in Haryana, where daughters were not always welcomed, to the first woman in the world to climb **Mount Everest twice**.
- **Part II — Maria Sharapova**: from Siberia, to a tennis academy in Florida at age nine, to **Wimbledon champion at seventeen** and world No. 1.

What do they share? **Grit, independence, sacrifice, and an unshakeable belief in their goals.**

**Before you read:** the textbook asks you to think about famous women achievers in sport, science, politics and the arts — and about what obstacles they had to cross that men often did not. Keep a list in your head as you read; you will be surprised how many of the same obstacles appear in both stories.

> This read: complete original retellings of both parts in textbook order, character sketches, a comparison, themes, the language exercises (word formation, personality adjectives), speaking and writing tasks, and model answers. The chapter is NCERT-written, so read the official text from the free PDF linked at the end.

check.q: What was unique about Santosh Yadav's achievement?
options: She was the first Indian to climb Everest
She was the first woman in the world to climb Everest twice
check.why: Santosh Yadav became the first woman in the world to climb Mount Everest twice, in 1992 and 1993.

sections.h: Part I, scene 1: a daughter nobody prayed for
sections.md:
Santosh Yadav was born in **Joniyawas**, a small village in the **Rewari district of Haryana**. She was the **sixth child** — after five sons. In that society a son was a blessing and a daughter often a worry. When a holy man visited and blessed her expecting mother with the wish of a son, something unusual happened: the grandmother, who was standing nearby, said the family did *not* want another son. The holy man was startled — but the blessing that came true was a girl. They named her **Santosh**, meaning *contentment*.

The irony is the heart of the opening: the girl called 'contentment' was **never content** with the narrow life expected of her. While other girls wore traditional dresses, she preferred **shorts**. Looking back she said she had decided early that if she was right about something, she would stick to her path and not bend.

**What this scene teaches:** a name does not define a person; character is chosen. And the family itself shows an early crack in the old prejudice — a grandmother who did not want only sons.

check.q: What does the name 'Santosh' mean, and why is it ironic?
options: Contentment — she was never content with a conventional life
check.why: Santosh means contentment, yet she refused to be content with the traditional life laid out for girls.

sections.h: Part I, scene 2: the bargain for education
sections.md:
Village schooling was limited, and her parents expected her to be **married at about sixteen**, as was usual in the area. Santosh refused. She told them clearly that she would **never marry** unless she was given a proper education. She left home and got herself **admitted to a school in Delhi**.

When her parents refused to pay her fees, she calmly announced that she would **earn the fees herself by doing part-time jobs**. Faced with such firmness, her parents gave in and agreed to pay.

After school she passed the high school exam and went to **Jaipur**, joining the **Maharani College** and staying in **Kasturba Hostel**.

**Language note:** the chapter calls her a 'tough' and 'determined' girl. The bargain scene shows three things at once — *clarity* (she knew what she wanted), *courage* (she defied custom) and *responsibility* (she offered to pay her way). Notice that she does not shout or run away; she negotiates.

check.q: How did Santosh convince her parents to let her study in Delhi?
options: She refused to marry unless allowed to study, offering to pay fees herself
check.why: She threatened not to marry at all unless they allowed her to study, and offered to earn her fees through part-time work.

sections.h: Part I, scene 3: the Aravallis call
sections.md:
From her room in Kasturba Hostel, Santosh could see the **Aravalli hills**. She noticed villagers walking up the slopes and, after a while, **disappearing** over the top. Curious, she decided to find out where they went. One day she followed — and found that they were **mountaineers**. She asked whether she could join them. They were encouraging, and soon she was climbing.

She saved money and enrolled in a course at the **Nehru Institute of Mountaineering, Uttarkashi**. She wrote to her father only *after* joining, apologising for going without his permission — and her father, seeing her conviction, gave his support.

After that she went on **an expedition every year**. Her climbing skills grew rapidly, and her instructors and team-mates noticed her remarkable **resistance to cold and altitude**, and her **mental toughness**.

**Did you know?** The Aravalli range is among the oldest fold mountains on Earth — far older than the Himalayas. Santosh's journey began on one of the oldest ranges and ended on the youngest and highest.

check.q: Where did Santosh train in mountaineering?
check.why: She saved money and enrolled at the Nehru Institute of Mountaineering in Uttarkashi.

sections.md:
**May 1992.** Barely twenty, Santosh climbed **Mount Everest** — at that time the **youngest woman in the world** to do so.

**Character on the mountain.** On that expedition a fellow climber was dying at the **South Col**; Santosh tried hard but could not save him. She did, however, save another climber, **Mohan Singh**, by **sharing her oxygen** with him. Her team-mates were moved: at extreme altitude, where every breath is precious, she thought of others first.

**May 1993.** Within twelve months she joined an **Indo-Nepalese Women's Expedition** and reached the summit again — becoming the **first woman in the world to climb Everest twice**. Her team-mates admired her skills and leadership.

**At the top**, she unfurled the **Indian tricolour** and held it high. She later described the moment as spiritual and indescribable — a feeling of being one with something vast — and of pride that the flag was flying on top of the world.

**Environment.** Pained by the trash on the mountains, she **collected and brought down about 500 kg of garbage** from the Himalayas, and became a voice for mountain ecology.

**Honour:** the Government of India awarded her the **Padma Shri** (2000).

sections.h: Part II, scene 1: Siberia to Florida at nine
sections.md:
**Maria Sharapova** was born in **1987** in **Siberia**, Russia. Tennis came early. At **nine**, she was sent with her father **Yuri** to **Florida, USA**, to train at a tennis academy. Her mother could not join them for **two years** because of **visa restrictions**.

Those years were hard. Maria was **lonely** and missed her mother terribly. Her father worked hard to pay for her training, so even he could not always be with her. She was **much younger** than the other trainees, and the older girls **bullied** her — they would wake her and order her to tidy the room, and send her to bed early. She later explained that she did not let it break her: she was very determined, she learnt to take care of herself, and she was *mentally tough*. She knew why she had come, and she would not quit.

**Key insight:** Maria's sacrifice is not one big moment but thousands of small ones — every lonely evening, every early morning, every refusal to cry and give up.

check.q: Why couldn't Maria's mother join her in the USA for two years?
check.why: Her mother was unable to get a visa, so Maria and her father were in Florida without her for two years.

sections.h: Part II, scene 2: the rise, and the girl off-court
sections.md:
**The rise:**
- **2004** — wins **Wimbledon** at **17**, beating Serena Williams in the final.
- **2005** — becomes **world No. 1** at 18.
- She becomes one of the highest-paid women athletes in the world.

The chapter describes her as having the poise and charm of a fashion model along with the hard focus of a champion.

**Off court:** She loves **fashion**, **singing**, **dancing** and reading the detective stories of **Arthur Conan Doyle**. She is **patriotic**: though she has lived in America for years, she says plainly that she is Russian, that Russia is in her blood, and that she would play for her country in the Olympics if asked.

**On money:** she is honest. She admits that money is a big motivation, but insists that she plays because she wants to be **the best**: she is extremely **competitive** and hates to lose.

**Why include this?** The chapter wants us to see a full person, not just a trophy — a teenager with hobbies, opinions and honesty about ambition.

sections.md:
**Santosh Yadav** — *determined, rebellious against unfair custom, self-reliant, brave, compassionate, patriotic, environment-conscious.* Evidence: refuses child marriage; pays her own way; joins mountaineering on her own; shares oxygen; carries down garbage; raises the tricolour.

**Santosh's parents** — traditional but ultimately supportive; they yield when they see her seriousness. The grandmother's line about not wanting a son shows that change can begin inside a traditional family.

**Maria Sharapova** — *focused, resilient, competitive, honest, patriotic, glamorous yet hard-working.* Evidence: endures loneliness and bullying at nine; trains relentlessly; wins Wimbledon at 17; admits money motivates her but values being the best.

**Yuri Sharapov** — a father who gave up his comfort, worked hard in a foreign land, and stayed beside his daughter.

**One-word tags for quick revision:** Santosh = *grit + grace*; Maria = *focus + frankness*.

check.q: Which incident best shows Santosh's compassion?
options: Sharing her oxygen with a fellow climber
check.why: At an altitude where every breath counts, she shared oxygen to save another climber's life.

sections.md:
Both stories show that **reaching the top demands sacrifice** — Santosh gave up a conventional life and fought her family's expectations; Maria gave up her childhood home and her mother's presence.

**Similarities:**
- **Determination** and self-belief from a young age.
- **Breaking norms** — Santosh against gender expectations; Maria against age and loneliness.
- **Hard training** — Uttarkashi expeditions; Florida academy.
- **Patriotism** — tricolour on Everest; pride in Russia.

**Differences:**
- Santosh's motivation is **personal freedom and the spirit of adventure**; Maria is candid about **competition and money**.
- Santosh's family began reluctant; Maria's father was deeply involved from the start.
- Santosh's sport is a battle with nature; Maria's is head-to-head competition.

left.title: Santosh Yadav
points: Cleaned ~500 kg Himalayan garbage; Padma Shri

right.title: Maria Sharapova
points: Moved to Florida at 9 with father

check.q: Which quality is common to both Santosh and Maria?
options: Both showed strong determination and made sacrifices
check.why: Both pursued their goals with great determination, sacrificing comfort, convention or family life to reach the top.

sections.h: Thinking about language: word formation and personality words
sections.md:
**1. Nouns from adjectives/verbs with suffixes.** The exercises ask you to find words like these in the chapter and form more:

| Suffix | Examples |
|---|---|
| -ism | patriot → **patriotism**, optimist → optimism, hero → heroism |
| -ity | able → ability, popular → **popularity**, capable → capability, sincere → sincerity |
| -ment | achieve → **achievement**, encourage → encouragement, commit → commitment |
| -ness | happy → happiness, aware → **awareness**, kind → kindness |
| -ion | determine → **determination**, motivate → motivation, decide → decision |

**2. Adjectives that describe personality** — choose from the chapter's spirit: *tough, determined, resilient, compassionate, focused, competitive, unconventional, patriotic, modest, frank, courageous*. Practise: *Santosh was ____ enough to defy custom.* (courageous)

**3. Words with a positive or negative shade.** *Stubborn* (negative) vs *determined* (positive); *proud* vs *confident*; *pushy* vs *ambitious*. Writers choose the shade to show their attitude.

**4. Vocabulary**

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| conventional | following accepted customs |
| resolve | firm decision |
| expedition | an organised journey for a purpose |
| altitude | height above sea level |
| resilience | ability to recover from hardship |
| ecological | relating to the environment |
| prodigy | a young person with exceptional ability |
| poise | calm, graceful self-control |
| unwavering | steady, not changing |

check.q: Which is the correct noun form of 'patriotic'?
check.why: The suffix -ism turns 'patriot' into the abstract noun 'patriotism'.

sections.md:
**Speaking — interview role-play.** One student is a journalist, the other Santosh (or Maria). Good questions: *What made you choose mountaineering? What did you feel at the summit? How did you cope with loneliness? What would you tell a girl in a village who wants to play sport?* Answer in character, using facts from the chapter.

**Writing — a profile of an achiever (100–150 words).** Structure:
1. Hook — a striking moment (summit, final point).
2. Background — birthplace, family, early obstacles.
3. Struggle and training.
4. Achievement with dates.
5. Values and a closing message.

**Model opening:** *At dawn on a May morning in 1993, a young woman from a Haryana village stood on the roof of the world for the second time in a year...*

**Writing — diary entry.** Date, day, time; first person; feelings + events; short reflective close. Try: Maria's diary on her first lonely night in Florida.

**Did you know?** Everest's height was officially remeasured as **8,848.86 m** in 2020 by China and Nepal jointly — commonly rounded to 8,849 m.

check.q: Which is the best hook for an achiever's profile?
options: A striking moment, like the final point at Wimbledon
check.why: A dramatic moment pulls the reader in before background details are given.

sections.md:
**Q. Why was the baby girl not unwelcome in Santosh's family?** Unusually, her grandmother said the family did not want another son; after five boys, the family welcomed a daughter.

**Q. 'Santosh was a woman of great will power.' Justify. (60 words)** She refused early marriage and fought to study in Delhi; she joined mountaineering training without first asking permission, then convinced her father; she climbed Everest twice within a year and even shared oxygen to save a fellow climber. These show extraordinary will power and courage.

**Q. What sacrifices did Maria make to reach the top? (60 words)** She left Siberia at nine, lived without her mother for two years, endured loneliness and bullying at the academy, and spent long hours training. Her father worked hard to fund her. These sacrifices made her determined and ultimately led to her Wimbledon win at seventeen.

**Q. How did Santosh show concern for the environment?** She collected and brought down about 500 kg of garbage from the Himalayas.

**Q. Compare the two achievers. (120 words)** Use the comparison above: background → obstacles → training → achievement → values. End with your own view on what young people can learn.

check.why: She was barely twenty in 1992, then the youngest woman to climb Everest.

summary: Two-part chapter: Santosh Yadav (Part I) and Maria Sharapova (Part II).
Santosh was born in Joniyawas, Rewari (Haryana), the sixth child after five sons; her grandmother did not want another son.
She refused early marriage, studied in Delhi offering to pay her own fees, then at Maharani College, Jaipur (Kasturba Hostel).
Watching climbers in the Aravallis led her to the Nehru Institute of Mountaineering, Uttarkashi.
She climbed Everest in May 1992 and May 1993 — the first woman to do it twice.
She shared oxygen with a fellow climber and brought down about 500 kg of garbage.
She received the Padma Shri.
Maria Sharapova, born 1987 in Siberia, moved to Florida at nine with her father Yuri.
Her mother could not join for two years because of visa issues; Maria faced loneliness and bullying.
She won Wimbledon in 2004 at 17 and became world No. 1 in 2005.
She loves fashion, singing and Conan Doyle; she is patriotic and frankly competitive.
Language: nouns with -ism, -ity, -ment, -ness, -ion; personality adjectives.
Shared values: determination, sacrifice, self-belief, breaking norms.

rd-school-c9-english-b.ch8-kathmandu.title: Kathmandu — Vikram Seth
rd-school-c9-english-b.ch8-kathmandu.subtitle: Two temples, a noisy bazaar, and a flute-seller whose music speaks every language

sections.md:
After months of hitchhiking across China and Tibet, a young Indian traveller finally reaches **Kathmandu**. He is exhausted, a little dirty, and very happy. He has a little time before going home — and he spends it doing what all great travellers do: **watching**.

**"Kathmandu"** is an extract from **Vikram Seth**'s award-winning travelogue **From Heaven Lake: Travels Through Sinkiang and Tibet** (1983). In a few pages he visits two famous holy places, wanders a busy market, plans his journey home and ends with a meditation on a humble bamboo flute.

The chapter is a lesson in **travel writing**: precise observation, contrast, humour, and reflection. It's also a quiet picture of **Nepal's coexistence of Hinduism and Buddhism**.

**Before you read:** the textbook invites you to think about a pilgrimage or a trip you have made. What did you *see*, *hear*, *smell*, *taste*? Good travel writing captures all five senses — watch how Seth does it.

> This read: author, a complete retelling in order, the two temples compared, the bazaar, the journey-home decision, the flute passage, style, language exercises (compound words, punctuation, tense), writing tasks and model answers. Vikram Seth is a living author, so we retell — read his own words in the free official PDF linked at the end.

check.q: 'Kathmandu' is an extract from which book?
check.why: The chapter comes from Vikram Seth's travelogue From Heaven Lake: Travels Through Sinkiang and Tibet.

sections.md:
**Vikram Seth (born 1952, Calcutta/Kolkata)** is one of India's best-known writers in English. He studied at Doon School, Oxford and Stanford, and also studied in **Nanjing, China**, which is how the journey in *From Heaven Lake* began — he hitchhiked home from China through Tibet and Nepal.

**Major works:**
- *From Heaven Lake* (1983) — travelogue; won the Thomas Cook Travel Book Award.
- *The Golden Gate* (1986) — a novel written entirely in verse (sonnets!).
- *A Suitable Boy* (1993) — one of the longest single-volume novels in English, set in 1950s India.
- *An Equal Music* (1999) — a novel about musicians.
- *Beastly Tales from Here and There* — fables in verse, loved by students.

He was awarded the **Padma Shri** (2007).

**Did you know?** *A Suitable Boy* runs to about 1,350 pages — and was adapted for television in 2020.

check.q: Vikram Seth's novel written entirely in verse is —
check.why: The Golden Gate (1986) is a novel told in sonnet stanzas.

sections.md:
Seth first visits **Pashupatinath**, the famous **Hindu** temple of **Lord Shiva** (as Pashupati, 'lord of animals') on the banks of the **Bagmati** river. A sign announces that **only Hindus** may enter. What he finds is an atmosphere of **feverish confusion**:

- **Priests** hawking their services, **devotees** jostling, **flower-sellers** and **vendors** everywhere.
- A group of **saffron-clad Westerners** struggling for permission to go in; the policeman at the gate is not convinced they are Hindus.
- A **fight breaks out between two monkeys**; one chases the other, jumps onto a Shivalinga, screams around the temples and down to the river.
- A **corpse** is being cremated on the riverbank.
- A **washerwoman** sits at her work; **children bathe** in the river.
- From a balcony, someone drops a basket of old flowers and leaves into the river; they float down past a corpse being burnt.

**A legend:** a small shrine partly protrudes from the stone platform on the river bank. People believe that when it **emerges fully**, the goddess inside will escape and the **evil period of the Kaliyug** will end on earth.

Notice how Seth places the sacred and the everyday side by side — cremation, laundry, monkeys and prayer, all at once. He doesn't judge; he shows. That restraint is a mark of a good travel writer.

check.q: According to the belief described, what will happen when the small shrine emerges fully?
options: The goddess will escape and the Kaliyug will end
check.why: Locals believe that when the shrine fully emerges, the goddess will escape and the evil age of Kaliyug will come to an end.

sections.md:
Next, Seth visits the **Baudhnath stupa**, the great **Buddhist** shrine of Kathmandu. Here everything is different:

- An **immense, whitewashed dome**, ringed by **a road** and small shops, many owned by **Tibetan immigrants**: felt bags, Tibetan prints, silver jewellery.
- **No crowds** — a haven of quietness in the busy streets around.
- **Prayer flags** flutter; there is a sense of **stillness**.

The contrast is the point. Seth doesn't say one is better; he simply lets us feel two religious moods: Hindu **fervour** and Buddhist **serenity**. And both exist in one city — a picture of **religious coexistence**.

**Did you know?** Both Pashupatinath and Boudhanath are part of the Kathmandu Valley UNESCO World Heritage Site. Many Nepalis visit both — devotion in Nepal often crosses the Hindu–Buddhist line.

sections.h: Scene 3: the bazaar — noise, colour, commerce
sections.md:
Back in the city, Seth plunges into Kathmandu's **vivid, mercenary, religious** streets. In small shrines along the lanes, flowers and offerings; next to them, the products of modern trade:

- **Fruit-sellers, flute-sellers, hawkers** of postcards.
- **Shops selling Western cosmetics, film rolls, chocolate**; **copper utensils** and **Nepalese antiques**.
- **Film songs** blaring from radios; **car horns**; bicycle bells; vendors shouting.

He treats himself: a bar of **marzipan**, a **corn-on-the-cob** roasted in a charcoal brazier, a **love-story comic**, and even a **Reader's Digest**. He washes it all down with **Coca-Cola** and an orange drink — small pleasures after a hard journey across the Tibetan plateau, where such things were unavailable.

**What it shows about Seth:** he is honest and human — tired, a bit homesick, happy to indulge simple cravings. The narrator is not a lofty sage but a real young man, and that makes us trust him.

check.q: How does Seth describe Kathmandu's streets?
check.why: He calls Kathmandu vivid, mercenary and religious — colourful, commercial and full of small shrines.

sections.h: Scene 4: the decision to fly home
sections.md:
Seth now weighs how to get home to **Delhi**. The overland route is long and tiring: by **bus and train** to the Indian border, on to **Patna**, a boat across the **Ganga**, then trains through **Benares (Varanasi)**, **Allahabad (Prayagraj)** and **Agra** to Delhi. He feels too **exhausted and homesick** for days of such travel, so he decides to **fly**. He goes and buys an air ticket.

**Why this short scene matters:** a traveller who has hitchhiked across Tibet suddenly chooses comfort. It is a believable, human moment — the adventure is over, and home is calling. It also prepares us for the closing passage: an ending that is calm, reflective and a little wistful.

items.what: Start: tired, ready to go home
Bus and train to the Indian border
Boat across the Ganga
Train onward
More long rail journeys
Home — but Seth decides to fly instead

fig.caption: The long overland route Seth decided not to take

check.q: Why did Seth decide to fly to Delhi?
check.why: The overland journey would have been long and tiring; tired and homesick, he chose to fly.

sections.h: Scene 5: the flute-seller — music of the world
sections.md:
The chapter's most beautiful passage comes near the end. In a square near his hotel stands a **flute-seller** with a pole like a huge **porcupine**, its 'quills' made of **bamboo flutes** — forty or fifty of them.

Every now and then the seller stops, puts one to his lips, and plays a **slow, meditative** tune. He doesn't shout to sell; he simply plays, and his music cuts through the noise of the market. He plays **unhurriedly**, without calling out, and sells a flute now and then.

The sound makes Seth reflect: the flute is the **most universal and most particular** of sounds. Every culture has its flute:
- the **reed neh** (Middle East),
- the **recorder** (Europe),
- the **Japanese shakuhachi**,
- the deep **bansuri** of Hindustani music,
- the clear or breathy **flutes of South America**,
- the high-pitched **Chinese** flutes.

Each has its own **fingering and playing technique**, but all share the most basic thing: **human breath** turned into music. Seth says the flute, more than any other instrument, gives voice to the **breath of human beings** — and that connects all people.

**This is the chapter's emotional summit:** after all the contrasts — Hindu/Buddhist, noise/quiet, East/West goods — the flute shows what is **common to all humanity**.

sections.md:
How does Seth make a short visit so vivid?

1. **Precise details** — not 'a crowd' but priests, westerners in saffron, a washerwoman, a monkey on a Shivalinga.
2. **Contrast** — Pashupatinath vs Baudhnath; noise vs one flute; traditional vs Western goods.
3. **Gentle humour** — monkeys fighting; the policeman deciding who is Hindu; his junk-food treats.
4. **Lists** — piling up sensory images to recreate the bazaar.
5. **Reflection** — the flute passage moves from description to philosophy.
6. **Present tense** in places, giving immediacy, as if we stand beside him.
7. **Personal voice** — tired, curious, honest about small cravings.
8. **Simile and imagery** — the flute pole 'like a porcupine'; the shrine 'emerging'.

sections.md:
**1. Compound words.** Seth uses many: *saffron-clad*, *corn-on-the-cob*, *flute-seller*, *whitewashed*, *love-story comic*, *high-pitched*. A compound joins two or more words into one meaning; hyphens often join compound adjectives before a noun (*a high-pitched flute*, but *the flute is high pitched* is also seen). Make your own: *rain-soaked street, sweet-smelling incense, sun-baked courtyard*.

**2. Punctuation for lists.** The bazaar passage piles up items with **commas**, and uses a **colon** to introduce a list and **semicolons** to separate longer list items. Try: *The lane was full of noise: vendors shouting; radios blaring film songs; bicycle bells ringing without pause.*

**3. Tense choice.** Seth narrates many scenes in the **simple present** (*a monkey jumps onto the Shivalinga*) — the 'historic present' — which makes travel writing feel live. Rewrite a past-tense paragraph of your own trip in the present and notice the change.

**4. Words for sounds and movement.** *jostle, hawk, scream, blare, flutter, float*. Strong verbs do more work than adjectives.

**Vocabulary**

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| hawk | sell goods by calling out |
| feverish | hurried, excited |
| sanctum | inner holy place |
| haven | place of safety and peace |
| mercenary | concerned mainly with money |
| brazier | a metal container for burning coal |
| porcupine | rodent covered with sharp quills |
| meditative | thoughtful, calm |
| fervour | intense religious feeling |

check.why: 'Saffron-clad' joins two words with a hyphen to describe the Westerners dressed in saffron.

sections.md:
**Travel account (120–150 words).** Pick a market, temple, mosque, gurdwara, church or fair you know — say Chandni Chowk, the Golden Temple, Mysuru Dasara or a village haat. Plan:
1. Arrival — first impression in one striking sentence.
2. Sights — three precise details, not general words.
3. Sounds and smells — at least two.
4. A small human moment — a child, a vendor, an animal.
5. Reflection — what the place made you feel or think.

**Model opening:** *The lanes of Chandni Chowk do not let you walk; they carry you — past a man frying jalebis in a wok wide as a cartwheel, past bangles stacked like rainbows...*

**Speaking idea:** describe aloud, for one minute, a place in your town to a visitor who has never been to India. Your classmates should be able to 'see' it.

check.q: Which detail would best improve a travel account?
options: 'A barefoot boy balanced a tray of chai glasses on his head.'
check.why: Precise, concrete detail creates a picture, exactly as Seth does.

sections.md:
**Q. Name the two temples Seth visits and the faith of each.** Pashupatinath — Hindu, dedicated to Lord Shiva; Baudhnath stupa — Buddhist.

**Q. Contrast the atmosphere at Pashupatinath and Baudhnath. (60 words)** Pashupatinath is full of feverish confusion — priests, hawkers, devotees, monkeys, westerners trying to enter, a cremation on the riverbank. Baudhnath, by contrast, is a calm, quiet haven: a great white stupa ringed by Tibetan shops, with little crowding. One shows fervour; the other serenity.

**Q. What reflections does the flute-seller inspire in Seth? (60 words)** The flute's sound makes him think of flutes across cultures — bansuri, shakuhachi, recorder, neh, South American and Chinese flutes. Each differs in technique, but all are played by human breath. The flute thus becomes a symbol of shared humanity.

**Q. How does the flute-seller sell his flutes?** He does not shout; he occasionally plays a slow, thoughtful tune and lets the music attract buyers.

**Q. What is the route Seth considers before flying?** Bus and train to the border, Patna, a boat across the Ganga, trains through Benares, Allahabad and Agra to Delhi.

check.q: 'Mercenary' in 'vivid, mercenary, religious' suggests the streets are —
check.why: Mercenary here means money-minded — the streets are full of commerce and trade.

summary: 'Kathmandu' is from Vikram Seth's travelogue From Heaven Lake (1983).

Its atmosphere is feverish: priests, hawkers, westerners, a monkey fight, a cremation, a washerwoman.

Kathmandu's streets are vivid, mercenary and religious; Seth enjoys marzipan, corn, comics, Coca-Cola.
He decides to fly home to Delhi rather than make the long overland journey via Patna, Benares and Agra.
A flute-seller with a pole of bamboo flutes plays unhurried tunes.

rd-school-c9-english-b.ch9-if-i-were-you.title: If I Were You — Douglas James
rd-school-c9-english-b.ch9-if-i-were-you.subtitle: A killer plans to steal an actor's identity. The actor has one weapon: his wit.

sections.h: A gun in a quiet cottage
sections.md:
A man is packing in his lonely country cottage. The door opens. A stranger steps in — holding a **revolver**. He has been watching the house. He knows the man lives alone. He knows his height, his build, his voice. And he has a chilling plan: **kill him and become him**.

This is the set-up of **"If I Were You"**, a short one-act **play** by **Douglas James**, the last chapter of *Beehive*. It is a battle not of guns but of **brains** — and of **acting**. The victim, **Vincent Gerrard**, is a playwright and actor. To survive, he must give the performance of his life.

**Before you read:** the textbook asks what you would do if you came face to face with an armed stranger. Most of us would freeze. Keep that honest answer in mind — it makes Gerrard's calm even more astonishing.

> In this read: what a one-act play is, the characters, a complete scene-by-scene retelling, how Gerrard wins, dramatic techniques, themes, the language exercises (informal speech, contractions, idioms), a guide to performing it, and model answers. The play is still in copyright, so we retell it in our own words — read the script in the free official PDF linked at the end.

check.q: What is the Intruder's plan?
options: To kill Gerrard and take on his identity
To hire Gerrard for a play
To hide in the cottage for a night
check.why: The Intruder, wanted for murder, plans to kill Gerrard and live as him so the police stop hunting him.

sections.md:
A play is written to be **performed**. When you read one, notice:

- **Characters** list at the start.
- **Stage directions** in italics/brackets — they tell actors what to do and how to speak (*smiling*, *with a sneer*), and describe the set.
- **Dialogue** carries the whole story; there's no narrator.
- **Dramatic tension** builds through conflict and suspense.

A **one-act play** is short and focused: one setting, a few characters, a single crisis that rises to a climax and resolves quickly. Its plot follows the classic curve: **exposition → rising action → climax → falling action → resolution**.

**Characters in this play:**
- **Gerrard** — a playwright and actor, living alone in a remote cottage.
- **Intruder** — a criminal on the run who resembles Gerrard in build.

**Setting:** A sparsely furnished room in Gerrard's cottage, in a lonely part of the countryside. Evening. Gerrard is packing a suitcase.

options: How characters move and speak, and what the set looks like
check.why: Stage directions guide actors on actions, tone and the set, since a play has no narrator.

sections.h: Scenes 1–2: the entrance and the Intruder's homework
sections.md:
**1. The entrance.** Gerrard is packing. The Intruder enters, gun in hand. Gerrard is strikingly **calm**: rather than panicking, he responds with **cool, witty remarks**, asking whether this is a social call or a hold-up, and teasing the stranger about his melodramatic manner. The Intruder is irritated — he wants Gerrard to be afraid, and he warns him that he is not here for jokes. Gerrard asks what he wants; the Intruder replies, in effect, that he wants Gerrard's *life* — not his money.

**2. The homework.** The Intruder shows he has watched the cottage carefully. He knows Gerrard's name, that he lives **alone**, rarely sees anyone, keeps odd hours, drives a car, gets supplies **delivered**, and **pays bills by post**. Tradesmen hardly see his face. He boasts that he has studied Gerrard's voice and manner too. Gerrard listens, says little, and lets the man talk — every boast tells him something.

**Did you know?** In drama, the opening minutes are called the **exposition**: the audience learns who, where and what the problem is. Here it is done entirely through tense, funny dialogue.

check.q: Why did the Intruder think he could easily take Gerrard's place?
options: Gerrard lived alone, rarely met people, and had supplies delivered
Gerrard was leaving the country for ever
The police had no photo of him
check.why: He had found out that Gerrard lived a solitary life and was rarely seen, so few would notice the switch.

sections.h: Scenes 3–4: the confession and the plan
sections.md:
**3. The confession.** Asked who he is, the Intruder admits he is a **killer**: he shot a **policeman**, and the police are hunting him. He complains bitterly about his hard life and blames society — a hint of self-pity Gerrard notices.

**4. The plan revealed.** He will **kill Gerrard**, dispose of the body, and **take his place**. Their height and build are similar; with Gerrard's car and clothes and his habit of being unseen, no one will know. With a new identity, the man the police are chasing will simply 'vanish'. That is the title's irony: he literally wants to *be* Gerrard — 'if I were you' turns from a polite phrase of advice into a death threat.

All the while, Gerrard keeps him talking — and, listening, he learns his weaknesses: the Intruder is **impatient**, **vain** about his cleverness, and **frightened of the police**. That last weakness is the door Gerrard will now push open.

check.q: What crime had the Intruder already committed?
check.why: He confesses that he killed a policeman and is on the run.

sections.md:
**5. The bluff.** Now Gerrard begins his performance. He calmly tells the Intruder that taking his identity would be a **terrible mistake** — because Gerrard himself is **a crook on the run**! His lonely life, odd hours, deliveries and secretiveness are not shyness: he is *hiding*. He hints that he too is wanted for a serious crime, a killing, and that the police are close.

He explains the packed suitcase: he was about to make a **getaway** that very evening. He even explains his disguises and his habit of never being seen in daylight as the tricks of a man on the run. The message to the Intruder is chilling: *become me, and you inherit my crimes — and the police will hang you for them.*

**6. Proof?** The Intruder is suspicious and demands proof. Gerrard points to the packed bag and to the **car** waiting in the garage. Then he raises the pressure: the police, he suggests, may arrive at any moment. The Intruder — the man who fears the police above all — grows rattled. Gerrard offers to help them *both* escape: there is a way out to the garage through a door in the room.

check.q: What story did Gerrard invent?
options: That he was a police officer
That he too was a criminal on the run, wanted by the police
That he had a twin brother
check.why: He bluffed that he was a wanted crook himself, so taking his identity would bring the police straight to the Intruder.

sections.h: Scenes 7–8: the trap and the phone call
sections.md:
**7. The trap.** The Intruder, now nervous and in a hurry, agrees to go by the 'exit'. Gerrard indicates the door; the Intruder opens it and moves to look — it is a **cupboard**. Gerrard **pushes him in and locks it**. The man with the gun is now trapped, banging and shouting inside. The threat is over without a shot being fired.

**8. The final touch.** Gerrard picks up the **telephone** and, in a cheerful, professional tone, calls a contact from his theatre world. He talks as if the whole episode were wonderful material — the plot for his next play, a real-life thriller with a surprise third act. The audience realises: **it was all an act**. Gerrard is no criminal; he is an actor and playwright who used his craft to survive, and then, true to form, turned it into a story. (In real life, the next call would surely be to the police — and the play implies they will come for the locked-up killer.)

sections.md:
**Vincent Gerrard**
- **Calm under pressure** — he jokes with a man holding a gun.
- **Witty and sarcastic** — his replies irritate and unsettle the Intruder.
- **Quick-thinking and resourceful** — he invents a convincing counter-story on the spot.
- **A skilled actor** — his 'performance' as a fellow criminal saves his life.
- **Observant** — he reads the Intruder's vanity and fear and uses them.
- **A true artist** — even danger becomes material for his writing.

**The Intruder**
- **Ruthless** — has already killed a policeman; ready to kill again.
- **Clever but over-confident** — has researched Gerrard but underestimates him.
- **Impatient and nervous** — easily rattled at the mention of police.
- **Self-pitying** — speaks of the hard life that made him a criminal.

**Contrast:** brute force vs intelligence. The gun loses to the mind.

left.title: Gerrard
points: Turns the tables with a story

check.q: Which quality of Gerrard is most important to his survival?
options: Presence of mind and acting skill
check.why: His calm presence of mind and skill at acting let him invent a believable story and trap the Intruder.

sections.md:
**Techniques:**
- **Suspense** — will Gerrard be shot? The gun is on stage from the start.
- **Dramatic irony** — the Intruder thinks *he* is in control; the audience slowly suspects Gerrard is playing him.
- **Reversal (twist)** — the hunter becomes the trapped.
- **Wit and dialogue** — humour relieves tension and characterises Gerrard.
- **Props** — gun, suitcase, cupboard, telephone: each matters to the plot (a principle called 'Chekhov's gun').

**Themes:**
1. **Presence of mind** — keeping cool in danger.
2. **Intelligence over force.**
3. **Identity** — can someone really 'become' another person? The title asks what it would mean to be someone else.
4. **Crime and its consequences** — the Intruder's past crime traps him in fear.
5. **Art and life** — an actor uses his art to survive, then treats the experience like a scene from a play.

**The title, three ways:** (a) the polite advice phrase 'if I were you, I would…', which Gerrard mocks; (b) the Intruder's literal wish to *be* Gerrard; (c) Gerrard 'being' a criminal for a while — the actor becoming someone else.

**Real-life safety note:** In a real emergency, don't play hero; your safety comes first — move away if you can and call **112** (India's emergency number).

check.q: The sudden switch where the Intruder becomes the one trapped is an example of —
check.why: The play's climax reverses the situation: the would-be killer ends up locked in the cupboard.

sections.md:
**1. Informal and colloquial speech.** Both men speak in everyday, sometimes slangy English. Words like *mug* (fool), *smart* (clever), *cut the funny stuff* (stop joking), *on the run*, *a getaway* are typical of crime dramas. In formal writing you would say *Stop joking*, *escaping from the police*, *an escape*.

**2. Contractions.** Speech uses *I'm, you're, he's, don't, can't, won't, I'll, it's* — they make dialogue sound natural. In a formal letter, expand them (*I am, do not, will not*). Remember: **it's** = it is; **its** = belonging to it.

**3. Tone in stage directions.** Words such as *smiling, sneering, quickly, angrily, with mock politeness* tell the actor *how* to say a line. Change the direction and the same line changes meaning: 'You're clever' said *admiringly* vs *sarcastically*.

**4. Idioms and phrases**

| Phrase | Meaning |
|---|---|
| on the run | escaping from the police |
| take somebody for a ride | deceive someone |
| turn the tables | reverse a situation to gain the upper hand |
| keep one's head | stay calm |
| the game is up | the trick has been discovered |

**5. Vocabulary**

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| intruder | someone who enters without permission |
| sarcastic | using irony to mock |
| sneer | a contemptuous smile |
| bluff | pretend in order to deceive |
| props | objects used on stage |

check.q: 'Turn the tables' means —
options: Reverse a situation to gain the advantage
check.why: Gerrard turns the tables: the man who held all the power ends up locked away.

sections.h: Act it out: a performance guide
sections.md:
The textbook encourages you to **perform** the play. Some tips:

- **Casting:** two actors, plus a director who reads the stage directions aloud in rehearsal.
- **Set:** a table, a chair, a suitcase, a 'cupboard' door (a cardboard screen works), a telephone. Use a toy or rolled-up paper for the gun — never anything that looks real in public.
- **Gerrard's voice:** relaxed, amused, never hurried — until the final push, which must be quick and sudden.
- **The Intruder's voice:** rough, tense, getting faster and higher as fear grows.
- **Pauses:** the most powerful moment is the silence after Gerrard says he too is wanted. Hold it for three seconds.
- **The phone call:** play it brightly; the contrast with the danger makes the audience laugh with relief.

**Writing task idea:** rewrite the climax from the Intruder's point of view inside the cupboard — his thoughts as he realises he has been fooled (100 words). Or write the next morning's newspaper report: *Actor Traps Wanted Killer in Cupboard*.

check.q: Why does the bright phone call work well on stage?
options: Its cheerful tone contrasts with the danger and releases tension
check.why: After the suspense, the playful call lets the audience relax and see that Gerrard was performing all along.

sections.md:
**Q. What is Gerrard's reaction when he first sees the Intruder?** He is calm and witty, asking jokingly whether it is a social call or a hold-up; he shows no fear.

**Q. How did the Intruder plan to escape the law? (40 words)** He planned to kill Gerrard, dispose of his body and live as Gerrard, since Gerrard lived alone and rarely met anyone. With a new identity, he hoped the police would stop searching for the man who had shot a policeman.

**Q. Why did the Intruder believe Gerrard's story?** It fitted the facts he himself had gathered — the lonely life, odd hours, deliveries, the packed bag and the car — and it played on his greatest fear, the police.

**Q. How did Gerrard outwit the Intruder? (120 words)** Plan: calm, witty opening → letting the Intruder reveal his plan and fears → inventing the story of being a criminal himself → packed bag and car as 'proof' → the threat of police → offering an escape route → locking him in the cupboard → the casual phone call showing it was an act.

check.q: 'Bluff' means —
options: To pretend in order to deceive
check.why: Gerrard bluffs — he pretends to be a criminal so the Intruder believes taking his identity is dangerous.

summary: 'If I Were You' is a one-act play by Douglas James.
Characters: Gerrard (playwright-actor) and the Intruder (a killer on the run).
Setting: Gerrard's lonely country cottage; he is packing a suitcase.
The Intruder, armed with a revolver, has studied Gerrard's solitary life.
He admits killing a policeman and plans to kill Gerrard and take his identity.
Gerrard stays calm and witty, keeping the Intruder talking and noting his fear of the police.
Gerrard bluffs that he too is a wanted criminal about to escape.
He uses the suitcase and a waiting car as 'proof' and offers an escape route.
He tricks the Intruder into a cupboard and locks him in.
His casual phone call reveals it was all a performance.
Themes: presence of mind, intelligence over force, identity, art and life.
Techniques: suspense, dramatic irony, reversal, witty dialogue, purposeful props.
Language: colloquial speech, contractions, idioms, tone in stage directions.

when the audience understands more than a character

rd-school-c9-english-c.grammar-modals-de.title: Grammar: Modals and Determiners
rd-school-c9-english-c.grammar-modals-de.subtitle: Can, could, must, might… and a, the, some, few, much — the small words that carry big meaning

sections.md:
Compare:

- *You **may** leave.* (permission)
- *You **must** leave.* (order)
- *You **might** leave.* (a possibility)
- *You **should** leave.* (advice)

Same subject, same verb — four completely different messages. Those small helpers are **modals**.

Now compare:

- *I have **a few** friends.* (some — good!)
- *I have **few** friends.* (hardly any — sad.)

One tiny word — **a** — flips the mood. These are **determiners**.

This read covers both topics as in the Class 9 grammar syllabus: **Part A — Modals** (rules, meanings, past modals, semi-modals, modals in real situations), **Part B — Determiners** (articles, demonstratives, possessives, quantifiers, numbers, distributives), then **Part C — exam formats** (gap-filling, editing, omission, sentence transformation) with worked examples.

check.q: 'You should see a doctor' expresses —
check.why: 'Should' is used to give advice or a recommendation.

sections.h: Part A: What makes a modal a modal
sections.md:
**Modal auxiliaries:** can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must, ought to (plus semi-modals: need, dare, used to, have to).

**Rules:**
1. A modal is followed by the **base form (V1)** of the verb: *She can **swim***. ✗ *She can swims / can to swim*.
2. Modals **don't change** with the subject: *I can, he can, they can*. (No *cans*.)
3. Negatives add *not*: *cannot (can't), should not (shouldn't), must not (mustn't)*.
4. Questions invert: ***Can** you help me?*
5. **Ought to** is the exception that keeps *to*: *You **ought to** respect elders.*
6. For the **past**, many modals use *have + V3*: *You **should have told** me.* *She **must have missed** the bus.*
7. Two modals never stand together: ✗ *will can* → ✓ *will be able to*.
8. Modals have **no -ing or -ed forms**; we borrow other verbs: *be able to*, *have to*, *be allowed to*. *I **will be able to** come tomorrow.* *We **had to** wait.*

check.q: Which sentence is correct?
check.why: Modals are followed by the base form of the verb and don't take -s: he can speak.

sections.md:
| Meaning | Modal(s) | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Ability (present)** | can | Neeraj **can** throw a javelin over 89 m. |
| **Ability (past)** | could | As a child she **could** climb trees easily. |
| **Permission** | may (formal), can (informal), could (polite) | **May** I come in, ma'am? **Can** I borrow your pen? |
| **Polite request** | could, would, will | **Could** you pass the salt? **Would** you open the window? |
| **Possibility** | may, might (less sure), could | It **may** rain today. He **might** be at the library. |
| **Certainty / deduction (positive)** | must | The lights are on; they **must** be home. |
| **Deduction (negative)** | can't | That **can't** be Rohan — he's in Goa. |
| **Obligation (strong, from speaker)** | must | You **must** wear a helmet. |
| **Obligation (external rule)** | have to | We **have to** wear uniforms on Mondays. |
| **Prohibition** | must not | You **must not** use phones in the exam hall. |
| **No necessity** | needn't, don't have to | You **needn't** bring lunch; it's provided. |
| **Advice / duty** | should, ought to | You **should** drink more water. We **ought to** help the needy. |
| **Offer / suggestion** | shall (I/we) | **Shall** I carry your bag? **Shall** we start? |
| **Future / willingness / promise** | will | I **will** finish it by tonight. |
| **Determination / command (formal)** | shall (2nd/3rd person) | You **shall** obey the rules. |
| **Past habit** | would, used to | Grandpa **would** tell us stories every night. |
| **Wish / hypothesis** | would | If I had wings, I **would** fly. |
| **Purpose** | may/might, can/could | He works hard **so that** he **may** succeed. |

**Key contrast — must not vs needn't:** *You mustn't run* = it's forbidden. *You needn't run* = it's not necessary (you can if you like).
