check.q: The teacher said, "Water boils at 100 °C." — Reported form?
options: The teacher said that water boiled at 100 °C.
The teacher said that water boils at 100 °C.
The teacher said that water had boiled at 100 °C.
The teacher told that water boils at 100 °C.
check.why: A universal scientific fact keeps its present tense even after a past reporting verb.

sections.md:
Words that point to *now* and *here* lose their meaning once the moment has passed. If your cousin in Jaipur said "here" on the phone, "here" was Jaipur — not your room in Chennai. So we swap them:

| Direct | Reported |
|---|---|
| now | then / at that time |
| today | that day |
| tonight | that night |
| yesterday | the day before / the previous day |
| tomorrow | the next day / the following day |
| last week | the week before / the previous week |
| next month | the following month |
| ago | before / earlier |
| here | there |
| this | that |
| these | those |
| come | go (when the place changes) |

Example: *Sana said, "I bought this kurta here yesterday."* → *Sana said that she had bought that kurta there the day before.*

### Common sense beats the table

If you report on the **same day** in the **same place**, you do not need to change them. If at 11 a.m. your friend says, "The match is today," and at noon you tell your brother, "Rohan said the match is today," that is perfectly correct English. Exams, however, usually assume a later time and place, so make the standard change unless the question says otherwise.

**Did you know?** Linguists call words like *here, now, this, you* **deictic** words — from a Greek word meaning "to point". Their meaning depends entirely on who is speaking, where and when.
keyTerms: Deictic words — pointing words whose meaning depends on the speaker's time and place
the previous day — standard reported form of yesterday
the following day — standard reported form of tomorrow

check.q: He said, "I will meet you here tomorrow." (to me) — reported?
options: He told me that he would meet me there the next day.
He told me that I would meet him here tomorrow.
He said me he will meet me there the next day.
He told me that he will meet you here tomorrow.
check.why: I → he, you → me, will → would, here → there, tomorrow → the next day, and told takes the listener me.

sections.md:
A reported question is **not a question any more** — it is a statement *about* a question. So it ends with a full stop, and the word order goes back to normal (subject before verb).

### 1. Yes/No questions → if / whether

- *She said to me, "Are you ready?"* → *She asked me **if** I was ready.*
- *He said, "Did you see the comet?"* → *He asked **whether** I had seen the comet.*

Notice that *do/does/did* vanish: the helping verb was only there to build the question.

### 2. Wh-questions → the wh-word joins the clauses

- *The guard asked, "Where are you going?"* → *The guard asked where I was going.* (not *where was I going*)
- *Mother asked, "Why did you come late?"* → *Mother asked why I had come late.*
- *Ira asked Dev, "How many runs has Kohli scored?"* → *Ira asked Dev how many runs Kohli had scored.*

### Reporting verbs for questions

*asked, enquired, wanted to know, wondered* — never *said* or *told*.

### Three errors examiners love

1. Keeping the question mark: *He asked where I lived?* ✗
2. Keeping question word order: *He asked where did I live.* ✗
3. Adding *that*: *He asked that whether I was free.* ✗

**Did you know?** *If* and *whether* are usually interchangeable, but use *whether* before *or not* and after prepositions: *They argued about whether to go.*

check.q: The doctor said to Anil, "How long have you had this cough?"
options: The doctor asked Anil how long had he had that cough.
The doctor asked Anil how long he had had that cough.
The doctor told Anil that how long he had had this cough?
The doctor asked Anil if how long he had that cough.
check.why: The wh-word links the clauses, word order becomes subject + verb, have had shifts to had had, and this becomes that.

sections.md:
For imperative sentences (orders, requests, advice) we use a **verb of command or request + object + to-infinitive**.

| Mood | Reporting verb | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Order | ordered, commanded, told | The officer said, "Stand in a line." → The officer **ordered** us **to stand** in a line. |
| Request | requested, asked, begged | She said, "Please lend me your notes." → She **requested** me **to lend** her my notes. |
| Advice | advised, urged | Dad said, "Drink more water." → Dad **advised** me **to drink** more water. |
| Warning | warned | The sign said, "Don't cross the track." → It **warned** people **not to cross** the track. |

**Negative commands:** *don't + verb* becomes **not to + verb**. *"Don't shout," said the librarian.* → *The librarian told us not to shout.*

**Drop *please*** — its meaning is now carried by *requested*.

### Let's: suggestions

*Let's* sentences become **suggested / proposed + that + should** or **suggested + -ing**:

- *Meera said, "Let's go to the Hampi ruins."* → *Meera suggested that we should go to the Hampi ruins.* / *Meera suggested going to the Hampi ruins.*

Never write *suggested us to go* — *suggest* does not take an object + to.

If *let* means *allow* (*"Let him play"*), report it with *allow*: *He asked them to let him play.*

right.title: Reported form
points: told me to close the window
warned us not to be late
suggested that we should start then

check.q: The coach said to the players, "Don't waste time."
options: The coach told the players don't waste time.
The coach told the players not to waste time.
The coach said the players to not waste time.
The coach told the players that not waste time.
check.why: Negative commands become not + to-infinitive after told/ordered/warned + object.

sections.md:
Exclamations carry feeling, so we report the feeling with a verb like **exclaimed with joy, exclaimed with sorrow, cried out, wished, prayed, thanked, congratulated**.

- *"Hurrah! We have won the trophy!" said the boys.* → *The boys **exclaimed with joy** that they had won the trophy.*
- *"Alas! The old banyan has fallen," said Grandpa.* → *Grandpa **exclaimed sadly** that the old banyan had fallen.*
- *"What a beautiful sunset!" she said.* → *She **exclaimed** that it was a very beautiful sunset.* (What/How a … becomes *very*.)
- *"May you live long!" said the grandmother.* → *The grandmother **blessed** me **that** I might live long.* / *wished me a long life.*
- *"Thank you," he said to me.* → *He **thanked** me.*
- *"Good morning, sir," said Asha.* → *Asha **wished** the teacher good morning.*

Interjections like *Oh, Alas, Wow, Hurrah* disappear; the reporting verb and an adverb carry them.

### Reporting a dialogue

Exams often give a four-line conversation and ask you to report it as a paragraph. Use varied verbs and connectors so it reads naturally:

> **Direct:**
> Shopkeeper: What would you like?
> Tara: Do you have notebooks with 200 pages?
> Shopkeeper: Yes, but only in blue.
> Tara: Give me three, please.

> **Reported:** The shopkeeper asked Tara what she would like. Tara asked whether he had notebooks with 200 pages. The shopkeeper **replied that** he did, but only in blue. Tara then **requested** him **to give** her three.

Useful verbs: *replied, answered, added, explained, agreed, refused, admitted, complained, promised, insisted, apologised.*

**Did you know?** Good journalists rarely use *said* twice in a row. Varying the verb also tells the reader *how* something was said.

check.q: "What a clever idea!" said Nisha. Best reported form:
options: Nisha said what a clever idea.
Nisha exclaimed that it was a very clever idea.
Nisha asked what a clever idea it was.
Nisha exclaimed what a clever idea!
check.why: Exclamations use exclaimed, What a… becomes very, and the sentence ends with a full stop.

sections.h: Mixed sentences, yes/no answers and reverse conversion
sections.md:
### Mixed sentences

Real speech mixes types. Report each part with its own verb and join them with *and*, *but*, *and added that*, *and asked*:

- *"I'm tired. Can you carry my bag?" said Dadi.* → *Dadi said that she was tired **and asked** me **if** I could carry her bag.*
- *"Sit down. Why are you standing?" said the teacher.* → *The teacher told me to sit down **and asked** why I was standing.*

### Short answers: yes and no

*Yes* and *no* vanish; use *replied in the affirmative/negative* or repeat the helping verb:

- *"Are you coming?" "Yes."* → *He asked if I was coming. I **replied that I was**.*
- *"Have you finished?" "No."* → *She asked whether I had finished. I **said that I had not**.*

### Vocatives (forms of address)

Words like *Sir, friends, my child, Ravi* used to address someone become part of the reporting clause: *"Friends, listen to me," said the leader.* → *The leader **addressed his friends and asked them** to listen to him.* / *Addressing them as friends, the leader asked them to listen.*

### Must, should and ought

- *must* (obligation) → *had to*: *"You must wear a mask," said the nurse.* → *The nurse said that I had to wear a mask.*
- *must* (deduction or permanent rule) usually stays: *He said that it must be late.*
- *should, ought to* stay unchanged.

### Reverse conversion: reported → direct

Some questions ask you to rebuild the exact words. Work backwards:

1. Choose the speaker's type (statement, question, command).
2. Put back the speaker's own pronouns (*he* → *I*, *me/us* → *you*).
3. Undo the backshift (*was* → *am*, *had seen* → *saw / have seen*, *would* → *will*).
4. Restore time words (*that day* → *today*, *the next day* → *tomorrow*).
5. Add quotation marks, a comma and the right end mark.

*The old man asked the boy whether he could help him cross the road.* → *The old man said to the boy, "Can you help me cross the road?"*

*She told us not to touch the painting.* → *She said to us, "Don't touch the painting."*

check.q: "Are you hungry?" asked Mother. "Yes," said Ravi. Best report of Ravi's answer:
options: Ravi said yes that he was.
Ravi said that yes he is hungry?
check.why: 'Yes' is dropped and replaced by a short clause that repeats the helping verb: he was.

sections.h: Integrated exam skills: gap-fills, editing and reports
sections.md:
The Class 9 paper rarely asks "change this sentence" alone. More often you will see:

**1. Dialogue completion.** A conversation is given, and a report with blanks: *The teacher asked Rahul (a) ______.* You must pick the right link word, tense and pronoun. Read the whole dialogue first so you know who is speaking to whom.

**2. Editing.** A paragraph with one error per line, often a tense not shifted or *said* used with an object.

**3. Notice / report writing** where you must report what an official said at an event.

### A five-step routine for any conversion

1. **Identify the sentence type** — statement, question (yes/no or wh), command/request, exclamation.
2. **Pick the reporting verb** — said/told, asked, ordered/requested/advised, exclaimed.
3. **Choose the linker** — that, if/whether, wh-word, to/not to.
4. **Shift** person (SON), tense (if reporting verb is past), and time/place words.
5. **Punctuate** — remove quotation marks, end with a full stop.

### Worked mini-dialogue

> Grandmother: Where were you all evening?
> Ishaan: I was practising at the cricket academy.
> Grandmother: Eat your dinner before it gets cold.

> Grandmother asked Ishaan where he had been all evening. Ishaan replied that he had been practising at the cricket academy. Grandmother told him to eat his dinner before it got cold.

Notice *gets* → *got*: the time clause also backshifts.

check.q: Find the error: "She asked me that whether I had finished my homework."
check.why: Reported yes/no questions are joined with if or whether alone; adding that is wrong.

workedExamples.q: Convert: Neha said, "I am reading a novel by R. K. Narayan now."
workedExamples.answer: Neha said that she was reading a novel by R. K. Narayan then.

workedExamples.q: Convert: The conductor said to the passengers, "Have you got your tickets?"
steps: you → they; have got → had got
workedExamples.answer: The conductor asked the passengers if they had got their tickets.

workedExamples.q: Convert: Father said to me, "Why didn't you call me yesterday?"
workedExamples.answer: Father asked me why I had not called him the previous day.

workedExamples.q: Convert: "Please don't disturb the baby," Mother said to us.
steps: Negative request → requested us not to
workedExamples.answer: Mother requested us not to disturb the baby.

workedExamples.q: Convert: Arjun said, "Let's play chess this evening."
workedExamples.answer: Arjun suggested that they should play chess that evening.

workedExamples.q: Convert: Kavya says, "I can solve this puzzle."
steps: Reporting verb is present (says) → no backshift
I → she; this stays this (same moment)
workedExamples.answer: Kavya says that she can solve this puzzle.

workedExamples.q: Convert: "I have lost my ticket. Will you lend me some money?" said Ali to Sam.
steps: Statement: told Sam that he had lost his ticket
Question: and asked if he would lend him some money
workedExamples.answer: Ali told Sam that he had lost his ticket and asked if he would lend him some money.

summary: Direct speech gives exact words in quotation marks; reported speech gives the meaning in the reporter's sentence.
Three things shift: person, tense and time/place words.
SON: first person follows the subject (speaker), second person follows the object (listener), third person usually stays.
After a past reporting verb, tenses move one step back (backshift); past perfect stays.
No backshift for present/future reporting verbs or universal truths.
will→would, can→could, may→might, must→had to; could/would/should/might stay.
now→then, today→that day, yesterday→the previous day, tomorrow→the next day, here→there, this→that.
Told needs a listener; said does not take a direct listener.
Yes/no questions use if/whether; wh-questions use the wh-word; no question mark and normal word order.
Commands and requests: ordered/requested/advised + object + (not) to + verb.
Let's → suggested that we should / suggested + -ing.
Exclamations: exclaimed with joy/sorrow; interjections are dropped; What a… becomes very.
Mixed sentences: report each part with its own verb, joined by 'and asked', 'and added that'.
Yes/No answers become short clauses: replied that he was / that she had not.
In dialogues, vary verbs: replied, added, explained, agreed, refused, promised.

glossary.d: Moving a verb one tense back in reported speech
Said, told, asked, ordered, etc.
A sentence that gives a command or request
A word expressing feeling, like Alas! or Hurrah!
A word used to address someone directly, like 'Sir' or 'friends'

rd-school-c9-english-d.reading-skills.title: Unseen Passages: Reading Like a Detective
rd-school-c9-english-d.reading-skills.subtitle: A passage you have never seen, ten minutes, and full marks — here is how

sections.h: Why the unseen passage scares people (and why it shouldn't)
sections.md:
Every other part of the English paper rewards what you prepared at home. The unseen passage seems to reward nothing — the text is a surprise, the topic could be anything from Himalayan glaciers to a grandmother's pickle recipe, and the clock is ticking. No wonder many students rush, skim, panic, and copy whole lines into their answers hoping something sticks.

Here is the secret: the unseen passage is the **most predictable** section of the paper. The topic changes, but the *questions* do not. Examiners test the same handful of skills every year:

1. Finding a stated fact (**literal comprehension**).
2. Working out something not stated directly (**inference**).
3. Guessing the meaning of a word from context (**vocabulary**).
4. Spotting the main idea or suitable title (**global understanding**).
5. Recognising the writer's tone, purpose or attitude (**evaluation**).
6. Sometimes, reading a chart or table (**data interpretation**).

There are two broad kinds of passage: **discursive/factual** (an article, report, or argument — about climate, health, technology, society) and **literary** (a story extract, memoir, or description). Some papers also include a **case-based** passage with a small table or graph.

If you train each skill separately, the surprise topic becomes irrelevant. A detective does not need to have seen the crime before; she needs a method. This read gives you that method: skimming and scanning, the three-pass routine, every question type and format, a factual and a literary practice run, and a plan to build reading stamina.

**Did you know?** Studies of skilled readers show they read *more slowly* at the start of a hard text and faster later — they invest early in understanding the frame, then everything else falls into place.
keyTerms: Literal question — answer is stated in the text
Inferential question — answer must be worked out from clues
Global question — about the whole passage: theme, title, purpose
Discursive passage — presents information or argument
Literary passage — narrative or descriptive writing

check.q: "Why do you think the author mentions her grandmother at the end?" is which type of question?
check.why: It asks you to work out the author's purpose, which is not stated directly, so it tests inference and evaluation.

sections.h: Skimming and scanning: two speeds of reading
sections.md:
Good readers change gear.

**Skimming** = reading fast for the **general idea**. Your eyes run over headings, first and last sentences of paragraphs, and words in bold or repeated. You are asking *What is this about? What is the writer's view?* You skim a newspaper page to decide which article to read, or a chapter before a test to remember its shape.

**Scanning** = reading fast for a **specific detail** — a name, number, date or key word. Your eyes jump down the page looking only for the target, like looking for your name on a result list or a train number on a departure board.

| | Skimming | Scanning |
|---|---|---|
| Goal | gist, main idea | one fact |
| Where the eyes go | openings, endings, headings | anywhere the key word might be |
| Exam use | Pass 1; title and purpose questions | literal questions with numbers, names |
| Speed | fast, but every paragraph | fastest; ignores most text |

**Close (intensive) reading** is the third gear: slow, careful, word-by-word — used for inference, tone and vocabulary questions.

**Practice drill:** take any newspaper article. Give yourself 30 seconds to skim and write one sentence on its main idea. Then set a scanning target (*How many people? Which city?*) and time how fast you find it. Repeat daily; your speed will double within weeks.

check.q: You need to find the year a dam was built in a long passage. You should:
check.why: Scanning hunts for a specific detail, such as a number or date, without reading everything.

sections.md:
Do not read the passage once, slowly, from top to bottom and then attack the questions. Use three passes.

### Pass 1 — Survey (about 1 minute)
Read the title (if any), the first two lines, the first line of every paragraph and the last two lines. Ask: *What is this about? Is it factual or a story? What is the writer's attitude?* You now have a skeleton.

### Pass 2 — Read the questions (about 1 minute)
Read every question *before* reading the passage fully. Underline key words in each: *why, how many, according to paragraph 3, the word that means…* Now your brain knows what to hunt for.

### Pass 3 — Read actively (3–4 minutes)
Read the whole passage with a pencil. Mark:
- names, numbers, dates;
- signal words (*however, therefore, because, but, on the other hand*);
- the sentence in each paragraph that carries the main point.

Then answer, going back to the exact paragraph each time. Never answer from memory of the passage — always check.

### Time budget for a 10-mark passage

| Step | Time |
|---|---|
| Survey + questions | 2 min |
| Active reading | 4 min |
| Answering | 8 min |
| Re-check | 1 min |
| **Total** | **15 min** |

The figure shows how your attention should move: a quick sweep, then targeted dives.

check.q: What should you do BEFORE reading the whole passage carefully?
options: Read the questions and underline key words
check.why: Knowing the questions in advance turns reading into a targeted search and saves time.

sections.md:
Literal questions are the easiest marks — and the most commonly *lost* because students copy a whole sentence that contains the answer plus three irrelevant clauses.

**Example passage (original):**

> Every winter, thousands of bar-headed geese fly over the Himalayas from Central Asia to the wetlands of Assam and Rajasthan. They cross passes higher than 7,000 metres, where the air holds less than half the oxygen found at sea level. Scientists once believed the birds used rising winds to help them; tracking studies now show they mostly fly at night and in the early morning, when the air is cooler and denser, which helps their wings grip.

**Q.** When do bar-headed geese mostly fly across the mountains, and why?

**Weak answer:** *Scientists once believed the birds used rising winds to help them; tracking studies now show they mostly fly at night…* (copied, includes a wrong belief)

**Strong answer:** *They fly mostly at night and early morning because the cooler, denser air helps their wings grip.*

### Rules for literal answers
1. Locate the line, then **rephrase** in your own short sentence.
2. Answer **every part** of the question (*when* AND *why*).
3. Keep the question's tense and subject.
4. If the question says "in about 30 words", stay within 25–35.

**Did you know?** Bar-headed geese really are among the highest-flying birds in the world — a fact your passage might use to hook you.

check.q: From the geese passage: why is flying at high passes difficult?
options: The air has less than half the oxygen of sea level
check.why: The passage states directly that the air at those heights holds less than half the oxygen found at sea level.

sections.md:
An inference is a conclusion you reach from **clues + common sense**. The text does not say it, but it *shows* it.

> Malati's hands moved quickly over the loom, but she kept glancing at the gate. When the postman's bicycle bell rang at last, she was on her feet before the shuttle stopped swinging.

Nothing says Malati is waiting for a letter, or that she is anxious. Yet you know both. The clues: *kept glancing at the gate*, *on her feet before the shuttle stopped*.

### The CLUE formula for answers
- **C**laim — state your inference: *Malati is anxiously expecting a letter.*
- **L**ink — point to the evidence: *She keeps glancing at the gate and jumps up when the postman arrives.*
- **U**nderstanding — briefly explain: *This shows her attention is not on the weaving.*
- **E**nd — keep it within the word limit.

### Traps
- **Over-reading:** inventing details not supported (*Malati's son is in the army*). Unless the text hints, it is a guess, not an inference.
- **Under-reading:** repeating the clue without the conclusion.

### Tone and attitude
Tone questions ask *how* the writer feels. Common answer words: *nostalgic, critical, humorous, sarcastic, optimistic, concerned, admiring, objective, sympathetic*. Find adjectives and verbs that carry emotion — a writer who calls a mall *glittering but soulless* is critical, not admiring.

check.q: A writer describes a new flyover as "yet another concrete monster swallowing the old neem trees". The tone is:
check.why: Words like monster and swallowing carry disapproval, so the writer's tone is critical.

sections.md:
You will be asked for a word in the passage that means X, or the meaning of a word as used in a given paragraph. You do not need a dictionary — you need the sentence around the word.

### Four context clues
1. **Definition:** *The village was arid — dry and almost without rain.*
2. **Synonym/restatement:** *He was frugal, careful never to waste a single rupee.*
3. **Contrast:** *Unlike his gregarious sister, Vikram preferred to be alone.* → gregarious = sociable.
4. **Example:** *Perishable goods such as milk, fruit and fish need cold storage.* → perishable = goes bad quickly.

### Find-the-word questions
- Note the paragraph number given.
- Match the **part of speech**: if the clue is an adjective (*very dry*), the answer must be an adjective (*arid*, not *aridity*).
- Match the **form**: if the meaning given is plural or past tense, so is the word.
- Write **only the word**, not the sentence.

### Substitution test
Put your chosen meaning back into the sentence. If it reads naturally, you are right.

### Word parts help too
Prefixes and suffixes give clues: *un-, in-, dis-* (not), *re-* (again), *pre-* (before), *-less* (without), *-ful* (full of), *-ous* (having). *Unprecedented* = un + precedent → never happened before.

**Did you know?** English borrows many words from Indian languages — *bungalow, shampoo, jungle, pyjamas, verandah, cot* — so you sometimes recognise more than you think.

check.q: "The usually boisterous classroom fell silent when the inspector entered." Boisterous most nearly means:
check.why: The contrast with fell silent shows the room is normally noisy and lively.

sections.md:
Global questions test whether you understood the whole, not just pieces.

### Main idea
Ask: *If I had to tell a friend this passage in one sentence, what would I say?* Often the main idea appears in the first or last paragraph. Each paragraph has its own **topic sentence**; together they build the central idea.

### Choosing a title
A good title is:
- **broad enough** to cover the whole passage (not just paragraph 2);
- **narrow enough** not to cover topics the passage never discusses;
- **short and catchy**.

For the geese passage: *Birds of India* is too broad; *Night Flights* is too narrow; *Conquering the Himalayas on Wings* fits.

### Writer's purpose
Common purposes: *to inform, to persuade, to warn, to entertain, to describe, to compare.* A passage full of statistics and a call to action at the end aims to **persuade**; a passage of facts in neutral language aims to **inform**.

### Fact or opinion?
A **fact** can be checked (*The Ganga is about 2,500 km long*). An **opinion** is a judgement (*The Ganga is the most beautiful river*). Signal words for opinion: *I believe, should, best, worst, beautiful, unfortunately*.

### MCQ elimination
In options, cross out:
- extreme words (*always, never, completely*) unless the passage uses them;
- options true in real life but **not in the passage**;
- options that mention only one detail.

check.q: A passage discusses why plastic bags clog drains in Mumbai, how cows swallow them, and ends by urging readers to carry cloth bags. The best purpose is:
options: To persuade readers to change a habit
check.why: It builds evidence of harm and ends with a call to action, which is the mark of persuasive writing.

sections.h: Question formats and how to answer each
sections.md:
| Format | What to do | Common slip |
|---|---|---|
| **MCQ** | Read all four options; eliminate; pick the one *the passage* supports | Choosing a 'true in life' option |
| **Short answer (30–40 words)** | One or two rephrased sentences, every part answered | Copying lines, going far over the limit |
| **Complete the sentence** | Continue grammatically from the given words | Repeating the stem; wrong tense |
| **True / False / Not given** | Check the exact claim; 'not given' if the passage is silent | Using outside knowledge |
| **Find the word / synonym / antonym** | Same part of speech and form; write one word | Writing the whole sentence |
| **Reason (Why…?)** | Begin with *because* or *since*; give the cause from the text | Giving the effect instead of the cause |
| **Assertion–reason** | Check each statement against the text, then whether the reason explains the assertion | Ticking 'both true' without checking the link |
| **Chart/table** | Read labels and units; compute; check totals | Mixing up number and percent |

**Example — complete the sentence:** *The writer believes that self-help groups are important because ______.* → *they lend small sums so that one bad season does not trap families in lifelong debt.*

**Example — True/False/Not given (geese passage):** *Bar-headed geese fly from Assam to Central Asia every winter.* → **False** (it's the other way). *Bar-headed geese live for 20 years.* → **Not given**.

check.q: The passage does not mention the topic of a statement at all. You should mark it:
check.why: If the passage is silent on a claim, the correct answer is 'not given', regardless of real-world truth.

sections.h: Case-based passages with charts and tables
sections.md:
Some passages include a small table or bar chart. The questions combine reading and simple numeracy.

**Example (made-up survey of 200 Class 9 students):**

The bar chart below shows how students travel to school. Questions might ask: *Which mode is most popular? What percentage walk? How many more use the bus than cycle?*

Work carefully:
- Bus: 80 of 200 = 40%
- Walk: 50 of 200 = 25%
- Cycle: 40 of 200 = 20%
- Car/auto: 30 of 200 = 15%
- Check: 80 + 50 + 40 + 30 = 200 ✓, and 40 + 25 + 20 + 15 = 100 ✓

*How many more use the bus than cycle?* 80 − 40 = **40 students**.

### Tips
1. Read the axis labels and the unit (number or percent?).
2. Use exact figures from the chart; do not round unless asked.
3. For *trend* questions, use words like *rose steadily, peaked, declined sharply, remained stable*.
4. Combine chart data with text: if the passage says buses are crowded, a question might ask you to infer why cycling is low.

check.why: 40 cyclists out of 200 students is 40 ÷ 200 × 100 = 20%.

sections.md:
**Passage (original):**

> (1) When the monsoon fails in Vidarbha, the first sign is not on the fields but in the market. Farmers stop buying new tools; tailors find fewer orders for wedding clothes; the bangle-seller packs up early.
>
> (2) Rekha Tai, who has sold seeds in the same shop in Akola for thirty years, says she can read the sky in her ledger. "When people pay in coins instead of notes," she laughs, "I know the rain is late."
>
> (3) Yet the region is learning to adapt. Farm ponds, drip irrigation and drought-resistant millets are spreading, slowly. Self-help groups of women now lend small sums so that one bad season need not mean a lifetime of debt.
>
> (4) Rain will always matter. But the story of Vidarbha is increasingly one of people refusing to let the sky decide everything.

**Questions and model answers:**

1. *What is the first sign of a failed monsoon, according to the writer?* — A slowdown in the market: people stop buying tools, clothes and bangles.
2. *What does Rekha Tai mean when she says she can "read the sky in her ledger"?* — Her sales records show how good the rains are, because people spend less when the monsoon is weak.
3. *Find a word in paragraph 3 meaning "adjust to new conditions".* — adapt
4. *Name two methods farmers use to cope with drought.* — Farm ponds and drip irrigation (also: millets).
5. *What is the tone of the last paragraph?* — Hopeful/determined.
6. *Suggest a title.* — Beyond the Sky: Vidarbha Learns to Adapt.

Notice how every answer is short, rephrased, and complete.

check.q: Why does Rekha Tai notice people paying in coins?
options: It shows people have less money because the rains are poor
check.why: Paying in small coins suggests shortage of money, which in a farming town signals a weak monsoon.

sections.md:
Literary passages test character, feeling and imagery more than facts.

**Passage (original):**

> (1) The last bus to Almora had gone, and the tea stall at the bend was shutting its shutters one by one. Kunal sat on his tin trunk, counting the coins in his pocket for the third time, as if they might multiply.
>
> (2) "First time away from home?" The old man who ran the stall did not wait for an answer. He poured a glass of tea so sweet it made Kunal's teeth ache, and set it on the trunk without a word about money.
>
> (3) Below them, the valley was filling with mist like a bowl with milk. Somewhere a dog barked, and the sound came back twice from the hills. Kunal wrapped his fingers round the warm glass and, for the first time that day, stopped counting.

**Questions and model answers:**

1. *How does Kunal feel at the start? Give evidence.* — Anxious and short of money: he counts his coins for the third time, hoping they might multiply.
2. *What does the stall-owner's action reveal about him?* — He is kind and understanding; he offers tea without asking for payment and guesses Kunal is new and lonely.
3. *Explain the comparison 'filling with mist like a bowl with milk'.* — A simile: the white mist slowly fills the hollow valley as milk fills a bowl, creating a calm, soft picture.
4. *What is the significance of 'stopped counting' in the last line?* — His worry eases; the small kindness and the peaceful scene comfort him. The counting coins symbolise anxiety.
5. *Find a word in paragraph 1 meaning 'increase in number'.* — multiply
6. *Choose the best title:* (a) Buses of Almora (b) A Glass of Kindness (c) Mountain Dogs (d) Counting Coins. — **(b)**: it covers the whole passage.

**Literary toolkit:** look for **simile/metaphor**, **sound** (echo, bark), **contrast** (cold night vs warm glass), **symbol** (coins = worry) and **shift in mood** from start to end.

check.q: In the Almora passage, the counting of coins symbolises:
check.why: He counts repeatedly out of worry; when comforted he 'stopped counting', so the action stands for anxiety.

sections.h: Building reading stamina for the year
sections.md:
No method replaces **reading regularly**. A plan that fits a busy Class 9 week:

| Day | 15-minute habit |
|---|---|
| Mon | One newspaper editorial: write its main idea in one sentence |
| Tue | A short story or a chapter of a novel for pleasure |
| Wed | A science or sports article: list 5 new words with meanings guessed from context |
| Thu | One timed unseen passage from a practice book |
| Fri | Read a poem aloud; note one image you liked |
| Sat | A long magazine feature; identify the writer's tone |
| Sun | Rest, or reread something you loved |

**Keep a word journal:** new word, the sentence you found it in, your guessed meaning, the dictionary meaning. Thirty words a month is 360 a year.

**Read widely:** Ruskin Bond and R. K. Narayan for stories; *The Hindu*'s or *Indian Express*'s student pages; NCERT's own supplementary readers; Tagore and Premchand in translation; science magazines.

**Did you know?** Reading 20 minutes a day exposes you to roughly 1.8 million words a year, according to a widely cited estimate — far more than any vocabulary list.

check.q: What is the best long-term way to improve at unseen passages?
options: Regular, varied reading with attention to new words
check.why: Regular varied reading builds speed, vocabulary and comprehension, which no shortcut replaces.

summary: Unseen passages test the same skills every year: literal, inference, vocabulary, global, tone, and sometimes data.
Skim for gist, scan for a detail, read closely for inference and tone.
Use three passes: survey, read the questions, then read actively with a pencil.
Budget about 15 minutes for a 10-mark passage.
Literal answers: locate, rephrase, answer every part, respect word limits.
Inference = clue + common sense; support every inference with evidence.
Tone words: critical, nostalgic, hopeful, humorous, sarcastic, objective, concerned.
Vocabulary: use definition, synonym, contrast, example and word-part clues; match part of speech and form.
A good title covers the whole passage, no more and no less.
Writer's purpose: inform, persuade, warn, entertain, describe; separate fact from opinion.
Know each format: MCQ, short answer, complete-the-sentence, true/false/not given, assertion–reason.
For charts, read labels and units, compute carefully and check totals.
Literary passages: watch imagery, symbol, contrast and mood shift.
Never copy whole sentences — examiners reward understanding.

glossary.d: The sentence that states the main point of a paragraph
Fast reading for the general idea
Fast reading to find a specific detail
The writer's attitude shown through word choice
A comparison using 'like' or 'as'

practice: Explain the difference between skimming and scanning with one example of when you would use each.
Write an original 150-word factual passage about a festival in your town and frame four questions on it (one literal, one inference, one vocabulary, one title).
Read today's newspaper editorial. Identify its purpose and tone, giving two words from the text as evidence.
Why is copying entire lines from the passage a poor strategy? Answer in 40 words.
Give three context-clue types and an original sentence illustrating each.
From the Vidarbha passage, infer why self-help groups are important, in about 30 words.
From the Almora passage, describe the change in Kunal's mood from beginning to end (40 words).
Write two facts and two opinions about your school.
A chart shows mobile phone users rising from 20 to 65 in a village of 100 over five years. Describe the trend in two sentences.
List four mistakes students make in unseen passages and how to avoid each.

rd-school-c9-english-d.revision-practice.subtitle: Beehive, Moments, grammar and writing — revised, connected and exam-ready

sections.h: How to use this revision read
sections.md:
It is February. The datesheet is on the fridge, and English feels like the subject you can "manage". That is exactly why marks leak away in English: students revise maths for weeks and English for an evening.

This read is built around the shape of a typical Class 9 English paper:

| Section | What it tests | Approx. weight |
|---|---|---|
| A. Reading | Unseen passages (discursive + case-based) | 20 |
| B. Writing & Grammar | Descriptive paragraph/diary/story; gap-fill, editing, reported speech | 20 |
| C. Literature | Beehive prose & poetry, Moments supplementary reader | 40 |

(Check your own school's blueprint — schemes change from year to year.)

We go through each in order: quick skill reminders for reading, writing and grammar; then a lesson-by-lesson revision map of the prose, poems and supplementary stories — each with the gist, key themes, characters and a likely exam angle; then long-answer technique and a mini mock paper. All summaries here are original retellings; read the actual chapters in your NCERT book (free online) alongside.

**A three-day plan:**
- **Day 1:** Reading + grammar practice (two passages, one editing task, ten reported-speech conversions).
- **Day 2:** Beehive — prose and poems, one long answer per chapter.
- **Day 3:** Moments + one timed full paper.

**Did you know?** Spaced revision — seeing material on day 1, day 3 and day 7 — beats cramming for long-term memory, according to decades of psychology research.

check.q: Which section usually carries the most marks in Class 9 English?
check.why: Literature (Beehive and Moments together) generally carries the largest share of the paper.

sections.h: Reading, writing and grammar — the 10-minute refresher
sections.md:
### Reading
- Survey → read questions → read actively.
- Literal answers: rephrase, answer all parts.
- Inference: claim + evidence.
- Vocabulary: match part of speech; substitute back.
- Title: covers the whole passage.
- Charts: read units, check totals.

### Writing
- **Descriptive paragraph** (100–150 words): topic sentence, five senses, ordered details, closing impression.
- **Diary entry**: day/date/time, Dear Diary, first person, event → feeling → reflection.
- **Story** (150–200 words): title, given opening, arc (opening, rising action, climax, resolution).

### Grammar checklist
| Topic | Golden rule |
|---|---|
| Tenses | Keep consistent; use present perfect for past actions with present result. |
| Modals | can/could (ability), may/might (possibility), must (necessity), should (advice). |
| Subject–verb agreement | *Each of the boys **is**…*; *The team **has**…* (as a unit). |
| Active–passive | Object becomes subject; *be* + past participle. |
| Reported speech | Person (SON), tense backshift, time/place words, correct linker. |
| Determiners | *few* (hardly any) vs *a few* (some); *much* (uncountable) vs *many* (countable). |

### Five editing errors you will meet
1. Missing article: *She is ~~honest girl~~ an honest girl.*
2. Wrong preposition: *~~discuss about~~ discuss the plan.*
3. Agreement: *One of my friends ~~are~~ is…*
4. Tense: *Yesterday he ~~go~~ went…*
5. Verb form after modal: *He can ~~sings~~ sing.*

check.q: Choose the correct sentence.
options: One of the players are injured.
One of the players is injured.
One of the player is injured.
One of the players were injured.
check.why: The subject is one, so the verb is singular, while players stays plural after of the.

sections.h: Writing: three model openings and a marking checklist
sections.md:
**Descriptive paragraph — 'A Railway Platform at Dawn'**
> *At five in the morning, Platform 3 of Lucknow Charbagh is a river of sound: the chai-wallah's clinking glasses, a porter's shout, the long sigh of a train easing in. Under yellow lamps, families sit on tin trunks...*
(Topic sentence → sights, sounds, smells in spatial order → closing impression.)

**Diary entry**
> *Saturday, 14 February, 9:30 p.m.*
> *Dear Diary, Today I finally did it — I sang on stage at the Annual Day. My knees shook so badly that...*
(Date + time, first person, past tense for events, present for feelings now, a short reflection to end.)

**Story — given opening: 'The lights went out just as...'**
> *The lights went out just as Ananya reached the last page of the mystery. Outside, the monsoon hammered the tin roof. Then, from the kitchen, came a soft, deliberate click...*
(Hook → build-up → twist/climax → resolution; a title; 150–200 words.)

**Checklist examiners use:**
| Criterion | Ask yourself |
|---|---|
| Format | Title/date/salutation present where required? |
| Content | All points in the question covered? |
| Organisation | Clear beginning, middle, end; paragraphs? |
| Language | Varied vocabulary, correct tenses and agreement? |
| Length | Within the word limit? |

check.q: Which tense should mainly carry the events in a diary entry about today?
check.why: Events that happened earlier in the day are narrated in the simple past; feelings now may be in the present.

sections.h: Beehive prose (part 1): Stories of childhood and wonder
sections.md:
### The Fun They Had — Isaac Asimov
**Gist:** In the year 2157, two children, Margie and Tommy, find a real printed book about old-fashioned schools. Their own schooling happens at home with a mechanical teacher fixed to the child's level. Margie, who dislikes her mechanical teacher (it kept giving her geography tests she did badly in, until the County Inspector adjusted it), imagines how much fun children must have had in the old days, learning together with human teachers.
**Themes:** technology vs human contact; the social joy of learning.
**Exam angle:** Why did Margie hate school? How is her school different from ours? Would you prefer a mechanical teacher? (Give balanced reasons.)

### The Sound of Music — Evelyn Glennie & Bismillah Khan
**Part I:** Evelyn Glennie, a Scottish percussionist, became profoundly deaf by about age eleven, yet learned to *feel* sound through her body, and went on to study at the Royal Academy of Music and become a world-famous solo percussionist.
**Part II:** Ustad Bismillah Khan took the shehnai — once played mainly at weddings and temples — to the classical concert stage. He loved Benaras and the Ganga and refused to settle abroad. He received the Bharat Ratna in 2001.
**Themes:** determination; music beyond hearing; love for one's roots.

### The Little Girl — Katherine Mansfield
**Gist:** Kezia fears her stern father, stammering in his presence. She is punished after tearing up his important papers to stuff a pin-cushion she meant as a birthday gift. One night, frightened by a nightmare while her mother is away, she is comforted by him and sees his tired, gentle side. She realises he works hard and has a "big heart".
**Themes:** a child's perception of a parent; misunderstanding and its healing.

### A Truly Beautiful Mind — on Albert Einstein
**Gist:** Einstein's school difficulties, his work as a patent-office clerk, the "miracle year" of 1905 papers including special relativity, the 1921 Nobel Prize (for the photoelectric effect), his letter to President Roosevelt about the possibility of an atomic bomb, and his later anguish over nuclear weapons and work for peace.
**Themes:** curiosity; science and conscience.

Signs letter to President Roosevelt warning of atomic bomb potential
Dies; remembered as scientist and campaigner for peace

check.q: For which work did Einstein receive the Nobel Prize?
check.why: The 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded for his explanation of the photoelectric effect, not relativity.

sections.h: Beehive prose (part 2): Courage, humour and journeys
sections.md:
### The Snake and the Mirror — Vaikom Muhammad Basheer
**Gist:** A poor homoeopath narrator, dreaming of a rich, fat wife and fine looks as he admires himself in a mirror, freezes in terror when a snake drops onto his shoulder and coils round his arm. Motionless, he prays; the snake is drawn to the mirror instead and slithers away. Humour comes from his vanity collapsing in fear.
**Themes:** vanity; humour in fear; self-mockery.

### My Childhood — A. P. J. Abdul Kalam
**Gist:** Growing up in Rameswaram in a modest, harmonious family; friendships across religions; a new teacher who tried to separate a Hindu and a Muslim boy and was corrected by the priest Lakshmana Sastry; a science teacher, Sivasubramania Iyer, who challenged caste barriers; his decision to leave home to study in Ramanathapuram.
**Themes:** communal harmony; values from family; education.

### Reach for the Top — Santosh Yadav & Maria Sharapova
**Part I:** Santosh Yadav from Haryana refused early marriage, studied, discovered mountaineering, and became the first woman to climb Everest twice (1992 and 1993).
**Part II:** Maria Sharapova left Russia at nine to train in tennis in the USA, endured loneliness, won Wimbledon at 17 and became world number one in 2005.
**Themes:** grit; breaking expectations.

### Kathmandu — Vikram Seth
**Gist:** A travel account contrasting the noisy, crowded Pashupatinath temple with the calm Buddhist Baudhnath stupa; the bustle of Kathmandu's streets; the decision to fly home; the narrator's fascination with a flute-seller and reflection on the universality of the flute.
**Themes:** contrasts; travel writing as observation.

### If I Were You — Douglas James (play)
**Gist:** Gerrard, an actor, is confronted by an intruder who plans to kill him and take over his identity. Gerrard outwits him with a made-up story that he himself is a wanted criminal, and locks him in a cupboard.
**Themes:** presence of mind; wit over force.

check.q: How does Gerrard defeat the intruder in 'If I Were You'?
options: He calls the police at once
He tricks him with a false story and locks him in a cupboard
check.why: Gerrard uses quick thinking, inventing a story about being a wanted man, and traps the intruder in a cupboard.

sections.h: Beehive poems: the map of meaning
sections.md:
For each poem, know the **poet, central idea, two poetic devices and one 'why' answer**. (Read the poem in your book — it is not reproduced here.)

| Poem | Poet | Central idea | Key devices |
|---|---|---|---|
| The Road Not Taken | Robert Frost | Choices shape life; we cannot take every road; a choice made becomes the difference | Extended metaphor (roads = choices), symbolism |
| Wind | Subramania Bharati (tr.) | Weak things are destroyed by wind; make the body and mind strong, then the wind becomes a friend | Personification, symbolism |
| Rain on the Roof | Coates Kinney | The sound of rain on a tin roof brings memories of the poet's mother | Imagery, onomatopoeia |
| The Lake Isle of Innisfree | W. B. Yeats | Longing to escape city life for peace in nature | Imagery, repetition |
| A Legend of the Northland | Phoebe Cary | A greedy old woman refuses even a small cake to Saint Peter and is turned into a woodpecker | Ballad form, moral |
| No Men Are Foreign | James Kirkup | All humans share one earth and one humanity; war hurts ourselves | Repetition, contrast |
| On Killing a Tree | Gieve Patel | A tree is not easily killed; only uprooting the root kills it | Irony, imagery |
| A Slumber Did My Spirit Seal | William Wordsworth | Grief at the death of a loved one, now part of the earth's motion | Contrast, imagery |

### How to write a poem answer (30–40 words)
1. Name the idea.
2. Point to the line/image (refer, don't copy at length).
3. Explain its effect.

*Example:* **What does the wind symbolise?** The wind symbolises hardships in life. Weak people, like fragile shutters and crumbling houses, are broken by it, but those who build strength of body and mind make the wind their friend.

*Example:* **Why does the speaker in 'On Killing a Tree' describe the process in such detail?** The step-by-step, almost surgical detail is ironic: it shows how strong and resilient a tree is, and makes us uneasy at the cruelty humans need to destroy it.

check.q: In 'The Road Not Taken', the two roads symbolise:
check.why: The diverging roads are an extended metaphor for decisions that shape the course of life.

sections.md:
### The Lost Child — Mulk Raj Anand
**Gist:** A little boy at a spring fair wants toys and sweets; his parents refuse. When he is separated from them in the crowd, he no longer wants anything except his mother and father, refusing every treat a kind stranger offers.
**Theme:** what a child truly needs is the security of parents.

### The Adventures of Toto — Ruskin Bond
**Gist:** The narrator's grandfather buys Toto, a mischievous monkey, from a tonga-driver for five rupees. Toto wrecks wallpaper, causes a fuss on a train journey (Grandfather pays for a dog ticket), nearly boils himself in a kettle and eats food meant for guests. Finally Grandfather sells him back for three rupees.
**Theme:** humour; wild animals are not pets.

### Iswaran the Storyteller — R. K. Laxman
**Gist:** Mahendra, a supervisor, has a cook, Iswaran, who tells thrilling tales — of a tusker running amok, and of ghosts. Iswaran's story of a female ghost frightens Mahendra so much one full-moon night that he decides to leave that haunted site.
**Theme:** the power of storytelling; suspense.

### In the Kingdom of Fools — folk tale retold by A. K. Ramanujan
**Gist:** In a kingdom where people sleep by day and work by night, a guru and disciple arrive. Absurd justice — a chain of blame after a thief dies when a wall collapses — leads to a death sentence that falls on the fat disciple. The clever guru claims that whoever dies first on the stake will be reborn as king; the foolish king and minister rush to die themselves, and the people make the guru and disciple their rulers.
**Theme:** wit vs foolishness; the danger of illogical rulers.

sections.md:
### The Happy Prince — Oscar Wilde
**Gist:** A gilded statue of a prince, seeing the misery of his city, asks a little swallow to carry away his ruby, sapphire eyes and gold leaf to the poor. The swallow stays too long into winter and dies; the statue's lead heart breaks. The town melts the shabby statue, but God declares the heart and the bird the two most precious things in the city.
**Themes:** compassion; sacrifice; true value vs appearance.

### The Last Leaf — O. Henry
**Gist:** Johnsy, ill with pneumonia, believes she will die when the last ivy leaf falls. Her friend Sue worries. Old painter Behrman, who always dreamed of a masterpiece, paints a leaf on the wall on a stormy night. Johnsy recovers, seeing the leaf survive; Behrman dies of pneumonia caught that night — the leaf was his masterpiece.
**Themes:** hope; self-sacrifice; art.

### A House Is Not a Home — Zan Gaudioso
**Gist:** A fourteen-year-old struggling at a new school loses his house to a fire, and his beloved cat goes missing. Classmates and the community rally with gifts and support; the cat is returned. He learns that people and love, not walls, make a home.
**Themes:** resilience; community.

### The Beggar — Anton Chekhov
**Gist:** Sergei, a lawyer, catches a beggar, Lushkoff, lying, and offers him wood-chopping work. Lushkoff works and eventually reforms. Years later he reveals that it was really Sergei's cook, Olga, who chopped the wood and whose kind scolding and tears changed him.
**Themes:** compassion; quiet kindness reforms people.

Who sacrifices?

check.why: Lushkoff reveals that Olga's compassion and tears, while she chopped the wood for him, changed him.

sections.md:
Literature papers often ask a 100–120 word answer linking a story to values: *How does Behrman's sacrifice show that true art lies in love?* or *Compare the childhood of Kalam with Kezia's.*

### The PEEL paragraph
- **P**oint: answer in one sentence.
- **E**vidence: one or two events from the text.
- **E**xplanation: why it matters.
- **L**ink: connect to the question/value or life today.

**Sample:** *What lesson does 'The Fun They Had' teach about technology?*

> Asimov suggests that technology can deliver information but not the warmth of shared learning. (P) Margie's mechanical teacher is efficient, tests her constantly, and even adjusts to her level, yet she hates it. (E) She longs for the old schools where children laughed, helped each other, and had a human teacher. (E) This shows that education is also social and emotional — something a machine cannot replace. (E) Today, as we use apps and online classes, the story reminds us to keep friendships and human mentors at the centre of learning. (L)

### Cross-text pairings worth preparing
- Courage: Santosh Yadav, Gerrard, Evelyn Glennie, Maria Sharapova.
- Childhood: Kalam, Kezia, the lost child, Margie.
- Compassion: Happy Prince, Olga, Behrman, Sivasubramania Iyer.
- Wit: the guru in Kingdom of Fools, Gerrard.

**Did you know?** Examiners reward *specific* evidence. "Behrman painted the leaf on a stormy night" beats "Behrman did something kind".

check.q: In a PEEL answer, what does 'Link' do?
options: Connects the point to the question's value or to real life
check.why: The link step ties the analysis back to the question and wider meaning, completing the argument.

**Section A — Reading (8 marks)**
> *Every evening at six, the lamplighter of old Shimla climbed his ladder, lit the gas lamp at the Mall corner, and moved on. Children followed him like a small parade. When electric lights came in the 1910s, his job vanished — but older residents say the Mall never felt quite so warm again.*
1. What did the lamplighter do every evening? (1)
2. Why did his job disappear? (1)
3. What does 'followed him like a small parade' suggest about the children? (2)
4. What is the writer's tone in the last sentence? (1)
5. Find a word meaning 'disappeared'. (1)
6. Suggest a title. (2)

**Section B — Grammar (6 marks)**
7. Fill in: *The Mall ___ (light) by gas lamps until electricity arrived.*
8. Report: *"Will you light the lamp early today?" the child asked the lamplighter.*
9. Correct: *Each of the lamps were lit by hand.*
10. Choose: *There were (few / a few) lamplighters left by 1920, so the job was dying.*

**Section B — Writing (6 marks)**
11. Write a diary entry (100–120 words) as the lamplighter on his last working day.

**Section C — Literature (20 marks)**
12. How did Evelyn Glennie 'hear' music? (3)
13. What is the central idea of 'No Men Are Foreign'? (3)
14. Why did Mahendra decide to leave the site in 'Iswaran the Storyteller'? (3)

**Self-marking hints:** Q2 — because electric lights replaced gas lamps; Q4 — nostalgic; Q5 — vanished; Q7 — was lit; Q8 — The child asked the lamplighter whether he would light the lamp early that day; Q9 — was lit; Q10 — few (hardly any, matching 'dying').

rd-school-c9-english-d.writing-skills.subtitle: Three formats, one secret — make the reader see, feel and turn the page

sections.md:
Ten marks. A topic like *Describe a busy railway platform* or *Write a diary entry about your first day at a new school*. You have the pen, you have twenty minutes, and your mind is as empty as the page.

Most weak writing fails for one reason: it **tells** instead of **shows**. *The platform was very crowded and noisy* tells. *A chaiwala's kettle hissed beside my ear while a thousand slippers slapped the concrete and a voice overhead announced, for the third time, that the Rajdhani was late* shows. The second sentence lets the reader stand there.

Class 9 writing asks for three forms:

| Form | Purpose | Person | Typical length |
|---|---|---|---|
| Descriptive paragraph | Paint a person, place, object or event | Usually 3rd or 1st | 100–150 words |
| Diary entry | Record personal experience and feelings | 1st person, informal | 100–150 words |
| Story | Narrate events with a beginning, middle, end | 1st or 3rd | 150–200 words |

Each has its own format and scoring points, but all three share one engine: **specific detail + controlled structure + clean language**. Examiners typically mark on *content* (ideas, relevance), *organisation* (order, paragraphing, format) and *accuracy* (grammar, spelling, vocabulary). Remember all three.

**A 20-minute exam routine:** 3 minutes planning (jot ideas, pick an order), 13 minutes writing, 4 minutes revising. Planning feels like lost time; it is the opposite.

**Did you know?** Many famous writers keep diaries — Anne Frank's diary, written by a teenager, became one of the most read books of the twentieth century. Diaries matter because honesty is powerful.
keyTerms: Show, don't tell — reveal through detail and action rather than labels
Content — ideas and relevance
Organisation — structure, order, format
Accuracy — grammar, spelling, punctuation

check.q: Which sentence SHOWS rather than tells?
options: The old man was very poor.
The old man counted his three coins twice before choosing the smaller roti.
The old man had a hard life.
check.why: It gives a concrete action that lets the reader infer poverty without being told.

sections.h: The descriptive paragraph: the five-senses camera
sections.md:
A descriptive paragraph is a photograph made of words — but a photograph that can also smell, sound and feel.

### Plan with the senses
Before writing, jot two details for each sense:
- **Sight:** colours, shapes, movement, light
- **Sound:** voices, machines, nature
- **Smell:** food, rain, smoke, flowers
- **Touch:** heat, texture, wind
- **Taste:** where natural (food, salt air)

### Choose an order
1. **Spatial** — near to far, left to right, top to bottom (good for places).
2. **Chronological** — as events unfold (good for an event like a festival).
3. **General to particular** — overall impression, then zoom in (good for people).

### Structure
- **Topic sentence** that sets the overall impression.
- **Supporting details** in your chosen order, using the senses.
- **Closing sentence** that leaves a feeling or reflection.

### Describing a person
Go beyond hair and height. Combine **appearance + habits + speech + personality**: *My grandfather's spectacles always rested at the very tip of his nose, as if ready to jump. He spoke slowly, chose every word as carefully as he chose mangoes at the market, and laughed with his whole body.*

### Language toolkit
- Precise nouns (*banyan*, not *tree*) and strong verbs (*trudged*, not *walked slowly*).
- Adjectives in moderation — one sharp adjective beats three vague ones.
- Figurative language: simile (*like*, *as*), metaphor, personification — one or two, not ten.
- Vary sentence length: long flowing sentences, then a short punch.
- **Tense:** present for a place as it usually is (*The market stretches…*); past for a particular visit (*The market was…*). Pick one and stay there.

sections.md:
**Topic:** Describe a vegetable market on a Sunday morning. (About 130 words)

> **Sunday at the Sabzi Mandi**
>
> By seven o'clock on Sunday, the sabzi mandi near our colony is already wide awake. Rows of wooden carts stretch down the lane like a painter's palette — scarlet tomatoes, emerald heaps of spinach, purple brinjals glossy as polished stones. The air smells of wet earth and crushed coriander. Vendors call out prices in a cheerful sing-song, each trying to outshout the next, while a radio somewhere plays old Kishore Kumar songs. Aunties in cotton sarees press each mango with an expert thumb and bargain over a single rupee as if it were a gold coin. A cow ambles past, nibbling a fallen cabbage leaf, and nobody stops her. By ten the crowd thins and the carts look tired, but for those three hours, the mandi is the liveliest place in town.

### Why it scores
- **Topic sentence** sets the scene and time.
- **Spatial + sensory** detail: sight (colours), smell, sound, touch (pressing mangoes).
- **Two similes**, used naturally.
- **Human touch** — aunties bargaining, the cow — adds humour without mockery.
- **Closing** gives a sense of time passing and an overall impression.
- Count: about 140 words — on target.

### Common errors to avoid
- Listing items without description (*There were tomatoes, potatoes, onions…*).
- Switching tense midway.
- Writing a story instead of a description — keep events minimal.

check.q: What does the final sentence of the model achieve?
options: Closes with an overall impression and sense of time
check.why: A good closing sentence rounds off the description with a reflection or impression.

sections.h: Models: describing a person and an event
sections.md:
**Topic:** Describe a person who has influenced you. (About 120 words)

> **Meena Ma'am**
>
> Meena Ma'am, our science teacher, is small enough to be lost in a crowd of Class 9 students — until she speaks. Her voice is low but somehow reaches the last bench, and her chalk moves across the board as fast as a cricket commentator's tongue. She wears the same green cardigan every winter and carries a battered steel tiffin that smells of lemon rice. What makes her unforgettable is her patience: she will explain photosynthesis five times, each time in a new way, until the slowest of us smiles. When I failed my first test, she wrote one line in the margin: *Try again — I know you can.* I still have that paper.

(General impression → appearance → habits → speech → personality → a defining moment.)

**Topic:** Describe the Republic Day celebration at your school. (Chronological order, about 120 words)

> At eight sharp on 26 January, the school ground was a sea of white uniforms. The band struck up, and the NCC cadets marched past, boots thudding in perfect rhythm. Our principal unfurled the tricolour; petals tumbled out of its folds and drifted onto the front row. We sang the national anthem, fifty-two seconds of complete stillness. Then came the cultural programme — a Bihu dance in swirling red and cream, a skit on road safety, and a poem recited by a nervous Class 3 girl who received the loudest applause of all. By eleven, laddoos were passed around in paper bags, sticky and sweet. As we left, the flag fluttered above the gate, bright against a clear winter sky.

(Time markers — *at eight, then, by eleven, as we left* — guide the reader through the event.)

check.q: Which order does the Republic Day model follow?
check.why: It moves through the event in time order, using markers like 'at eight', 'then' and 'by eleven'.

sections.h: The diary entry: format and voice
sections.md:
A diary is a conversation with yourself. It is personal, honest, informal and reflective — but in an exam it also has a **fixed format** that carries marks.

### Format
```
Thursday, 26 November 2026          (day and date)
9:30 p.m.                            (time — optional but good)

Dear Diary,                          (optional; many teachers accept)

Body — 2 or 3 short paragraphs:
  1. What happened (the event)
  2. How I felt / what I thought
  3. What I learned / resolve / looking ahead

Ananya                               (name or initial — optional)
```

### Voice
- **First person** (*I, me, my*).
- **Past tense** for events of the day; **present** for feelings now; **future** for plans.
- Informal but not slangy — contractions are fine (*I'm, couldn't*); text-speak (*gr8, lol*) is not.
- Emotions are the heart: *I felt a knot in my stomach*; *I couldn't stop smiling*.
- **Reflection** lifts a diary from a report to writing: *Maybe being nervous is just my brain getting ready.*

### Kinds of diary topics
- **An event** (a match, a trip, a festival).
- **An experience with feelings** (an argument, an achievement, a loss).
- **A character's diary** from a lesson — e.g., *Kezia's diary after her father comforted her* or *Santosh Yadav's diary on the summit*. Stay true to the text's facts and add believable feelings.

### Diary vs. other formats

The compare box shows how a diary differs from a formal report of the same event.

check.q: Which element is essential in a diary entry format?
check.why: A diary is a dated personal record, so the date (and usually day and time) is part of its format.

sections.md:
**Topic:** You helped an elderly neighbour during a power cut. Write a diary entry. (About 130 words)

> **Saturday, 14 June 2026**
> **10:15 p.m.**
>
> Dear Diary,
>
> The lights went out at seven today, right in the middle of my maths homework. While I was grumbling and hunting for a torch, I heard a faint knock. It was Sharma Dadi from next door, holding a candle that kept flickering out. Her inverter had failed, and she couldn't find her blood-pressure tablets in the dark.
>
> I lit our emergency lamp, found her medicine box and sat with her until the power came back two hours later. She told me stories about Lucknow in the 1970s — lanterns, crowded tongas, and a cinema hall where tickets cost one rupee!
>
> I came home feeling strangely light. I had always thought of Dadi as just the lady who scolds us for noisy cricket. Tonight I realised how lonely she must be. I'll visit her every Sunday now.
>
> Riya

### Why it scores
- Correct format: day, date, time, salutation, name.
- Three paragraphs: event → experience → reflection/resolve.
- Feelings are shown (*grumbling*, *strangely light*).
- Tense control: past for events, present for realisation, future for resolve.
- A small surprise (Dadi's stories) makes it memorable.

check.q: Why does the last paragraph of the model add value?
options: It reflects on a change in the writer's understanding and makes a resolve
check.why: Reflection and resolve are what distinguish a strong diary entry from a plain account of events.

sections.md:
In the exam you usually get either a **beginning** (*As the bus stopped at the deserted village, I noticed…*) or a set of **cues/outline**, or a **title** like *An Unexpected Friend*. You must write 150–200 words.

### The five-step arc
1. **Opening / exposition** — who, where, when; hook the reader in the first line.
2. **Rising action** — a problem or desire appears.
3. **Climax** — the moment of highest tension or decision.
4. **Falling action** — consequences unfold.
5. **Resolution** — the problem ends; often a lesson or twist.

### Hooks that work
- Start with dialogue: *"Don't open that box," Nani whispered.*
- Start with action: *The ball smashed through Mr Iyer's window.*
- Start with a mystery: *Nobody had entered the old library for twenty years — until the lights came on.*

### Rules for exam stories
- Use the **given beginning word-for-word** if one is provided.
- Give your story a **title** (it earns a mark in many schemes).
- **Past tense** for narration; keep it consistent.
- Use dialogue sparingly — one or two exchanges, punctuated correctly.
- Keep to **two or three characters**; you have no space for ten.
- End **satisfyingly** — avoid *and then I woke up, it was a dream* unless you make it clever.

Watch the arc rise and fall below — a plot is a hill the reader climbs.

sections.h: Model: a story from a given beginning
sections.md:
**Beginning given:** *The rain had not stopped for three days, and the river was rising.*

> **The Boat of Tin**
>
> The rain had not stopped for three days, and the river was rising. In the little Assamese village of Majuli Char, fourteen-year-old Bikash watched the water creep past the bamboo fence, then the well, then the steps of the school.
>
> At noon, the siren from the panchayat office wailed: everyone must move to the high ground. Bikash was halfway up the slope with his mother when he heard a thin cry. Old Hiren Kaka, who could barely walk, was still on his roof.
>
> There was no boat. But behind the school lay the huge tin sheet the carpenter had kept for the new roof. Bikash and his friend Moni tied empty oil cans beneath it with jute rope, their fingers numb. Pushing with a bamboo pole, they wobbled across the brown current. Twice the raft tilted; twice they held on.
>
> When they finally hauled Kaka onto the hill, the whole village cheered. That evening the carpenter only smiled. "I'll find another sheet," he said. "Some roofs are meant to float."

### Why it scores
- Uses the given opening exactly.
- Clear arc: rising water → cry for help → raft-building (climax) → rescue → warm ending.
- Concrete setting (Majuli, bamboo fence, jute rope) and senses.
- One line of dialogue, perfectly punctuated, giving a memorable close.
- About 200 words.

check.q: Which detail best shows the danger during the climax?
options: Twice the raft tilted; twice they held on
check.why: The repeated tilting of the raft shows the peak of physical danger in the story.

sections.md:
**Cues given:** *new girl in class — doesn't speak Hindi or English well — others laugh — narrator helps — school science fair — surprise.*

**Plan (1 minute):** Opening: new girl Lhamo from Sikkim. Rising: teasing, narrator's guilt. Climax: science fair, partner drops out. Resolution: Lhamo's brilliant model; lesson about judging people.

> **The Quiet Scientist**
>
> Lhamo joined our class in July, all the way from a village near Gangtok. She spoke softly, in short, careful sentences, and some boys at the back copied her accent until the whole row giggled. I laughed too — and hated myself for it all evening.
>
> The next day I sat beside her at lunch and offered her half my aloo paratha. She smiled and shared her momos. Slowly, between bites, she told me about the small water-mill her father had built on their stream.
>
> In September, my partner for the science fair fell ill. With three days left, I asked Lhamo to help. She drew a perfect diagram of a mini hydro-generator, and we built it with a plastic bottle, a toy motor and an old CFL holder.
>
> When the judges poured water and the tiny bulb glowed, the hall went silent — then burst into applause. We won second prize. The boys from the back row came up to shake her hand. That day I learnt that a quiet voice can hold the brightest ideas.

**Cue-story tips:** use **every cue** in order; you may add names, places and details; don't add a cue that changes the outline; end with a natural lesson, not a lecture.

check.q: When writing a story from cues, you should:
options: Use only the cues you like
Use every cue, in order, adding details
check.why: Examiners check that all cues are developed in sequence; details may be added around them.

sections.h: From weak to strong: a revision demonstration
sections.md:
**Weak draft (diary, 60 words):**
> *Today was my first day in new school. It was very nice. The teachers was very nice and the students was also nice. I made a friend. We ate lunch. Then I came home. I was very happy. I think I will like this school very much.*

**Problems:** no date/time; *nice* ×3, *very* ×4; agreement errors (*teachers was*); no feelings shown; flat ending.

**Strong revision (about 120 words):**
> *Monday, 2 June 2026, 8:00 p.m.*
>
> *Dear Diary,*
>
> *My stomach was doing somersaults when Papa dropped me at the gate of Kendriya Vidyalaya this morning. Six hundred strangers, and not one familiar face.*
>
> *Then Ms D'Souza, our class teacher, asked who could solve a riddle, and before I knew it my hand was up. I got it right — and a boy named Arjun grinned at me across the room. At lunch he showed me the secret corner behind the library where the mango tree drops its fruit.*
>
> *I came home tired but lighter. Maybe new places are only frightening until someone smiles.*
>
> *Kavya*

**What changed:** format added; feelings shown (*stomach doing somersaults*); specific people and places; agreement fixed; reflective close.

### Rubric at a glance
| Band | Content | Organisation | Accuracy |
|---|---|---|---|
| Excellent | Rich, relevant details; all points | Clear format, paragraphs, flow | Almost error-free, varied vocabulary |
| Good | Mostly relevant | Some paragraphing | Minor errors |
| Weak | Thin, repetitive | Missing format | Frequent errors |

check.q: Which change most improved the weak diary draft?
options: Adding specific details and shown feelings with correct format
check.why: Specific details, shown emotion and proper format address content, organisation and accuracy together.

sections.h: Polishing: language, editing and the last two minutes
sections.md:
### Ten-point self-check before you move on
1. Did I follow the **format** (title for story/paragraph; date for diary)?
2. Is the **word limit** respected (±10%)?
3. Is the **tense** consistent?
4. Are there **paragraphs** (at least two for diary/story)?
5. Did I **show** with at least three concrete details?
6. Did I avoid **repetition** of the same adjective (very, nice, good)?
7. Are **dialogues** punctuated: opening/closing quotation marks, comma before closing mark, new paragraph for new speaker?
8. Did I check **spellings** of common traps: *their/there, its/it's, quiet/quite, lose/loose*?
9. Is the **ending** satisfying?
10. Is the handwriting legible and are cuttings neat?

### Upgrade words
| Instead of | Try |
|---|---|
| very big | enormous, vast |
| very happy | overjoyed, delighted |
| said loudly | shouted, bellowed |
| walked slowly | trudged, ambled, strolled |
| very scared | terrified, petrified |
| nice | pleasant, charming, warm |

Use them where they fit — an *enormous* pencil sounds silly.

### Linking words that make writing flow
*Time:* first, then, soon, meanwhile, finally. *Contrast:* however, yet, although. *Addition:* moreover, besides, also. *Result:* so, therefore, as a result.

**Did you know?** Professional writers revise far more than they write. Even two minutes of rereading can catch the one error that costs a mark.

check.q: Which dialogue is correctly punctuated?
check.why: In standard English the comma goes inside the closing quotation mark before the reporting clause.

summary: All three forms reward specific detail, clear structure and accurate language.
Show, don't tell: use actions and sensory details instead of labels.
Spend about 3 minutes planning, 13 writing and 4 revising.
Descriptive paragraph: topic sentence, ordered sensory details, closing impression; 100–150 words.
Choose spatial (places), chronological (events) or general-to-particular (people) order.
Describe people through appearance, habits, speech, personality and one defining moment.
Diary: day, date, time, Dear Diary, first person, informal, reflective, optional name.
Diary paragraphs: event → feelings → reflection or resolve; character diaries must fit the text.
Story arc: opening, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution.
Use the given beginning exactly, or every cue in order; add a title; keep tense consistent.
Limit characters; use dialogue sparingly and punctuate it correctly.
Use one or two similes or metaphors, not dozens.
Revise for format, word limit, tense, agreement, spelling and repetition.

sections.h: शुरुआत: गधा सचमुच मूर्ख है क्या?
sections.md:
सोचिए, किसी को "गधा" कह दिया जाए तो वह नाराज़ क्यों होता है? प्रेमचंद इस कहानी की शुरुआत ठीक इसी सवाल से करते हैं — बड़े मज़ेदार, व्यंग्य भरे अंदाज़ में। वे कहते हैं कि जानवरों में गधे को हम सबसे बड़ा मूर्ख मानते हैं, जबकि असल में वह सबसे सीधा, सहनशील और संतोषी जीव है। उसे मारो, भूखा रखो, सूखी घास दो — वह कभी शिकायत नहीं करता, कभी गुस्सा नहीं दिखाता। गाय तक कभी-कभी सींग मार देती है, कुत्ता भी काट लेता है, पर गधे को किसी ने बिगड़ते नहीं देखा।

फिर लेखक एक चुभती बात कहते हैं — दुनिया में सीधेपन की क़द्र नहीं होती। जो अपने हक़ के लिए नहीं बोलता, उसे लोग "बेवकूफ़" कहकर ठुकरा देते हैं। लेखक यहाँ तक इशारा करते हैं कि भारतीयों को भी विदेशों में (जैसे अफ़्रीका, अमेरिका में) इसी सीधेपन और सहनशीलता के कारण अपमान सहना पड़ा; अगर वे भी ईंट का जवाब पत्थर से देना जानते तो शायद उन्हें "सभ्य" माना जाता। यह भूमिका पूरी कहानी की कुंजी है: **सहनशीलता अच्छी है, पर अन्याय सहते जाना कमज़ोरी है।**

लेखक यह भी कहते हैं कि गधे का एक छोटा भाई भी है जो उससे "कुछ ही कम गधा" है — वह है **बैल**। पर बैल कभी-कभी अड़ भी जाता है, मारता भी है। इसी के बाद कहानी उन दो बैलों की ओर मुड़ती है — **हीरा और मोती**।

### लेखक के बारे में
**मुंशी प्रेमचंद** (1880–1936) का असली नाम धनपत राय श्रीवास्तव था। उनका जन्म बनारस के पास **लमही** गाँव में हुआ। उन्हें "उपन्यास सम्राट" कहा जाता है। *गोदान*, *गबन*, *निर्मला*, *सेवासदन*, *रंगभूमि* जैसे उपन्यास और *ईदगाह*, *पूस की रात*, *कफ़न*, *नमक का दारोगा* जैसी लगभग तीन सौ कहानियाँ उन्होंने लिखीं, जो "मानसरोवर" के आठ खंडों में संकलित हैं। उन्होंने *हंस* और *जागरण* पत्रिकाओं का संपादन भी किया। उनकी भाषा आम बोलचाल की हिंदुस्तानी है — उर्दू और हिंदी का सहज मेल।

### कहानी कब की है?
यह कहानी उस दौर में लिखी गई जब भारत अंग्रेज़ों का गुलाम था और आज़ादी का आंदोलन ज़ोरों पर था। इसलिए कई आलोचक मानते हैं कि हीरा-मोती का संघर्ष असल में **आज़ादी के लिए लड़ते भारतीयों** का प्रतीक है। कहानी सीधे राजनीति की बात नहीं करती, पर उसकी गूँज हर पन्ने पर है।

**क्या आप जानते हैं?** प्रेमचंद के जन्मदिन, 31 जुलाई, को कई स्कूल "प्रेमचंद जयंती" के रूप में मनाते हैं। इस कहानी पर 1959 में हिंदी फ़िल्म *हीरा मोती* भी बनी थी।

**नोट:** प्रेमचंद की रचनाएँ अब सार्वजनिक (पब्लिक डोमेन) हैं, पर पाठ्यपुस्तक के सटीक शब्दों के लिए यहाँ हम कहानी को अपने शब्दों में, दृश्य-दर-दृश्य समझा रहे हैं। मूल पाठ NCERT की मुफ़्त पुस्तक *क्षितिज* (भाग 1) में पढ़ें।

sections.h: हीरा और मोती: दो शरीर, एक मन
sections.md:
झूरी नाम के एक काछी (किसान) के पास पछाईं जाति के दो सुंदर, ताक़तवर बैल थे — हीरा और मोती। दोनों देखने में सुंदर, काम में चौकस और डील में ऊँचे थे। बरसों साथ रहते-रहते वे ऐसे दोस्त बन गए थे कि बिना बोले एक-दूसरे के मन की बात समझ लेते थे। लेखक कहते हैं कि उनके पास कोई ऐसी गुप्त शक्ति थी जिससे वे मूक भाषा में विचार-विनिमय कर लेते थे — यह शक्ति मनुष्य के पास भी नहीं, जो खुद को "जीवों में श्रेष्ठ" कहता है।

वे एक-दूसरे को चाटकर, सूँघकर प्यार जताते; कभी-कभी सींग मिलाकर खेल-खेल में धक्का-मुक्की करते — दोस्ती में ज़रा-सी छेड़छाड़ ज़रूरी है, नहीं तो वह फीकी लगती है। हल या गाड़ी में जुतते तो दोनों की कोशिश रहती कि ज़्यादा बोझ ख़ुद उठाए ताकि दोस्त को आराम मिले। शाम को नाँद पर एक साथ खाते, एक साथ उठते; अगर एक मुँह हटा लेता तो दूसरा भी खाना छोड़ देता।

### दोनों का स्वभाव
दोनों में दोस्ती तो गहरी थी, पर स्वभाव थोड़ा अलग था — यही अंतर कहानी को रोचक बनाता है। हीरा विवेक से काम लेता है, मोती भावना से। कहानी में बार-बार मोती कोई उग्र कदम उठाना चाहता है और हीरा उसे रोकता है; फिर भी संकट आने पर मोती ही सबसे पहले जान की बाज़ी लगाता है।

**क्या आप जानते हैं?** "पछाईं" बैल पश्चिमी (पछाँह) प्रदेशों के अच्छी नस्ल के बैलों को कहा जाता था, जो मज़बूत और सुंदर माने जाते थे।
